News.title: Italy heatwave sees all 27 major cities on 'red alert' as country faces 39C - full list
News.content:
Italy heatwave sees all 27 major cities on 'red alert' as country faces 39C - full list

Italy's Health Ministry has placed all 27 of its major cities under a maximum red warning as the country's fourth heatwave of the summer intensifies, with temperatures climbing towards 40C

View 3 Images Italy has been hit by another scorching hot spell (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

All 27 of Italy's major cities are set to be placed under the country's highest heat alert on Thursday, as the nation's fourth heatwave of the summer threatens to hit 39C.

‌



It marks the first time this year that every city monitored by Italy's Health Ministry heat surveillance system has been put on maximum red warning.

‌



Authorities confirmed that 25 cities were already on the highest alert on Wednesday, with a further two set to join the list on Thursday.

‌



In Italy, a red alert is triggered when prolonged spells of extreme heat are expected to pose a health risk to the entire population, raising the likelihood of heat-related emergencies rather than solely affecting vulnerable groups. Temperatures across parts of the country have soared towards 40C in recent days, prompting authorities to roll out a series of public health guidance measures aimed at reducing the dangers posed by the sweltering conditions.

Residents have been advised to stay out of direct sunlight between 11am and 6pm, remain indoors wherever possible and drink at least 1.5 litres of water daily.

View 3 Images Milan, where tourists are pictured above, is among the affected cities (Image: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock)

‌



UK weather maps show possible hottest day of year as 8 counties hit 37C or more READ MORE :

Officials have also urged people to steer clear of fizzy drinks, coffee, alcohol and heavy meals, wear light clothing and never leave children or animals inside parked cars.

Forecasters say there is no sign of the scorching temperatures letting up for at least another week. The current heatwave has been blamed for four deaths in recent days, among them a 19-year-old tomato picker and a 40-year-old carpenter working in Lombardy, while a security guard in Bologna is also thought to have died from a heat-related illness.

The prolonged spell of scorching weather has also worsened drought conditions in the Po Valley, with more than 100 towns in Piedmont and Lombardy experiencing water shortages and some having to rely on tanker trucks for supplies.

‌



Farmers report that crop yields are being hit, grape ripening has sped up and milk production has dropped by around 10 per cent as dairy cows eat less in the sweltering heat.

View 3 Images Low water levels and increased algae are visible along the Tiber River, which runs through Rome, after prolonged dry weather (Image: Marcello Valeri/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

In Rome, authorities are offering free entry to air-conditioned cinemas and cultural venues, while evening opening hours have been extended at the Colosseum and Pantheon.

‌



Forecasters have also warned there is little prospect of relief before next week.

Lorenzo Giovannini, an atmospheric physicist at the University of Trento, told Ansa the heatwaves were above average in both intensity and duration, adding that the climate crisis was making them "longer and more intense".

Scientists have connected the growing frequency and severity of heatwaves to human-driven climate change.

Article continues below

According to the Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization, Europe has warmed at more than twice the global average since the 1980s.

News.title: Brothels crackdown in Oldham as two shut down and man tries to run from police
News.content:
Brothels crackdown in Oldham as two shut down and man tries to run from police

Sites on the town's Balfour Street and Miriam Street were closed down by officers after reports of men loitering while waiting to enter

View 2 Images Notices displayed at the property on Balfour Street, Oldham (Image: Manchester Evening News)

Brothels in Greater Manchester causing "significant distress" to neighbours have been shut by police after reports of men loitering outside.

Police raided properties in Balfour Street and Miriam Street, Oldham, arresting four people and detaining one man as he tried to run from one of the addresses. Greater Manchester Police had received reports from residents and councillors about "suspicious activity" at the two addresses.

These included concerns about men arriving throughout the day and night, staying for short periods of time and then leaving. This caused "significant distress" to those living nearby, the police said.

On July 27, officers attended the property on Balfour Street in relation to a "concern for welfare". A brothel was found to be operating from the address and one man tried to flee through the rear of the property before he was detained.

View 2 Images The closures will be in place for three months (Image: Manchester Evening News)

Two people were arrested on suspicion of controlling prostitution for gain. The next day, officers executed a warrant at the Miriam Street address following reports from the local community.

Two women were arrested and bailed as an investigation remains ongoing. In both cases, a 48-hour closure notice was authorised, followed by a three-month closure order.

The orders were granted by Tameside Magistrates' Court on July 29. It is a criminal offence to enter or remain in either of the two properties during the three-month period.

Article continues below

Neighbourhood Inspector for Oldham South and West, Amie Whitehead, said: "These two premises had a significant impact on people living nearby, with men attending the addresses throughout the day and night and loitering outside neighbouring homes while waiting to enter.

"Residents told us this behaviour was causing considerable distress within the community and affecting their quality of life." Insp Whitehead said the orders will prevent further criminality in the area, protecting the local community.

News.title: Covent Garden stabbing live: Police arrest woman in London as four men attacked
News.content:
A woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed with a weapon believed to be a pair of scissors in Covent Garden, central London

A 47-year-old woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in what police think was an "isolated mental health-related incident" in central London.

The woman has been held on suspicion of possessing an offensive weapon – believed to be a pair of scissors – and assault after the Wednesday lunchtime incident in busy Covent Garden, an area filled with bars, theatres and restaurants.

Two men are being treated in hospital for injuries which are not life-threatening or life-changing and the other two were discharged.

They are aged 34, 39, 42 and 52. The woman was held by officers from the Metropolitan Police's Parliamentary and Diplomatic Protection unit, who happened to be in the area at the time of the attack.

Members of the elite armed police unit drew their Tasers during the incident. The highly trained officers normally protect high-profile individuals and sites of national importance.

News.title: PM Andy Burnham: 'Mental health system piles pressure on NHS - this needs to change'
News.content:
We’ve all had some experience of struggles with mental health. Maybe you’ve stood by a loved one in a time of need. Maybe you’ve been through tough moments yourself.

Too often, illness is only half the challenge, with people forced to wait too long and fight too hard to get the help they need.

The simple fact is that mental health services haven’t kept pace with rising demand. The result is a system that waits to step in only when someone reaches crisis, leaving their family under unbearable strain and piling more pressure on our NHS. This needs to change.

Today, we’re announcing a major expansion of NHS mental health services so people can get help earlier and closer to home.

‌



This includes 100 new community mental health centres, where people with severe needs can walk in without a referral and get support without waiting months. In addition, we’re setting up 59 dedicated mental health emergency departments, giving people in crisis fast, same-day specialist care.

How to get perfect night's sleep as one third of Brits experience problems at least once a week READ MORE :

View 2 Images 'We’re announcing a major expansion of NHS mental health services,' says Andy Burnham (Image: Getty Images)

Community-led, community-based support is an approach we used to great effect in Greater Manchester. These services will make it much easier for people to get the right support, at the right time, in the right place. Mental health specialists will work alongside GPs, councils, charities and families, and provide direct links to housing and employment support.

The first of these new facilities will open their doors and offer their help later this year.

‌



We know there’s a profound mental health crisis impacting younger generations. There are those who are quick to criticise young people today, but that’s never been my way. Our country’s future depends on them – and they will have this government’s support.

The overwhelming majority of the one million young people not in education, employment or training want the chance to build their future. But poor mental health, combined with a system that can’t keep up, robs them of that opportunity. These new NHS facilities will help get lives moving again.

When I spoke outside Downing Street on day one of the job, I promised we’d help people live well. I said we’d invest in success, rather than pay for failure. This is what that promise looks like.

And to everyone who’s struggling with their mental health today: don’t give up hope. Help is out there and more is on the way.

News.title: PM Andy Burnham promises families 'help is on way' with more than 150 new NHS mental health centres to open
News.content:
PM Andy Burnham promises families 'help is on way' with more than 150 new NHS mental health centres to open

The shake-up is being billed by the new government as the "biggest redesign of mental health services in a generation" to prevent people reaching a crisis point in the first place

View 4 Images A man has a difficult conversation with a doctor (file image) (Image: Getty Images)

More than 150 new lifeline NHS mental health centres will open across England from the autumn relieving pressure on overstretched A&Es.

Announcing the shake-up, new Prime Minister Andy Burnham said current services were leaving families under “unbearable strain and piling more pressure on our NHS”.

In an article for The Mirror, he added: “This needs to change. Today, we’re announcing a major expansion of NHS mental health services so people can get help earlier and closer to home.”

‌



Under the plans, the government will massively expand an existing pilot scheme of six round-the-clock community based mental health centres (CMHCs) to 106.

The first opened in Tower Hamlets, east London, in 2025 providing patients, including those with schizophrenia or bipolar, vital support.

People can walk-in seven days a week without an appointment to the centres, which also offer employment and housing advice and have access to a small number of overnight beds.

Some of the community hubs will be new facilities while others will be in libraries, banks and other high street locations, the government said.

Channel 4 slammed as fans fume new ADHD documentary sends 'dangerous' message READ MORE :

View 4 Images Andy Burnham said current mental health services were leaving families under 'unbearable strain and piling more pressure on our NHS' (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Wire)

'Biggest redesign of mental health services in a generation'

At the same time, 59 new mental health emergency departments (MHEDs) will provide same-day support for those experiencing a moment of crisis.

‌



The announcement brings the total number of units, which are located within A&E units and work with the police and ambulance services, to 82.

It is being billed by the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) as the biggest redesign of mental health services in a generation.

And the aim is that both mental health units will relieve pressure on busy A&Es while preventing people reaching a mental health crisis point in the first place.

‌



Mr Burnham said in statement: "Nobody should be left to struggle with their mental health alone. But every day, thousands of people are waiting months for help, then finding the only door open to them is a busy A&E. These new centres will be a lifeline for so many.”

According to NHS figures, 2.36 million people in England had an open referral with mental health services at the end of May 2026, up from 2.10 million a year earlier and 1.95 million in May 2024.

Last year, The Mirror also reported warnings from nurses that some patients were suffering the “torture” of waiting up to three days in emergency department in “utterly degrading” conditions for a mental health bed.

‌



The Royal College of Nursing said at the time nearly 5,300 mental health patients waited at least 12 hours after a decision had been made to admit them at A&E departments in England last year - up from around 1,000 in 2019.

Previous RCN research also showed a staggering half a million children suffering with mental ill health also attended A&E between 2019 and 2025, with some waiting over 12 hours or even three days.

Writing for The Mirror, Mr Burnham recognised the “profound mental health crisis impacting younger generations”. He said poor mental health was also robbing young people, including the one million not in education, employment or training (Neets) opportunities.

‌



He added: “There are those who are quick to criticise young people today, but that’s never been my way. Our country’s future depends on them – and they will have this government’s support.”

View 4 Images It is hoped the new mental health units will help ease pressure on A&E departments (Image: PA)

More work to be done

DHSC said the move is the first phase of a wider roll-out set in the 10-year health plan in 2025 and backed by over £343million in funding.

‌



It also forms part of a upcoming mental health strategy in an attempt to reduce the number of people in England reaching crisis point. The strategy will be informed by the independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, which is expected in the autumn.

RCN Head of Nursing Practice Stephen Jones told The Mirror: “Today's announcement must begin to turn the page on a sorry chapter which has seen so many people go without the specialist support they need in the community, only to end up in crisis in loud, bright emergency departments waiting days for essential care.

"More services closer to people’s homes and new dedicated emergency departments are a crucial step towards more humane care. To succeed, both will need specialist mental health nurses at the centre.

‌



“Improving accessibility to mental health services is crucial to improving people’s quality of life and helping them access things like work and education. With the right investment, including in growing the workforce to deliver an expansion of services, we can also save the NHS money in the long run by bringing down waiting lists and preventing unnecessary hospitalisations.”

New Health Secretary, Yvette Cooper, also said: "Too many people are only getting mental health support when they reach crisis point, after struggling for far too long to get the help they need."

View 4 Images UK Head of Nursing Practice, Dr Stephen Jones, spoke to the Mirror (Image: LINKEDIN)

‌



'Mental health at crisis point'

She added: "These new community mental health centres will help people get support earlier and closer to home, making it easier to get the right care before problems escalate. A

“And when someone does need urgent help, new mental health emergency departments will be able to make sure they are seen quickly by specialist teams in the right setting.

"This is how we can turn the tide on mental ill health - preventing more people from reaching crisis, cutting waits for care, and building an NHS which is there for everyone when they need it”

‌



DHSC said the first facilities are set to open from autumn 2026 while further sites will open from March 2027.

Lynn Perry, Chief Executive at Barnardo's, said: "The mental health of far too many children and young people is at crisis point. We urgently need to shift focus from response to prevention – helping children and young people get the support they need before reaching crisis point.

"That's why we welcome the rollout of new mental health centres that are embedded into the neighbourhoods that need them, and hope that the needs of children and young people are placed right at the heart.

"This is an important step towards giving every child and young person the opportunity to grow up healthier, happier and able to thrive, with support that improves outcomes for life."

News.title: Met Office's striking weather maps lay bare UK's dire need for rain as drought continues
News.content:
Met Office's striking weather maps lay bare UK's dire need for rain as drought continues

The drought crisis gripping the UK is revealed in a new Met Office map showing areas where just 3% of expected rainfall came during the entire month of July as farmers warned of impending food shortages

View 5 Images Drought conditions have transformed the typically lush green colour of Primrose Hill, north London (Image: Akira Suemori/Shutterstock)

Britain's drought crisis is laid bare in new weather maps showing a frightening lack of rainfall across the country.

‌



Half of England is currently under official drought conditions after some areas recorded almost no rainfall in the entire month of July.

‌



While rain has fallen in areas further north in recent days, helping boost reservoirs and alleviate some of the severe impacts on farming, forecasts show more dry, hot weather in the Southeast of England - the hardest-hit region.

‌



One weather map, issued by the Met Office, shows that rainfall was 65% below average across the UK last month. New maps issued by the service this week indicate the lack of rain has hampered soil moisture, which is causing havoc for farmers across the UK.

England transformed into barren Western-like frontier as dramatic photos capture horror extent of drought READ MORE :

Olympic stadium provides shelter for dogs rescued from Greece wildfires READ MORE :

View 5 Images Met Office soil moisture map (Image: Met office)

Large swathes of the UK is in a brown hue in the graphic, which indicates soil moisture is low - as much as 1% in some parts of the East of England and the Southeast of England - at the moment.

‌



Soil moisture is a measurement favoured for showing the exact amount of water available in the ground to sustain plant life and agriculture. The benchmark required for supporting plants and wildlife is typically around 30%.

Reacting to this data, Met Office meteorologist Aidan McGovern said in a forecast bulletin: "It's not good news - we really need the rain... You obviously need soil moisture for those plants to continue to thrive and we are seriously lacking in soil moisture across a large part of England and Wales.

"I've just picked a point there, but it's representative of a large area of England or Wales, 1% soil moisture in that top 40 centimetres, less than 30% supposedly over a long period time. It really isn't good news for plants and all sorts of wildlife that need plant life and so on."

‌



View 5 Images The NFU has warned of food shortages as a result of the drought (Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Wire)

Southern England experienced just 3% of its long-term average rainfall for the month - its driest month ever recorded - while Wales was on 9%.

Only the far north of Scotland bucked the trend, recording 69% of its average rainfall after continued downpours and more changeable conditions.

‌



Farmers sounded the warning this week that some everyday food staples - such as wheat, barley, and potatoes - could be set to jump in price due to shortages in the coming months after the worst summer harvest in living memory.

View 5 Images A young dairy herd walk across a field of dry grass near Ashford, Kent (Image: Getty Images)

NFU president Tom Bradshaw said: "We have taken food production for granted for too long; we must create a more resilient food system to feed the 29 million households across the country, and we can’t produce food without water.

‌



“Those other countries around the world that we currently rely on to produce our food and vegetables, their climates are changing as well. It does feel like there is going be some shortages of products."

Hosepipe bans have been in place across the Southeast of England and East Anglia for several weeks - and in Whitstable and Herne Bay, Kent, local residents have been urged to use water for essential purposes only to prevent a sudden loss of water supply.

South East Water's Matthew Dean said: "Due to the prolonged period of hot and dry weather, water levels in our local drinking water storage tank in the Whitstable and Herne Bay areas continue to be extremely low.

‌



"This may soon impact our ability to pump fresh drinking water to our customers. All customers are currently in supply. However, if demand for water continues to remain high, there is a risk of supply interruptions."

View 5 Images Janesmoor Pond, which is in the New Forest, has dried-up (Image: Andrew Matthews/PA Wire)

He continued: "We’re continuing to ask customers to use water for essential purposes only: drinking, cooking and hygiene. This is in line with our temporary usage ban that is now in place for all of our 2.4 million customers across our supply area.

Article continues below

"To safeguard our shared resource and help prevent any homes from facing a sudden loss of water, we are incredibly grateful to everyone helping us protect water supplies in Kent."

Showers are forecast across the Northeast of England on Thursday, but not enough to improve soil moisture significantly. Temperatures are likely to rise next week too, with 35C expected across the East of England and parts of the Southeast of England.

News.title: Young son made desperate attempt to save mum-of-three's life after she 'went for nap'
News.content:
Young son made desperate attempt to save mum-of-three's life after she 'went for nap'

'Beautiful' mum-of-three Sophie Whitehurst was pronounced dead by paramedics at her home in Stoke-on-Trent, leaving behind her three children - two teenagers and a baby

View 3 Images Sophie Whitehurst was 33 years old and leaves behind her three children following her sudden death (Image: BPM Media)

A young and "beautiful" mum-of-three suddenly died after she went to have a nap, with one of her children desperately attempting to resuscitate her.

‌



Epileptic Sophie Whitehurst had been up all night caring for her baby and decided to take a nap during the day to recharge before watching a football match with her son Connor. But when he later went into her bedroom to ask her something, he noticed his mum wasn't breathing.

‌



Despite the 15-year-old's desperate attempts to save his mother's life, Sophie was pronounced dead by paramedics at her home in Stoke-on-Trent on Saturday. The 33-year-old leaves behind Connor, Allie-May, 16, and baby Harper, with her cause of death not yet officially confirmed.

‌



Neighbour Sophia Berrow, aged 20, witnessed the tragedy and also tried to save Sophie's life. She told The Sentinel: "I live with my boyfriend and his family, who have lived next door to Sophie for 13 years.

"We’re all really close. Everyone on the street loved Sophie. She was the life of the party! She was so beautiful, bubbly, and friendly and she always put her kids first. You couldn’t picture Sophie without thinking of her kids."

View 3 Images Sophie's children - daughters Ellie-Mai and Harper and son Connor (Image: BPM Media)

‌



Mum sobs as autistic son is turned away from summer holiday club - with thousands of disabled children missing out READ MORE :

Ms Berrow explained that Sophie suffered from epilepsy and "often" had seizures when she was feeling tired. Her dog was trained to alert people when she was having one.

She said: "She was doing quite well recently and wasn’t getting seizures as often. And when she did have a seizure she would come around quite quickly."

But this appears not to have been the case on Saturday. Ms Berrow added: "Sophie had decided to go for a nap because she'd been up all night with the baby.

‌



"She was meant to be watching the Stoke City game with her son later that day, so she wanted to be refreshed for it. Sophie went into her room and fell asleep.

"She had the bedroom window open and we think the breeze shut the door. That meant her dog wasn't inside with her. Everything was quiet upstairs and everyone assumed she was just asleep.

"Connor went upstairs to ask her something. He opened the door and saw that something wasn’t right. Sophie wasn’t breathing. Connor began CPR straight away while Allie-May went to get help.

‌



View 3 Images Sophie with her two daughters (Image: BPM Media)

Ms Berrow's bedroom window was also open, so she could hear the commotion. As she's training to be a veterinary nurse, she is qualified in human and animal CPR and didn't hesitate to go and help straight away.

She said: "I took Sophie off the bed to continue doing CPR on the floor. But it was clear to me straightaway that something was seriously wrong.

‌



"I performed CPR for 18 minutes until the paramedics arrived and took over. They carried on for 30 minutes before they told everyone the awful news."

Sophia says the news devastated Sophie's children. She explained: "Everything went by in a total blur. Part of me knew she wasn’t going to make it, but I was hoping for a miracle. Hearing she’d passed away was absolutely awful. It still doesn't feel real.

"Sophie's kids were in the living room when the news was delivered. I had gone back next door with my mum. When we were told the immediate family had been asked to wait, I knew it was bad news.

‌



"Then I heard them all screaming and breaking down. I’ve never heard something so awful. I broke down too."

Ms Berrow has now launched a fundraiser to give Sophie a "really, really good funeral" and allow her children to say goodbye to their mother "properly". She said: "My biggest worry after the news had sunk in was that her children wouldn’t get to give her a good send-off.

"Nobody wants a council funeral to be the last memory of their mum. They deserve to say goodbye properly. Any money that is left over will go to the kids too. I know that Sophie’s biggest concern would be what would happen to the kids.

‌



"So our priority has to be supporting them and making sure they’re looked after. That’s what this is all about."

Ms Berrow explained that Sophie's children have received a "massive outpouring of support". "They’re still absolutely distraught, but having that support is definitely helping," she said.

So far, the page has fundraised more than £4,700 out of its £7,000 goal from 255 donations.

News.title: Do you need special glasses to watch Solar Eclipse 2026? How to watch safely
News.content:
Do you need special glasses to watch Solar Eclipse 2026? How to watch safely

The UK is just days away from its most dramatic solar eclipse since 1999 - but before you look up, here's what you need to know about protecting your eyes

This is what a solar eclipse looks like from space

With the most dramatic solar eclipse visible from the UK since 1999 just days away, many skygazers will be wondering if they can watch the spectacular event safely.

‌



Health experts have warned people against using ordinary sunglasses to watch the eclipse as they can still allow harmful solar radiation to damage eyes.

‌



But there are other many ways people will be able to enjoy the eclipse - including special glasses and homemade pinhole viewers.

‌



Where and when will the eclipse be visible?

On Wednesday, August 12, people across much of Europe, including the UK and Ireland, will be treated to an impressive partial solar eclipse, with around 90 per cent of the Sun covered by the Moon.

A total solar eclipse, where the Moon completely covers the Sun, will be visible from parts of Spain, Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia and a small area of northern Portugal.

The exact timings will vary depending on location. In London, Bristol and Cardiff, the eclipse will begin at around 6.17pm, reach its maximum at around 7.12pm and finish at around 8.06pm, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.

‌



Viewers in Cornwall will witness around 95 per cent coverage at 7.16pm, with the south-west set to experience the greatest eclipse coverage in the UK, according to the Royal Observatory Greenwich.

View 2 Images The UK will see an approximately 96% solar eclipse on Wednesday

When is the solar eclipse 2026 in UK and how to watch safely - complete guide READ MORE :

Stunning new images offer glimpse of the Sun's surface in unprecedented detail READ MORE :

Do I need special glasses to watch the solar eclipse safely?

Health officials have warned that even cloudy skies do not make it safe to look directly at the Sun during the eclipse, urging people to take the necessary precautions.

‌



You should use specially designed eclipse glasses or handheld solar viewers to watch a solar eclipse safely as they are "thousands of times" darker than regular sunglasses, according to NASA.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has also warned that looking directly at the Sun during an eclipse without proper protection can cause serious eye damage.

It said: "Ordinary sunglasses – no matter how dark – do not provide adequate protection for viewing a solar eclipse."

‌



A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, blocking some or all of the Sun's light from reaching our planet.

During an eclipse, the sky becomes darker and the Sun may appear less bright, which can make people more likely to stare at it for longer. But the remaining visible part of the Sun still emits intense ultraviolet, visible and infrared radiation that can damage the retina, the UKHSA warned.

View 2 Images (Image: Colin Davey/Getty Images)

‌



The Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported around 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after viewing the 1999 total solar eclipse. Around 40 per cent of those affected had observed it for less than a minute.

Even when wearing eclipse glasses or using a handheld solar viewer, NASA says people should never look at the Sun through a camera lens, telescope, binoculars or any other optical device.

Can I use cameras or binoculars to get a closer look?

NASA has warned people not to look at the Sun through cameras, telescopes or binoculars while wearing eclipse glasses.

‌



The space agency said the concentrated rays of the Sun can burn through eclipse filters and cause severe eye injuries if optical devices are used without correct front-mounted filters.

It advises anyone planning to use cameras, telescopes or binoculars to "seek expert advice" and ensure the correct solar filter is securely fitted to the front of the equipment before observing the eclipse.

Experts also recommend checking eclipse glasses before use and discarding them if they are torn, scratched or otherwise damaged.

‌



Are there other ways to watch the solar eclipse safely?

For those without eclipse glasses, there are some other cheap and cheerful ways to watch the phenomenon safely using items you may already have at home.

The UKHSA recommends the following options:

Making a pinhole viewer at home . To do this you need a long cardboard box, such as a cereal box, white paper, aluminium foil, tape, scissors, and a push pin. Tape white paper inside the bottom of the box as a screen. Seal the top, cut two small holes on opposite ends, cover one with foil, and poke a clean pinhole in it

Viewing the Sun's image projected through a colander or the gaps between tree leaves

Projecting the Sun's image onto a sheet of paper using a simple pinhole projector

Article continues below

You can also watch the eclipse online. The European Space Agency is hosting a live webcast from Spain's Astrophysical Observatory of Javalambre, alongside a public celebration in León. NASA will also provide coverage, as will the Italy-based Virtual Telescope Project, among others.

News.title: Ex neo-Nazi activist withdraws as Tory election candidate
News.content:
A former neo-Nazi selected by the Conservatives to fight a council election next year has pulled out after a backlash against his candidacy.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine was convicted of racially harassing Jewish former Labour MP Luciana Berger in 2016, while already serving a separate jail sentence for sharing antisemitic posts.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch had defended the decision to select him as a candidate for the new Somerset Council seat of Crewkerne South, saying he had been rehabilitated and her party "believes in second chances".

But Bonehill-Paine said he had now withdrawn his candidacy, and had been offered a position as an anti-extremism adviser to the party.

In a social media post, he said the position with the Conservative Party's Culture and Integration Commission would focus on advising on how to prevent young men from being radicalised.

Berger, who now sits as Baroness Berger in the House of Lords, described the appointment as an "insult," adding that making him a party adviser was "no better than allowing him to stand as a council candidate".

The position as an anti-extremism adviser to the party is unpaid, the BBC understands.

Bonehill-Paine spent three years in prison after he was jailed in 2015 for posting antisemitic material ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally. He was convicted of racially harassing then-Labour MP Berger the following year.

News.title: Woman arrested after four stabbed in central London
News.content:
A 47-year-old woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden in central London, the Metropolitan Police said.

The men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, were taken to hospital after emergency services were called to reports of a stabbing in Endell Street at about 12:30 BST.

The force said two men remain in hospital with injuries not thought to be life threatening or life changing while the other two have been discharged.

The woman was arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon and assault. The Met said it was believed to have been a mental health-related incident.

News.title: University of Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns
News.content:
The University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row has resigned "with immediate effect".

Prof Jason Arday said he had "concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".

Earlier, the university said it had launched an investigation "following new information" about Arday's "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

It comes after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in Arday's work and questioned some of his stated achievements. The academic has admitted errors in his work, but has insisted he is not "a liar".

In a statement posted by the Good Law Project on Wednesday, Arday said that being appointed professor had been "without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life".

"The years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack," he said, adding "there comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great".

He said his resignation should not "be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge.

"Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

Thanking his students and colleagues, he said that "for my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".

Arday said "this is not the end of my work" and that he needed "time to heal".

"When that time comes, I will return," he added.

Earlier on Wednesday, the university said its inquiry had begun "following new information" about Arday's "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

"Separately, there remains a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct, which are being handled in line with our Misconduct in Research policy," the University of Cambridge said in a statement.

It added: "While we are fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter, it remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both university policies and employment law.

"We also fully recognise that there is a person at the centre of this situation, and we continue to provide support to him."

Jesus College, where Arday is a fellow, has said it is launching its own process "parallel" to the university's investigation.

In 2023, the then 37-year-old sociologist became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge.

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He claimed on Substack that he had put Arday's work through a plagiarism detection software, which found that "many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source".

On Saturday, Arday told the Times in an interview that he was accountable for those mistakes, but that "what I am not is a liar".

He told the newspaper: "There has been, since I arrived at Cambridge, a very well orchestrated and co-ordinated campaign to unseat me from my position."

He suggested that this was "racially motivated" and that he had become a "lightning rod" for criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policy.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work was because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information, and that similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics.

"We're talking about academia here. I didn't murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I've experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable," he told the newspaper.

Earlier on Wednesday, publisher Simon & Schuster - which is set to publish Arday's memoir later this month - defended Arday in a statement to AFP news agency.

"We are proud to publish Professor Jason Arday. We have worked closely with him... and can speak to the professionalism and integrity he has brought to every stage of the publication," Simon & Schuster said.

News.title: Walk-in mental health centres to open in banks and libraries across England
News.content:
People in England needing immediate care for mental health problems will be able to access specialist walk-in hubs close to their home, the government is promising.

Ministers have set out plans to create a network of nearly 200 community mental health centres and mental health A&Es by 2029.

The aim is to give those experiencing a mental health crisis or significant distress somewhere to go to get help when they need it - with plans to open dozens of the hubs in high street locations like banks and libraries.

One in five people struggle with their mental health and thousands of people turn up at A&E when they get to crisis point because they cannot find help elsewhere.

The government believes its plans, which build on pilots that have been run over recent years, will help tackle this issue and ensure people receive expert care when they need it.

The government said there will be 100 new community mental health centres opened in a variety of locations, from libraries and banks. Some will be set up in new buildings.

They will bring together existing teams of nurses, therapists and support workers.

Many of the hubs are expected to be open seven days a week and some will have short-stay bed facilities.

Six areas have trialled the approach since 2024.

The government is also pledging to set up another 59 dedicated mental health A&Es, on top of the 23 which are already operational. Many will be attached to existing A&Es.

News.title: See the Sun like never before with most detailed images yet
News.content:
Scientists using the world's most powerful solar telescope have captured the surface of our Sun in new, unprecedented detail.

Images and footage show "whirlpools" of activity that it has not been possible to see before.

It is the Sun's magnetic field being twisted and moved by the motion of hot gas.

That constant swirling is a driving force behind bursts of energy from the Sun, creating so-called space weather, that can disrupt Earth's power grids and satellites, and could even injure astronauts.

"The Sun is the source of that energy and of all of that space weather," explained Dr David Boboltz from the US National Solar Observatory, external (NSO).

Capturing more detailed pictures of our solar system's star will help in responding to that weather, he said.

"To figure out and eventually predict space weather, we want to understand the physics of the Sun, all the way down to the smallest scales."

News.title: Student loan repayment rates an 'unsustainable burden', chancellor told
News.content:
More than 120 MPs and peers have asked the chancellor to carry out an "urgent review" of the student loan repayment system.

An open letter coordinated by the campaign group Rethink Repayment says the current set-up places an "unsustainable burden on the next generation of workers".

Among the cross-party signatories are MPs with their own Plan 2 student loans, which have come under particular scrutiny this year.

Last week, Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the interest rate on those loans was "egregious" and the issue was at the top of her in-tray.

Current and former students have different student loan plans depending on where they live in the UK and when they went to university.

The letter to Chancellor John Healey does not specify a particular plan signatories would like to be reformed, nor does it name a particular nation.

However, the debate has centred around Plan 2 loans, which were taken out by students in England between September 2012 and July 2023 and are still issued in Wales. Graduates pay back what they earn above the repayment threshold at a rate of 9%.

The letter says that "successive governments' adjustments to repayment thresholds â together with high interest and marginal tax rates â are placing an unsustainable burden on the next generation of workers".

It says many middle-income graduates "see less than half of any hard-earned pay rise due to a combination of income tax, national insurance and student loan repayments".

It adds: "We are united in the belief that the current repayment framework requires urgent review... to ensure it is fair, sustainable, and supportive of aspiration."

News.title: Family 'devastated' by death of girl, 9, as man charged with murder
News.content:
The family of a nine-year-old girl who died after being found seriously injured in Arbroath have said they are "devastated" at her loss, as a man appeared in court charged with her murder.

Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, died in Dundee's Ninewells Hospital on Monday.

A 35-year-old man, who police said was known to the girl, has appeared in court charged with her murder.

Christopher Rice from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, made no plea during an appearance in private at Forfar Sheriff Court and was remanded in custody.

News.title: AI or real? BBC analyses viral China disaster videos
News.content:
As weather events become more extreme, fake videos are being shared rapidly online, and itâs causing real world problems in China.

The government has vowed to crack down on misinformation, but as our China correspondent Stephen McDonell explains, identifying AI-generated content is becoming increasingly difficult.

News.title: Miliband says reopening Strait of Hormuz 'essential' as he meets Rubio
News.content:
Reopening the Strait of Hormuz is essential to bringing down the cost of living in the UK, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said as he met his US counterpart Marco Rubio.

The Labour minister is in Washington for his first official one-on-one meeting with Rubio.

The pair were expected to discuss the war in Ukraine and the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

Miliband was invited to the US capital by Rubio after they met on the sidelines of a foreign ministers' summit in the Philippines, where the former Labour leader made his debut as foreign secretary.

The White House was reported to be concerned about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision to hand Miliband the Foreign Office brief, given his previous criticism of US President Donald Trump as a racist and a misogynist.

Trump is also a trenchant opponent of wind farms and supports the opening up North Sea oil and use of fossil fuels, whereas in his former role as UK energy secretary, Miliband championed net zero and renewables.

Burnham has signalled a shift in North Sea oil policy, earning praise from the Oval Office, but the dynamic between Miliband and Rubio was set to be closely watched.

Last month, Washington's top diplomat in London, Warren Stephens, said Miliband had been "wrong" in 2016 to call Trump "a racist, misogynistic self-confessed groper" and added "hopefully his views have changed".

Following their meeting, US state department spokesman Tommy Pigott said: "The two discussed the importance of Europe taking on a greater role in its own security.

"They reiterated their shared commitment to safe transit in the Strait of Hormuz and ensuring Iran never develops or obtains a nuclear weapon."

In a statement after the meeting, Miliband thanked Rubio for a "warm, productive meeting" and said he was "hopeful" that the Strait may be re-opened.

"The number one priority for this government is to tackle the cost of living crisis that people are facing and my job as foreign secretary most immediately is to work with our closest ally the United States on getting a lasting ceasefire in relation to the Iran war.

"We are working night and day to make that happen - that was a large part of our discussions today - I am hopeful that this may happen, but we are not there yet."

He added: "People should be in no doubt, I know as foreign secretary that the British people are worried about what's happened to petrol prices, diesel prices, energy bills, and the single biggest thing we can do is get that ceasefire in relation to Iran."

The strategic sea route, which had been open before the US and Israel launched the war in February, has been a flashpoint in the Middle East conflict and disruption to trade has driven up fuel and food prices.

Miliband added: "We also discussed standing together with Ukraine in the face of Putin's war, and spoke about the intolerable situation in Gaza and the urgent need to address the humanitarian situation there, as we work towards a lasting peace for Palestinians and Israelis."

News.title: Gary Glitter appears in court over historical sex offence charges
News.content:
Dressed in a blue shirt and wearing sunglasses, Glitter appeared by video link from His Majesty's Prison Channings Wood for the 11-minute hearing.

Under his real name, Gadd was told of the charges against him and spoke only to confirm his name and date of birth.

The prosecutor, Jonathan Polnay KC, told the court that Gadd said in a police interview he did not know the complainant, and that the allegations against him were false.

He also told the court that the offences involved one person, and are said to have taken place between the years of 1978 and 1981 when the complainant was eight to 11 years old.

He said she lived near where Glitter lived and that was how he came to know her. She says he gave her chocolate and that he invited her into his house where the offences occurred.

The allegations were first reported to the Metropolitan Police on 9 January 2025 and an investigation into the circumstances was launched.

Gadd was first interviewed on 22 July last year in relation to the investigation.

The 82-year-old was one of the biggest pop stars of the 1970s with a string of number one hits.

The Met said in July that the alleged victim was being supported by specialist officers and had been made aware that Glitter had been charged.

The singer is currently being held in HMP Channings Wood in Devon.

News.title: Police chief considers joining legal action over PC Harper killers' early release
News.content:
The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and is not eligible for early release.

Speaking on the Today programme, Thames Valley Police chief Jason Hogg urged the government to reconsider its position.

Only prisoners convicted of murder, rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from the scheme in England and Wales - while those convicted of manslaughter remain eligible.

"I fully understand the challenges around the crisis in the prison system," he said.

"But the decision made and where that line has been drawn, I do not believe that people responsible for taking the life of another citizen in our country should be released early."

He said: "I was informed yesterday that the Police Federation are considering legal action, I am in discussions with the Police Federation with regards to this matter".

Asked whether this meant he would join them, he said: "I think we need to get some legal advice in relation to this. This is something I certainly would consider."

Following PC Harper's death and a campaign by his widow Lissie, Parliament passed "Harper's Law", which gives mandatory life sentences to the killers of emergency services workers. It also doubles the maximum penalty from 12 months to two years for those who assault police or other emergency workers.

But the new rules - introduced in 2022 - did not apply retrospectively to the sentencing of PC Harper's killers, and so do not prevent them from being released early.

Hogg said: "The law isn't retrospective and we all understand that, but the fact that they are released early simply seems perverse."

Aileen O'Connor, branch chairman of Thames Valley Police Federation told BBC Breakfast her organisation was exploring whether legal action was an option.

"If it is an avenue we can explore then I'll get behind that 110%," she said.

As for what shape a potential legal challenge might take, she said: "Ultimately that's for the specialists, the barristers and those in that legal sector to make that decision whether there is a challenge there.

"If there is a challenge then we will look to take that challenge."

Sentencing minister Jake Richards told the BBC it would be wrong to pick out individual cases and block two of PC Harper's killers from early release.

Although the government had reviewed what sentences would be excluded from the early release scheme, he confirmed "manslaughter is not one of those offences".

On Wednesday the Ministry of Justice released a new list of exclusions that will be exempt from the early release scheme.

It said rapists, as well as criminals sentenced for child sex offences and grooming and conspiracy offences for these crimes, will no longer be eligible to leave prison early.

Murderers and terrorists were already not eligible for the early release scheme.

Richards said: "It would be wrong to pick out individual cases within different offending cohorts. That wouldn't be right. It wouldn't be lawful either. So it is correct that those two individuals will be subject to the new regime from October".

News.title: Apology after carer fed dog food to elderly woman by mistake
News.content:
A home carer unintentionally fed an elderly woman microwaved dog food, an investigation has found.

The Radis Community Care worker logged the meal, from the client's freezer, as a "lamb dinner", before a second carer saw the packaging and realised the mistake, the report said.

The food was just one instance of poor care over three months with some "abysmal failures", the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman concluded.

Portsmouth City Council said it no longer commissioned services from Radis. Both organisations have apologised.

The woman ate three mouthfuls of the food in June 2024, a month before she died from frailty of old age, the ombudsman's report said.

The meal came from a pack which was labelled "fresh take on dog food" and "for adult dogs and puppies", it added.

Previously, in April 2024, the council opened a safeguarding inquiry following complaints from the woman's family.

It eventually found concerns that Radis staff had logged visits that did not happen, fed the woman stale and inedible food and left her wet or in darkness overnight.

The woman's Do Not Attempt Resuscitation document was also found scrunched up in a cupboard, the report added.

News.title: Traitors star Joe Marler to become BBC's first celebrity Gladiator
News.content:
Former rugby star Joe Marler is to become the first ever celebrity Gladiator on the BBC's popular entertainment series.

The 36-year-old, who also took part in the first series of Celebrity Traitors, will be known as Mauler and face contenders when the fourth series of Gladiators begins in 2027.

"Mauler will see you now," Marler said in a video posted on Instagram, external announcing the news, recorded in the Gladiators dressing room.

The BBC said Marler will make his debut with a series of "special appearances packed with power, personality and plenty of surprises".

Filming for the fourth series is currently under way in Sheffield, the BBC confirmed in a statement.

"Known for his uncompromising style of play and larger-than-life sense of humour, Joe has built a reputation as one of the UK's most entertaining sporting personalities," the corporation said.

"Now, he's taking on an entirely new challenge as he joins the ranks of the Gladiators, bringing his trademark physicality and competitive spirit to one of television's toughest arenas."

The former England rugby international star, who is from Heathfield, Sussex, will join fellow Gladiators such as Nitro, Viper, Diamond and Sabre in battle when the show returns next year.

Gladiators was a hugely successful show on ITV in the 1990s, and saw members of the public take on a group of elite athletes who each had their own on-screen persona.

Olympic swimmer Sharron Davies, who like Marler was already known as a famous sports personality, joined that iteration of the show in 1995 as the character Amazon.

The format was revived by Sky for two series in 2008, before the current iteration launched in 2024, quickly becoming a hit for BBC One.

A celebrity spin-off is separately in the works, featuring contestants including presenter AJ Odudu, comedian Sara Pascoe, podcaster Chris Ramsey and social media star George Clarke.

News.title: No misconduct case for officer who shot Chris Kaba
News.content:
The Met police officer who shot Chris Kaba will not face misconduct proceedings, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has said.

Sgt Martyn Blake shot the 24-year-old in Streatham, south London, in 2022 after Kaba tried to ram his way past police cars. Blake was cleared of murder following a trial in 2024.

A decision was made in January to pause any proceedings involving Blake until a law change relating to the use of force in misconduct cases was introduced and its impact was clear, the IOPC said.

Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the IOPC's decision brought an end to "almost four years of uncertainty" for Blake, calling the accountability process for police officers "disgraceful".

In June the use of force test in such cases changed from the civil law test to the criminal law test, meaning actions that did not amount to a crime should not amount to misconduct either.

Referring to Blake by his cypher NX121, Rowley said: "Today's decision finally brings to an end almost four years of uncertainty for NX121, his family and the wider firearms command, with all the considerable worry and stress that has brought.

"We also recognise the profound impact on Chris Kaba's family, who continue to grieve their loss."

News.title: Restrict sale of pet flea treatments, government urged
News.content:
Pet flea treatments should be banned from general sale, a Lords committee has urged, after an inquiry raised concerns about their impact on their environment.

Spot-on treatments to prevent parasite infestations in fur and on skin are currently widely available for pet owners to buy in supermarkets and online.

But the House of Lords environment committee said their sale should be restricted, adding widespread use posed a potential threat to natural ecosystems.

The government said it was continuing to assess the availability of the treatments in order to ensure "correct usage by owners".

Currently, dog and cat owners are frequently advised to use preventative spot-on treatments every month to avoid parasite infestations.

But in a series of evidence sessions, the committee heard such blanket usage is not supported by robust scientific evidence and is likely to be harming the environment.

Many vets do not treat their own pets monthly, the committee heard, instead regularly checking their pets' fur with flea combs and restricting use to when fleas were spotted.

The committee heard that high volumes of fipronil and imidacloprid, common active ingredients in spot-on treatments, have been found in UK streams and rivers, killing off aquatic life, with a knock-on effect on wildlife higher up the food chain.

These chemicals have already been banned for use as agricultural pesticides because of their impact on wildlife such as bees, while the committee said "very little is known" about the impacts of newer chemicals such as isoxazolines.

In a report, external, the cross-party committee recommended that only vets, pharmacists and other qualified professionals should be able to sell such treatments, with pet owners advised to take a precautionary approach to using them.

News.title: Man gets third-degree burns from hot sand after using disposable beach BBQ
News.content:
Warning: This article contains a distressing image

A man who suffered third-degree burns from hot sand after using a disposable barbecue on a beach has warned others to be aware of the dangers.

Sam Knight had been using it on Cefn Sidan Beach, Carmarthenshire, with his family and stepped on sand that was still hot.

The 27-year-old had to be carried off the beach after suffering badly blistered feet and needed weeks of treatment.

Experts at a burns centre say injuries such as this are becoming increasingly common and warned beach goers to take precautions.

Knight told Radio Wales Breakfast he was not aware that sand could be a "real hazard".

He had used tongs to move the barbecue to one side and extinguished it, so he thought it was safe.

"When I returned to the area, I stepped on a boiling hot patch of sand, and had to be carried off the beach," he added.

Knight was taken to Neath Port Talbot Hospital referred to a burns specialist.

"I couldn't walk for a couple of weeks so I had to take a fortnight off work," he added.

David Fligelstone and Menna Davies are physiotherapists who work with the burns centre at Swansea Bay University Health Board.

Fligelstone said the number of incidents they are seeing is "going up year on year".

"The key thing is that people don't understand is that sand stays hot for such a long time after a barbecue is moved," he said.

"When you look at the evidence it's always the sand that hasn't been cooled that ends up causing that injury."

Davies said injuries like this can be "quite painful" and need to be dressed for a "long period of time".

President Donald Trump slammed Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed during a speech on Wednesday in Las Vegas after the Democrat notched a primary win in a closely watched race.

The president accused El-Sayed of being part of a wave of a “communists” who would bring “squalor” and “death” to America.

“When I watch Abdul, he's full of s***,” Trump told a crowd at the Red Rock Casino Resort.

El-Sayed is not a communist, but rather a progressive who is campaigning on issues including Medicare for all and removing corporate money from politics.

Elsewhere in his remarks, Trump accused El-Sayed, who has been critical of the U.S. supporting Israel’s “genocide” in Gaza, of being hateful and antisemitic.

open image in gallery President Trump aggressively attacked Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed during a speech on Wednesday in Las Vegas, accusing the Democrat of being ‘full of s***’ and antisemitic ( AFP/Getty )

“Put him in office, you're going to find out what he loves,” Trump said. “He doesn't love Israel. He doesn't love Jewish people. He hates them. He hates them with a passion that burns in his heart.”

The Independent has contacted the El-Sayed campaign for comment.

The Michigan primary race was a key target of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israel lobbying group whose super PAC spent an estimated $32 million spreading the message that El-Sayed was pursuing a “radical anti-Israel agenda.”

El-Sayed, a former public health official, has argued U.S. money would be better spent on domestic priorities like healthcare than on supporting Israel’s military.

In a victory speech on Wednesday after his primary win over Rep. Haley Stevens, El-Sayed thanked Jewish supporters of his campaign and affirmed his commitment to representing people of all faiths in Michigan.

open image in gallery El-Sayed beat Rep. Haley Stevens this week in the Democratic primary for Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat. The former public health official has vowed to protect Michiganders of all faiths and has sharply criticized U.S. support for the Israeli ‘genocide’ in Gaza ( Reuters )

“To all of my sisters and brothers of the Jewish faith, or any faith at all, or no faith at all, I want you to know that my commitment to your safety, my commitment to Jewish safety, is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters,” he said.

He added that he had been “listening to sisters and brothers who said, ‘I want to join this movement because AIPAC doesn’t speak for me, because I understand that self-determination for one people does not require the quenching of self-determination for another people.”

This is a breaking news story and will be updated with new information.

A new study suggests giving Mounjaro to type 2 diabetes patients could reduce the risk of heart attacks in people also living with heart disease.

Those receiving the drug were found to be 33% less likely to suffer a heart attack when compared to patients on another type 2 diabetes medication.

Mounjaro, a GLP-1 receptor agonist also known as tirzepatide, is currently used on the NHS to treat both type 2 diabetes and severe obesity.

The US study, published in The BMJ, involved almost 53,000 people diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Researchers meticulously tracked major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) – which includes heart attacks, strokes, and death from any cause – comparing outcomes for those starting Mounjaro with patients on sitagliptin, another common diabetes drug.

After a year, the risk of Mace was 2.9% among those on Mounjaro compared to 4.4% in the sitagliptin group.

Mounjaro, a GLP-1 receptor agonist also known as tirzepatide, is currently used on the NHS to treat both type 2 diabetes and severe obesity ( PA )

Researchers estimate that this is the equivalent of preventing one case per every 70 people.

Mounjaro slashed the risk of heart attacks by a third, although there was no meaningful difference found in cases of stroke.

However, Mounjaro did lower cases of hospital admissions due to infections, the analysis found.

One hospital admission was prevented for every 48 patients, according to researchers.

It also prevented one death from any cause for every 122 patients.

Researchers said: “This study shows how trial-anchored evidence from clinical practice can estimate the expected cardiovascular benefit of initiating tirzepatide beyond standard background treatment and inform shared decision making.”

A study released last month claimed that weight loss drugs were linked to hair loss.

People on GLP-1 agonist drugs such as Mounjaro, Ozempic and Wegovy reported hair loss to regulators – and July’s study on around 50,000 people appeared to support the link.

Experts used data to compare rates of alopecia hair loss in adults using GLP-1s to manage diabetes with those on other drugs.

The team from the University of Pennsylvania Health System noted that regulators in the US have been informed of the link between the drugs and hair loss, particularly for semaglutide (Wegovy and Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro).

So far in 2026, the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has received 399 reports of hair loss relating to tirzepatide, alongside 541 last year.

It has also received 148 reports of hair loss linked to semaglutide, alongside 164 reports last year.

News.content:

After a hard-fought and bitter campaign and a real nailbiter of an evening, Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic nominee in the Michigan Senate race.

Polls leading up to Tuesday’s primary in the Great Lakes State put El-Sayed, the former Wayne County health department director, comfortably ahead of his opponent by a double-digit margin. Campaign officials working for Rep. Haley Stevens reportedly viewed the race as more of a toss-up heading into the final hours.

They were right, and the polls were very, very wrong.

In the end, El-Sayed won by a one-point margin of victory. Though he led Stevens for almost the entire evening, the exceedingly narrow margin sapped much of the energy out of progressive social media spaces as votes continued to trickle in.

So what does this mean for the left?

Progressives can win in purple states

All naysaying from the center-left will focus on El-Sayed’s very slim margin of victory, in no small part due to the illusions about the race created by the polling environment prior to Tuesday. But make no mistake: this is a historic achievement for the American left. The victory of a firmly progressive Bernie Sanders-endorsed candidate in a statewide election, in the Midwest, will electrify left-leaning organizations in Michigan and elsewhere as narratives about the brand being confined to deep-blue strongholds just took a major blow.

It’s no general election victory; not yet. But pollsters and the mainstream media — and Republicans, despite their bluster — are far from counting him out in November. And regardless, many assumptions about Democratic voters in purple states were just torn to pieces.

open image in gallery Abdul El-Sayed won the Michigan Senate primary on Tuesday and appeared Wednesday morning at a press conference to declare victory ( Reuters )

open image in gallery Rep. Haley Stevens was fired up at her watch party on Tuesday evening, but ultimately was unable to overcome El-Sayed’s lead ( Getty )

Ok, but just barely

We would be remiss to talk about El-Sayed’s victory like it was anything more than it was: A slim, but not translucent, margin of victory separated him from Stevens, despite all of the criticism that the congresswoman was a poor candidate. Stevens eschewed in-person events and was never able to turn out the kinds of crowds El-Sayed did when appearing alongside national progressive figures like Sanders or streamer Hasan Piker. None of that really seemed to push her into obscurity, however, and as she nipped at his heels Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning in the vote returns it was clear that the massive flood of PAC money, including from the pro-Israel lobby, had made for a far more competitive race than almost anyone had forseen.

There’s a lesson there for progressives. El-Sayed is a candidate whose reputation (so far) is squeaky-clean, free of the damaging past comments that dogged other progressive candidates like Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York or William Lawrence in Michigan’s 7th district. To win statewide against a massive flood of AIPAC money it took a number of stars aligning for progressives, not least being the unpopularity of the Iran war and Israel’s war in Gaza, and a year when frustration towards party leaders was at its zenith.

None of those factors were insignificant. El-Sayed crossed the finish line, yes, but by the skin of his teeth and with the wind at his back. Others may not be so lucky.

open image in gallery Nervous supporters of Abdul El-Sayed watched for hours as vote returns showed Haley Stevens to be much closer than any polls showed ( AFP/Getty )

Everyone’s ‘DSA’ now

If there’s one group that was feeling genuinely confident on Wednesday it’s probably the Democratic Socialists of America. Aside from the aforementioned proof that a Medicare-for-All-supporting Democrat can win a statewide race in a midwestern swing state, even when massively outspent, there was one other reason for the Democratic Party’s far left flank to feel good about Tuesday’s results.

That’s because truth and fiction are blending together and both El-Sayed and his onetime rival, fellow progressive Mallory McMorrow, were linked closely with the DSA brand in the waning weeks of the campaign. Some of it came from surprising sources — like Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, chair of the Senate Democratic campaign arm, who reportedly was telling donors that McMorrow was a DSA member as a means of dissuading the party’s moneyed elite from backing here.

The DSA is now watching as two fairly mainstream progressive Democrats get branded with their logo, willingly or not. That only helps their brand among less politically-connected voters in the long run.

open image in gallery El-Sayed was flanked by Mallory McMorrow, his onetime opponent, at a victory press conference on Wednesday ( Reuters )

“The lesson the left should take away from last night is the same as what moderates should be heeding: this is Michigan,” Rodericka Applewhaite of Majority Democrats, which supported Mallory McMorrow during the primary, told The Independent on Wednesday.

“Both factions will need the other in order to bring independents into the fold and beat Mike Rogers in November. Leaders from state Senator McMorrow to Governor Whitmer understand the stakes, which is why they moved quickly this morning to present a united front. Abdul will win this if he uses that support to do what he does best and stay focused on costs and corruption.”

In the end, El-Sayed’s victory is a mixed bag for the party overall. It’s definitely a blow for party leaders like Chuck Schumer and pro-Israel groups like AIPAC, whose combined reputations were a major drag on Stevens’s campaign and a major animating factor for the left. But it wasn’t the blowout victory the left wanted, and the center left is largely looking at Michigan’s results as a sign that they aren’t out of the fight just yet -- far from it.

Progressives are riding the contrasting highs and lows of another night of an undeniable shift in the Democratic Party’s membership, as El-Sayed’s victory was accompanied by other victories for the left such as the ousting of another sitting member of Congress, Shri Thanedar of Michigan’s 13th district, in a race that took place far outside of New York.

Donavan McKinney, Thanedar’s opponent, just won a majority-Black district with the endorsement of the DSA, dealing another blow to narratives about the group (whose membership skews white, according to internal surveys).

Overall, though, the lesson for Democrats of all stripes seems to be that they really can’t afford too many fights like this in the future, especially as the presidential election cycle nears. AIPAC alone burned tens of millions of dollars backing Stevens, and the race turned ugly and divisive quickly as supporters of the two candidates waged war online in a manner all too reminiscent of the 2016 presidential primary. The result could be a demotivating effect across voters of one or even both candidates in future contests.

“Glad it’s over, thrilled by the results, and, I regret to inform you: The MI Senate primary (much like the TX one) is pretty good foreshadowing for what the 2028 Democratic presidential primary is going to feel like,” wrote Amanda Litman, a backer of El-Sayed and founder of the left-leaning group Run For Something, on Wednesday.

After 2024 and the debacle around Joe Biden, Democrats know all too well the dangers of having toxic intraparty political fights at the wrong moment. Whether the party can avoid that in 2028, and keep themselves from losing the White House for a second time in a row, remains to be seen.

House Speaker Mike Johnson says he won't get involved in the abuse allegations against embattled Republican Representative Max Miller — describing them as “domestic events” that happen “all the time.”

“I haven’t spoken to Max about this in the last few days. Of course, I will,” Johnson said in an interview with Politico. “There’s all sorts of domestic events going on with 435 members of Congress all the time, it’s not my business to get engaged in it.”

When pressed about accusations that the Ohio Republican held a gun to the head of ex-wife Emily Moreno and broke their two-year-old daughter's collarbone, Johnson acknowledged the claims were “serious,” Politico reported Wednesday.

Moreno’s father is Republican Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, who said Sunday that his former son-in-law should drop his re-election bid, resign from Congress and get “serious psychological help.”

"He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter," Senator Moreno wrote on social media. "If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them."

open image in gallery House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledges the allegations against Rep. Max Miller are ‘serious’ but says he won’t get involved because ‘domestic events’ happen ‘all the time’ ( Getty )

The remarks led several Republican colleagues to echo the call, with Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas saying: “I trust Bernie so much as a good friend, and his family has such high values” that “to go through with this, it makes me think that they’re telling the whole truth and nothing but the truth.”

President Donald Trump privately told Miller that “things aren’t looking good,” Axios reported Monday. The president also told reporters the same day that the situation involving him was “a very sad thing.”

At Miller’s request, the House Ethics Committee said Tuesday that it's looking into whether the 37-year-old lawmaker “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use.” Johnson said that investigation would get to the bottom of the allegations.

“I think Max is taking them seriously. I think our colleagues are,” the speaker said. “But, again, we have to allow this process to play out. It’s just begun.”

Hours after the Ethics Committee announcement, Miller appeared Tuesday on CNN, where he denied any wrongdoing and called the claims against him “politically motivated.”

open image in gallery Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio called Sunday for Miller, his former son-in-law, to resign from Congress and drop his re-election bid ( Getty )

Miller also said he wouldn't drop his campaign for a third term in the House ahead of Tuesday’s deadline, saying: “I will never back down.”

"I am never going to give up, and what I mean by that is my daughter is going to grow up one day, and she's going to see all of this, and she's not going to see that her father caved to political and social media pressures for something that he never did," he added.

Emily Moreno’s accusations, contained in police reports and court documents, led to the resurfacing of a 2021 Politico report in which unidentified sources alleged that Miller had pushed and slapped then-girlfriend and former Trump White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham during an April 2021 domestic dispute, and had also shoved a high school classmate down a flight of stairs when she refused his advances.

Miller, through an attorney, denied those allegations at the time and later sued Grisham for defamation after she wrote about an abusive relationship with an ex-boyfriend, without identifying Miller by name.

They settled out of court, with both sides agreeing not to disparage each other but Grisham sued Miller last month, alleging he violated that deal.

open image in gallery Former Trump White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham is suing Miller for allegedly violating a non-disparagement agreement tied to their former relationship ( AFP/Getty )

Grisham also filed a motion Monday for a temporary restraining order against Miller to prevent further alleged violations.

During his Tuesday CNN appearance, Miller acknowledged that Trump had called him the day before and told him “it’s going to be a tough race” but didn’t tell him to drop out.

Miller also said that “Speaker Mike Johnson, everyone else — they’re standing behind me.”

Johnson told Politico that he thought that “what Max is suggesting there is that I’ve been intellectually consistent.”

“We don’t take disciplinary action against members for allegations,” the speaker said. “But he’s saying the same things privately to members that he is publicly, that he denies all this.”

Johnson also said that the allegations “don’t look good right now, of course,” adding, “Look, I pine for the days when we don’t have these kinds of disturbances, when we got people who act in accordance with the dignity of their office. “

“But people have domestic disputes,” he said. “It’s part of being flawed humans, as we are, and we have to let those processes play out.”

The U.S. National Domestic Violence Hotline offers support at 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In the U.K., the national domestic abuse helpline offers support for women on 0808 2000 247, or you can visit the Refuge website. There is a dedicated men's advice line on 0808 8010 327. Other international helplines can be found via www.befrienders.org
