World.title: ‘The Dog-Gone Girl Is Mine’: Love triangle lands man in court after allegedly kicking ex-girlfriend’s new man off his cycle and throwing bottle at ex
World.content:
‘The Dog-Gone Girl Is Mine’: Love triangle lands man in court after allegedly kicking ex-girlfriend’s new man off his cycle and throwing bottle at ex

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man accused of attacking his former girlfriend and injuring her new boyfriend in two separate incidents has been granted bail after appearing in the Magistrate’s Court.

Raheem Tray Gibson, 22, a runman of North Front Street, was arraigned on charges of aggravated assault and harm when he appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate on Tuesday. He pleaded not guilty to both charges.

The aggravated assault charge relates to an allegation made by Gibson’s former girlfriend, a 24-year-old sales clerk.

Yearwood reported that at about 6:30 p.m. on Sunday, August 2, she was at a park on Matron Roberts Street with her five-year-old son and her current boyfriend when Gibson arrived on a motorcycle.

She alleged that Gibson stopped several feet away, cursed at her and threw a glass pint bottle in her direction. The bottle reportedly missed her, and Gibson then rode away.

The harm charge stems from an incident reported by the woman’s current boyfriend, a 24-year-old security guard.

He told police that on the morning of Saturday, August 1, he was riding his motorcycle toward Douglas Jones Street when another motorcyclist began following him.

He alleged that the rider drove directly behind him and kicked the rear tyre of his motorcycle, causing him to crash. Flowers reportedly suffered abrasions to his right palm, elbow, ankle and hip.

His motorcycle was also damaged, including a bent handlebar and front wheel, as well as broken lights, indicators and a rear-view mirror.

Flowers identified the alleged attacker as Gibson, whom he knew as his girlfriend’s former boyfriend.

There was no objection to bail, and Gibson was offered bail of $1,500 for the aggravated assault charge and $1,000 for the harm charge. He was required to provide separate sureties for each matter.

His bail conditions include staying at least 100 yards away from Yearwood, her home and workplace, and avoiding all contact with her, her relatives and prosecution witnesses, including through social media.

Gibson must also report to the Queen Street Police Station every Wednesday and must not be charged with any other offence while on bail.

Both matters were adjourned until September 16, 2026.

World.title: National Commission for Families and Children launches child protection training
World.content:
National Commission for Families and Children launches child protection training

By Zoila Palma: The National Commission for Families and Children (NCFC), with the support of the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, launched the first child protection training session for teachers from Wesley College, Excelsior High School, and Gwen Lizarraga High School.

The NCFC explained that as mandatory reporters and a critical line of defense for vulnerable children, teachers play a vital role in recognizing signs of abuse, reporting concerns, and safeguarding children’s rights and well-being.

This initiative will strengthen educators’ knowledge of child protection, safeguarding, and their responsibilities under Belize’s child protection framework, with a total of 80 teachers expected to be trained to help ensure every child is protected, heard, and supported.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture hosts soil sampling methodologies training in San Antonio, Cayo
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture hosts soil sampling methodologies training in San Antonio, Cayo

By Zoila Palma: On August 4th 2026, a Soil Sampling Methodologies training was conducted in San Antonio, Cayo with the SAYAB Farmer’s Cooperative.

A total of 16 cooperative members comprising the SAYAB cooperative were present this morning in the execution of Soil Sampling Methodologies.

The cooperative was founded in 2017 as non-traditional producer of vegetables and spices such as arugula, thyme, basil and other nice spices that are very much used in both Belizean and American cuisine.

Today, Enrique Rivas and Israel Pech delivered a Soils Sampling Methodologies training; and their experiences so that the cooperative members would be able to make more educated decisions when it comes to their soils and fertilizer amendments.

Soils are very rich in nutrients nevertheless as years pass; the producers need to make better amendments to compensate for those that are being depleted by the different crops cultivated.

The Ministry says that the cooperative is now fully capable of doing their samples and ship them to the different laboratories to get the results of their soil samples.

Once this information is received, they will also get the recommendations from the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries in the amends that they will need to conduct so they are safer and more productive in their production parcels.

The collaboration between MAFSNGI and IICA focuses on assisting farmers with the knowledge for them to make better decisions in their farms.

The event was coordinated with Dale Pech, extension officer of the COSAL Project for the Inter American Institute for Cooperation on Agriculture (IICA).

World.title: Galen University, Transparent BPO partner with Corazon Creek Technical High School to expand higher education and employment opportunities
World.content:
Galen University, Transparent BPO partner with Corazon Creek Technical High School to expand higher education and employment opportunities

By Zoila Palma: Representatives from Galen University and Transparent BPO visited Corazon Creek Technical High School (CCTHS) on Monday, August 3, to advance a new initiative aimed at expanding access to higher education and employment opportunities for students in Corazon Creek and neighboring communities.

The partnership will allow the first cohort of Galen University students to begin classes during the upcoming fall semester while working at Transparent BPO, which will operate from the CCTHS campus.

The program is designed to enable students to earn an income, gain valuable professional experience, and pursue their university education at the same time.

Representing Galen University during the visit were Dr. Cynthia Eve Aird, Provost, and Hiram Ochaeta, Director of Digital Strategy and Strategic Management. Transparent BPO was represented by Angie Westby, Human Resources Business Partner, and Abraham Middleton, Vice President of Network Infrastructure.

The initiative reflects a collaborative effort to create new educational and career pathways for young people in southern Belize, helping to reduce barriers to higher education while preparing students for the workforce through practical experience.

Galen University said it looks forward to strengthening its partnership with Corazon Creek Technical High School under the leadership of Board of Management Chairman Justo Veliz Jr., as the institutions work together to provide students with greater opportunities for academic and professional success.

World.title: We bid, we lost: Recinos Group answers procurement questions
World.content:
We bid, we lost: Recinos Group answers procurement questions

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Recinos Group of Companies has issued a public statement addressing what it describes as recent questions concerning its participation in government procurement processes, declaring that its construction arm submitted a proposal in the process at issue, did not win the bid, and was not awarded the contract.

The statement, dated August 3, 2026, responds to public commentary which, according to the group, has referred to a well-known entrepreneur from the Cayo District whose career began in the beauty industry. The group says it considers it important to provide a more complete understanding of the businesses involved and their history.

According to the statement, Maria Estella Recinos has built and expanded a diverse group of businesses over more than three decades, operating across retail trade, construction, importation, exportation, distribution, beauty services, logistics, and entrepreneurship initiatives. The group includes K&M Construction Company Ltd., Salon Essentials Ltd., Maria Estella’s Beauty Salon, and other affiliated enterprises and initiatives, including Women in Business. K&M Construction is described as a Belizean construction company engaged in construction-related works and services, including the execution and support of building and infrastructure projects.

The group states that its businesses have maintained commercial relationships with customers, suppliers, contractors, and institutions in Belize and abroad, including partners in Guatemala, El Salvador, the United States, and Guyana, and that, like many established Belizean companies, members of the group have participated in public procurement processes, supplying goods and services to both public and private sector clients in the ordinary course of business.

On the matter driving the commentary, the statement is direct: “The receipt of an invitation to participate in a procurement process is not, in itself, evidence of wrongdoing, nor does the submission of a proposal guarantee that a contract will ultimately be awarded.” It continues, “In this instance, K&M Construction Company Ltd. submitted a proposal but did not win the bid and was not awarded the contract.”

The statement closes on the principle at the heart of the season’s procurement debates: “The public has every right to expect transparency and accountability, and we support that principle fully. Equally, however, we believe that the public is entitled to receive complete, accurate, and properly contextualized information concerning the work that our businesses have undertaken over many years.”

It should be noted that the statement does not identify the specific procurement process in question or the source of the public commentary it addresses, and no allegation of wrongdoing against the group has been established in any official forum. The statement represents the group’s account of its position.

The exchange lands amid a period of heightened public attention on government procurement across several ministries, a climate in which established businesses and public institutions alike are finding their processes under the microscope, and in which, as this statement illustrates, the right of reply is being exercised as vigorously as the scrutiny itself.

World.title: One month of summer left: Cahal Pech Village Resort is the family’s last hurrah
World.content:
One month of summer left: Cahal Pech Village Resort is the family’s last hurrah

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP):The school year is coming, uniforms are being fitted, and the summer holidays have entered their final stretch. Cahal Pech Village Resort in San Ignacio is making the case that August deserves one proper family escape before the routine returns.

The hilltop resort above San Ignacio is built for exactly that kind of trip. The pools handle the day shift, keeping children happily occupied for hours, while the views across the Cayo countryside handle the parents’ end of the bargain, best enjoyed from the bar with a cold drink as the sun drops. On-site dining means nobody has to cook on holiday, and the thatched cabana setting delivers the away-from-it-all feeling minutes from town.

For families who want one more adventure in the memory bank, the location does the heavy lifting: the ancient Maya site of Cahal Pech sits right beside the resort, with Xunantunich, cave adventures and the San Ignacio market all within easy reach.

Bookings are one call away at 824-3740, on WhatsApp at 671-5737, or online at www.cahalpech.com.

Summer is not over yet. Close it out on the hilltop.

World.title: Galen University opens MBA applications with online delivery built for working Belizeans
World.content:
Galen University opens MBA applications with online delivery built for working Belizeans

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizean professionals eyeing the next rung on the career ladder have a homegrown option on the table. Galen University is accepting applications for its Master in Social Work, a two year programme delivered fully online and, in the university’s own words, designed for Belize and Belizeans.

The structure targets the working professional squarely. Online delivery means managers, public officers and business owners can pursue the degree without leaving their jobs or relocating to campus, and the two year duration gives a clear finish line. Galen has also put its pricing in plain view: $600 BZD per credit hour, allowing applicants to plan the investment semester by semester.

The localization is the quiet selling point. A masters designed for the Belizean context means coursework and case discussion grounded in the economy graduates will actually lead in, and classmates drawn from the country’s own professional ranks, the network that pays dividends long after graduation.

The timing carries urgency. Galen’s admissions window for the September intake closes August 19, with classes beginning September 7, leaving roughly two weeks to apply.

Applications and information are available at www.galen.edu.bz, by email at [email protected], or by phone at +501 614-6415. This could be you.

World.title: Jamaica plants 100 Kenyan Wambugu apple trees in import substitution drive – Green
World.content:
Designed for resilience, the Wambugu apple tree flourishes in both hot and cold conditions, making it ideally suited for tropical environments.

One hundred Wambugu apple trees were recently imported to Jamaica from Kenya and planted across agro parks at Amity Hall, Ebony Park and Parnassu, as the Caribbean island steps up its programme to support import substitution of apples and to diversify the earning potential of farmers.

Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining, Floyd Green made the announcement at the 72nd staging of the annual Denbigh Agricultural Industrial and Food Show in Clarendon last weekend.

“These demonstration plots will allow us to evaluate performance while encouraging wider adoption among farmers,” Green said of the development.

“A single acre can accommodate as many as 500 trees,” he continued, adding that “Within approximately five years, each tree can produce up to 500 apples and, with proper care and management, yields can reach between 30 and 40 tonnes per acre annually.”

The Wambugu apple is a crisp, juicy red variety similar to American apples. It was developed by Kenyan farmer Peter Wambugu to grow in warmer, tropical climates, which makes it suitable for Jamaica.

In the project spearheaded by the Agro-Investment Corporation (AIC), Jamaica aims for the crop to become a viable addition to local fruit production, contributing to agricultural diversification and farmer profitability.

Peter Wambugu’s daughter, Catherine conducted training sessions in Jamaica last year and distributed seedlings to agro park farmers as part of the programme.

Emphasising the potential of the initiative, Green noted that last year alone, Jamaica imported more than 1.4 million kilogrammes of apples at a cost of more than J$260 million.

“Just imagine what could happen if even a portion of that market could be supplied by Jamaican farmers,” he said.

“The Wambugu apple gives us an opportunity to do precisely that,” he added, noting that the fruit has demonstrated tremendous potential as a commercial crop.

The agriculture minister stressed that the introduction of a new crop “requires more than simply putting trees into the ground”.

“It requires research, training, monitoring and strong partnerships. That is why the Agro-Invest Corporation will continue to work closely with farmers as we assess the long-term potential of this crop under local conditions,” he said.

Green urged farmers who are interested in participating to contact the Agro-Invest Corporation to learn more about the programme and the opportunities that it presents.

World.title: UHWI at fault
World.content:
A view of the University Hospital of the West Indies

The University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) has been ordered to pay millions in damages after the Supreme Court found that the facility “fell below the standard of care” expected of it and also “breached the duty of care” provided to a 16-year-old girl, who died six days after being admitted to the hospital in March 2018.

The girl’s parents later sued the hospital’s board of management for failing to “use all proper professional skill, care, competence, and diligence during their investigation, diagnosis, management, and treatment of their only child”.

The court on Friday awarded $1,687,380.19 “for pain and suffering” endured by the child prior to her death. For loss of life/loss of expectation of life, the court awarded $344,127.70 with interest at three per cent per annum from April 15, 2021 to July 31 this year. In assessing how much the child, who was described as “a perennial high achiever” and a “polyglot” (a person who knows, speaks, or writes several different languages) would have lost in terms of earnings from before the trial to the last hearing date the court awarded $6 million. In satisfying the parent’s claims for special damages, the court awarded $975,573.41 plus interest of three per cent per annum, from the date she died to the date the judgement was handed down. It also awarded US$8,000 in respect of the report prepared by the expert witness relied on in the case.

The teenager who was described as “an accomplished and promising fifth-form student at Campion College, St Andrew” was preparing to sit the May/June sitting of the Caribbean Secondary Examination Council (CSEC) examinations at the time of her passing. She was said to have “entrepreneurial dreams and aspirations to become a scientist or a medical researcher”.

According to the civil negligence and estate lawsuit filed by her parents in the civil division of the Supreme Court in 2021, the young girl, on or around March 30, 2018 was admitted by the UHWI for treatment at its medical facility. Her mother said the ordeal began on March 27, 2018 when her daughter complained of what had become a persistent headache. She said after being examined by the family doctor, her daughter — who had also been warm to the touch — was prescribed medication. When that headache persisted three days later, along with weakness the parents — who said they began to “suspect that their daughter was suffering from another bout of meningitis, an illness with which she had been diagnosed at the age of eight years” — decided to take her to the UHWI.

Once there, they said they informed medical staff of her symptoms and history of meningitis as well as their suspicions. The parents said on March 31 after blood samples, a CT scan and an unsuccessful lumbar puncture procedure (which was to be done over), they were informed that their daughter was suffering from hemiplegic migraine. After some 18 seizures and two heart attacks, the teen who had also been placed on life support was pronounced dead on April 5, 2018.

Unmoored and set adrift by the loss of their child, the parents asserted that they suffered emotional and psychiatric distress. The father alleged that he became unable to focus, depressed and angry, making it difficult for him to hold onto a job. His wife maintained that, as a sales manager, the mental distress caused by, and the toll of, her daughter’s death affected her so drastically that she could not do her job as well as she did before.

According to court documents two medical professionals who gave evidence on behalf of the hospital maintained that the UHWI and its medical teams acted in accordance with standard practices and that there were no actions of negligence in the diagnosis, treatment and/or management of the teen.

However the court, in choosing to rely on the evidence of an expert witness called by the parents, said there were “aspects of negligence on the part of the UHWI, which are of great concern”.

“The documentary evidence discloses that, during the course of [her] admission to the UHWI, it was noted on three separate occasions that a diagnosis of meningitis was to be ruled out… in fact, it is readily apparent from the medical docket that no further attempt was made to rule out or to exclude the differential diagnosis of meningitis. This court is of the view that there is an absolute need for a physician to ensure that sufficient tests and detailed investigations are conducted before ruling out one disease over another. Negligence must be ascribed to the UHWI, by its servants and/or agents, for its failure to properly employ all usual diagnostic aids in ruling out the possibility of meningitis, including a lumbar puncture test,” the court said.

“The court finds that the UHWI was negligent in the failure on the part of its servants and/or agents to recognise that [name withheld] was brain-dead on 1 April 2018 at 11:00 pm. The evidence of the rapid deterioration in [the child’s] condition in the five days following her admission to the UHWI is concerning,” said the ruling handed down by Supreme Court Justice Anne-Marie Nembhard.

“The court finds that there was no clear plan of treatment, on the part of the servants and/or agents of the UHWI, to treat [her] in the face of her rapid deterioration, whilst being admitted as a patient to the UHWI. Nor does there seem to have been a corresponding, commensurate escalation in the UHWI’s plan of treatment or course of treatment in the face of her rapid deterioration,” the justice added.

In additional findings, the court said based on the evidence of the expert witness, an accurate diagnosis could have been arrived at, had a lumbar puncture been performed.

World.title: Power in unity
World.content:
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama (left) shakes hands with Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness after addressing a joint sitting of the Houses of Parliament at Gordon House on Tuesday. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama is urging Africa and the Caribbean to speak with one voice on the global stage, saying stronger cooperation is essential to reform the United Nations (UN) and international financial institutions to secure fairer treatment for developing countries.

Addressing a joint sitting of Jamaica’s Parliament, Tuesday during his State visit, Mahama argued that the historic relationship between Africa and the Caribbean must now evolve into a strategic partnership capable of influencing international decision-making, reducing global inequality and creating greater economic opportunities for developing nations.

Rather than allowing the relationship to remain rooted solely in a shared history of slavery and colonialism, the Ghanaian leader said the two regions should work together to influence policies on climate change, global finance, trade, food security and public health, areas in which he believes developing countries have long struggled to make their voices heard.

“We must strengthen cooperation between the African Union and Caricom. We must deepen our collaboration within the United Nations and other multilateral institutions, and we must coordinate our positions on issues that will define the future of humanity. Whether the challenge is climate change, reform of the international financial architecture, food security, public health, or digital transformation, our voices will carry greater weight if we speak together,” he declared.

Caricom and the African Union have steadily expanded cooperation in recent years, driven by shared positions on reparatory justice, climate finance, sustainable development and reform of the international financial system.

In 2021, the two regional organisations signed a memorandum of understanding aimed at strengthening political and economic cooperation, while regular Africa-Caricom summits have sought to deepen collaboration on trade, investment, education and technology.

Mahama said that cooperation must now extend beyond diplomacy and deliver meaningful change for citizens across both regions.

“The partnership between Africa and the Caribbean should therefore no longer be defined only by our shared past, but also by our shared future. It should be recognised for the future we are determined to build together. It is this conviction that inspired me to call the Accra Reset Conference recently,” he said.

He used his address to criticise what he described as persistent inequalities within the international system, arguing that many of the institutions governing global finance and politics were created in a different era and no longer adequately reflect the realities of today’s developing world.

The Accra Reset, launched by Ghana earlier this year, calls for reforms to international governance and development financing, with greater emphasis on productive investment, industrialisation and fairer representation for developing countries.

“The Accra Reset reflects our belief that institutions governing the world must evolve to reflect the realities and aspirations of the 21st century. Too many developing countries continue to confront structural barriers to financing, unequal trading arrangements, and inadequate representation in global decision-making bodies. These inequities cannot define our future,” Mahama argued.

He said Africa and the Caribbean should work together to change those conditions rather than continue operating within a system that limits their economic potential.

“The Accra Reset calls for a new development paradigm founded on mutual respect, productive investment, and genuine partnership. It seeks to accelerate industrialisation, promote value addition, encourage innovation, exercise national sovereignty over our resources, and equip our young people with the knowledge and skills to compete successfully in the global economy. But above all, it calls for a more balanced international order in which developing countries participate as equal partners in shaping global solutions,” he added.

Among the reforms he proposed was a renewed push to restructure the United Nations Security Council, which has remained largely unchanged since its creation after the Second World War. Africa, despite representing 54 sovereign states, does not hold a permanent seat on the council, a long-standing concern raised by African leaders.

Mahama also called for changes to international financial institutions, arguing that developing countries should have greater influence over decisions that affect access to financing and economic development.

Although much of Mahama’s address reflected on the historical ties between Africa and Jamaica, he repeatedly stressed that history alone would not improve the lives of future generations.

Instead, he said both regions should use their shared experiences to build stronger economic partnerships, coordinate their positions on major international issues and pursue reforms that give developing countries a more equal role in shaping global policies.

“When we work together, our partnership becomes more than just a historical connection. It becomes a powerful force for global progress, for shared prosperity, and for lasting justice,” he added.

World.title: Daydreams shows up white-hot before YUSH nostalgia
World.content:
Dexta Daps holds a vibe onstage at Daydreams on Saturday at the Montego Bay Convention Centre.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Dream Wknd transformed the Montego Bay Convention Centre into two completely different worlds on Saturday. From the elegance and romance of Daydreams to the nostalgic throwback energy of YUSH, patrons experienced a seamless journey through two distinct eras of music and celebration.

The afternoon belonged to Daydreams, where thousands dressed in all white filled the venue for one of the festival’s most-anticipated events. Against a backdrop of premium décor, unlimited drinks, and an atmosphere that balanced sophistication with celebration, patrons eagerly awaited dancehall’s leading man, Dexta Daps. And the singer delivered exactly what fans had come for.

Opening to deafening screams, Dexta Daps commanded the stage with a performance that blended passion, charisma, and crowd interaction. Couples embraced, friends sang ‘at the top of their lungs’, and phones lit up the venue as fans captured every moment.

His catalogue of hits, including WIFI, Owner, Call Me If, and Breaking News, had the ladies in the audience swooning and singing every word.

For nearly an hour the space became less of a concert venue and more of a shared celebration of music, romance, and dancehall culture, led by Dexta Daps.

For Sophia Khan, who flew in from Birmingham, Daydreams stood out as one of the highlights of Dream Wknd.

“This is my first-ever Dream Wknd, and Daydreams has definitely lived up to the hype. The vibe was amazing, the all-white theme looked so good, and Dexta Daps gave us everything we wanted. It’s one of those events you don’t want to leave,” she said.

As the sun went down, the atmosphere shifted from polished and elegant to playful and nostalgic as YUSH took over.

Presented by Casamigos, the throwback event invited patrons to relive their school days with a uniform dress code that saw party-goers arriving in creative takes on the classic classroom looks. This set the tone for an evening dedicated to celebrating the unforgettable sounds, style, and spirit of the late 1990s and early 2000s.

The nostalgia only intensified once the music started. Dancehall star Tifa took to the stage first, delivering a high-energy performance from the opening song. She set the tone for the night with a string of crowd-favourites before passing the baton to dancehall veteran Elephant Man, who raised the energy even further with his trademark infectious hits and signature dance moves. Together, the performances perfectly complemented the event’s retro concept, transporting the audience back to one of dancehall’s most celebrated eras.

The seamless transition highlighted the festival’s ability to deliver distinctly different experiences, each with its own unique personality while maintaining the premium standard patrons have come to expect.

Scott Dunn, group managing director of Dream Entertainment, expressed that, “Saturday really showcased what Dream Wknd is all about, offering completely different experiences within the same festival while maintaining the same level of quality. Daydreams delivered the premium, feel-good atmosphere we envisioned, and then YUSH allowed patrons to relive the music and culture that defined an era. Watching thousands of people fully embrace both concepts is incredibly rewarding and reinforces why Dream continues to evolve year after year.”

World.title: CREDIT CARD BALANCES HIT RECORD $94B
World.content:
Commercial banks are being urged to tighten their credit card lending practices after outstanding balances climbed to a record $94 billion, with one economist warning that the trend could push more households into financial distress.

Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) data show that commercial banks’ credit card receivables more than doubled in nominal terms, rising from $40.2 billion in 2017 to $94 billion as at April 2026. The central bank’s record shows 435,883 credit cards were in circulation at the end of 2025.

Economist and researcher Janiel McEwan in an interview with the Jamaica Observer said that while consumers must take responsibility for managing their finances, financial institutions should also shoulder some of the blame for encouraging borrowing through aggressive marketing and automatic credit-limit increases, while charging what he described as some of the highest credit card interest rates in the region.

“Banks have made borrowing much easier to say yes to, which from a marketing perspective is not inherently harmful, but they also have a fiduciary responsibility to ensure that they are lending responsibly. If they know someone is consistently struggling to meet repayments, there should be programmes to restructure those obligations before the debt spirals out of control,” he told the Business Observer.

“Credit by itself is not the enemy. Used wisely, it can open doors to opportunity. But without proper understanding, it can become a burden,” he added.

McEwan said the persistent rise in credit card balances could not be attributed solely to reckless spending, pointing to a combination of stagnant wage growth, persistent inflation, high transportation and living costs, and elevated borrowing costs as contributing factors.

“Wage growth is not keeping pace with the cost of living for many people. As such credit cards have increasingly become a backup plan or a social safety net for many households that are trying to manage everyday expenses,” he said, adding that credit card debt in Jamaica has not spiked overnight but has climbed steadily for about a decade, interrupted only briefly by the pandemic, with growth accelerating since 2023.

McEwan said annual credit card interest rates in Jamaica typically range from 35 and 40 per cent, which he contrasted with average rates of about 20 per cent in the United States.

“These interest rates are among the highest consumers will encounter in the financial system. Once people are unable to pay the balance in full, the debt accumulates very quickly,” McEwan noted.

Criticising what he described as aggressive marketing practices by some financial institutions, he said consumers are routinely encouraged to take up new credit cards or accept higher credit limits while receiving little guidance on responsible borrowing.

“They tell you that you can get the card without paying anything upfront and encourage you to spend beyond your income. But many people do not fully understand how interest compounds once the payment period expires,” he said.

Stressing the need for lenders to undertake more robust affordability assessments before issuing cards or increasing credit limits, McEwan deemed this a more worthwhile strategy than relying primarily on customers’ banking relationships.

“They should not simply look at someone’s salary and decide they qualify for a larger limit. Banks need to determine whether that person can realistically service the debt,” he said.

While acknowledging that lenders face genuine risks from loan defaults, he argued that profitability should not come at the expense of responsible lending.

As he called on the central bank to strengthen oversight of consumer lending, he said there is an immediate need for the BOJ as regulator to require that financial institutions adopt stricter affordability standards and more responsible credit practices.

Beyond regulation, McEwan also said Jamaica urgently needs financial literacy programmes that focus specifically on the responsible use of credit rather than general savings education.

“We have spent years promoting saving, but we also need to teach people how credit works, how interest accumulates and the long-term consequences of carrying balances month after month,” he said.

He argued that financial education should begin at an early age and become a core part of the local school curriculum, while public awareness campaigns should also be rolled out to target existing credit card users.

McEwan suggested that while higher-income earners may use credit cards strategically to earn rewards while investing their cash elsewhere, much of the country’s growing credit card debt is likely concentrated among middle- and lower-income households struggling with rising living costs.

“The people who understand credit tend to use it as a financial tool. The concern, however, is with those who are relying on it simply to make ends meet,” he said.

While stopping short of declaring that Jamaica has entered a full-scale debt crisis, McEwan warned that current trends suggest the country is moving in that direction if borrowing continues to outpace repayment.

“When one looks at the size of the outstanding balance, the number of repossessions by banks now taking place and the financial pressures households are facing… we are moving dangerously close to a debt crisis,” he said.

To this end, he urged banks to adopt more responsible lending practices and to tailor credit limits that are in line with the customers’ ability to repay and where possible to offer debt restructuring options for those borrowers showing signs of financial distress.

“Financial institutions should also be more considerate in deciding who gets a credit card and also what limit they receive. Better guardrails now could help to prevent much bigger problems later,” McEwan concluded.

World.title: ON THE ROPES
World.content:
Bowler Ali Usman (right) of Pakistan celebrates after he caught and bowled batter Roston Chase (unseen) of West Indies as non-striking batter Justin Greaves (left) looks on during the third day of their second Test match at Queen’s Park Oval in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, on Tuesday. (Photo: AFP)

PORT OF SPAIN, Trinidad (CMC) — Jomel Warrican continued his love affair with Pakistan’s batters, but the visitors’ spinning duo of Sajid Khan and Ali Usman grabbed six wickets in the final session to leave West Indies on the brink of defeat in the second and final Test here on Tuesday.

On a pitch offering significant assistance to the spinners, Khan and Usman bemused the Windies’ batters to leave them reeling on 103 for six at the end of day three at the Queen’s Park Oval — an overall lead of only 60 runs.

Those late strikes overshadowed an earlier impressive bowling spell by Warrican, that saw him record his second-best figures of 6-112 and claim his third five-wicket haul in Tests — all of them against Pakistan.

His efforts helped the home side fight their way back into the match after Pakistan, who resumed the day comfortably placed at 266 for two, were bowled out for 387 in reply to the Windies’ 344.

West Indies reaped success early on when Pakistan captain Babar Azam, who failed to add to his overnight score of 88, was run out by a direct throw from Brandon King at cover, following a mix up with Abdullah Shafique.

That proved to be a bittersweet moment for the Windies, as King was injured in the process and had to be stretchered off the field.

An update from Cricket West Indies (CWI) revealed that the opener was experiencing lower back spasms and he did not return to the field for the remainder of the day.

Warrican then bowled Awais Zafar and Mohammad Rizwan, while pacer Shamar Joseph trapped Salman Agha lbw for a duck to see Pakistan slip to 311 for six.

However, Shafique continued to defy the Windies’ bowlers and he reached 150 during a 59-run partnership with Khan that gave them the lead.

But once Jayden Seales had Khan caught behind for 30, Warrican cleaned up the tail by dismissing Usman, Ubaid Shah and Mohammad Ali in the space of four deliveries.

Shafique remained unbeaten on 160 off 323 balls and hit 15 fours and three sixes.

Faced with a slender deficit of 43 runs, West Indies made a positive start with Tagenarine Chanderpaul and makeshift opener Kavem Hodge all but erasing it during a stand of 40 runs for the first wicket.

However, the introduction of Khan in the 10th over changed the complexion of the match as he had Chanderpaul lbw with his second ball.

Amir Jangoo and Hodge ensured the Windies wiped away the deficit, but shortly after Khan struck again by bowling Jangoo for 13 with a delivery that straightened to leave them 62 for two.

Usman then got the key wicket of Hodge for 34. A voracious appeal for lbw was turned down by the umpire, but the review showed the ball crashing into the stumps to make it 74 for three.

Shai Hope was then undone by a delivery from Khan that kept low to be lbw for 15 and two runs later Khan also accounted for the wicket of nightwatchman Jayden Seales for a duck.

With the close of play in sight, Roston Chase drove a delivery straight back into the hands of Usman in what turned out to be the last ball of the day, with the Windies essentially 60 for six heading into the penultimate day of play.

Khan has so far taken 4-32, while Usman has grabbed 2-29.

World.title: Paramount pursues international lubricant deal
World.content:
Lubricant being poured from a container. Paramount Trading (Jamaica) Limited is negotiating to manufacture lubricant brands for an international marketer serving local and export markets. .

PARAMOUNT Trading (Jamaica) Limited is negotiating with an unnamed international lubricant marketer to manufacture its brands in Jamaica for local and export markets, a prospective arrangement that could reshape the company’s lubricant operation, although there is no timetable for concluding the negotiations.

Chief Executive Officer Hugh Graham said Paramount deliberately reduced some existing lubricant production to preserve blending capacity for the prospective customer.

“We have a big player at the table that would take up all the capacity that we have,” Graham told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday.

If an agreement is reached, he said, Paramount may eventually have to expand its plant.

Graham did not identify the customer or disclose the proposed contract’s value, duration, production volumes or export markets. He also did not say whether the parties had signed a preliminary agreement.

He said Paramount had obtained certification to standards developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) as part of its preparations. Graham described the prospective customer as “one of the biggest marketers in the world”.

Graham said he hoped the negotiations would conclude soon but could not provide a timetable, citing the war in West Asia and volatility in the global oil industry.

His explanation provides context for the 43.1 per cent decline in lubricant revenue during the year ended May 31, 2026. Sales from the division fell to $60.6 million from $106.4 million a year earlier. Paramount has not quantified how much of that decline resulted from the production cut or disclosed when the reduction began.

The discussions form part of Paramount’s plan to shift towards contract manufacturing. Under that model, the company blends and packages lubricants for customers that already have established brands and distribution networks.

“We prefer to produce and have someone else market it,” Graham told the Business Observer.

Paramount already manufactures Futrol lubricants for Future Energy Source Company Limited (Fesco) and the ALTRA brand for Allegheny Petroleum Products Company. Based on Graham’s description, the proposed international arrangement would apply that model on a much larger scale, with production intended for Jamaica and export markets.

The negotiations come after a financial year in which Paramount’s profit recovered but revenue declined.

Total revenue fell 2.1 per cent to $1.69 billion. Chemicals, the company’s largest division, declined 6.9 per cent to $1.13 billion, while lubricants recorded the steepest contraction.

Growth in smaller divisions partly offset those declines. Revenue from construction products and adhesives increased 26.7 per cent to $251.3 million, while manufacturing revenue rose 16.8 per cent to $228.2 million.

Graham expects sales of construction chemicals to benefit from high-rise developments, underground parking facilities, water-storage projects and hotel renovations. Paramount distributes Sika-branded construction products.

He also expects demand to recover among hotels and industrial and water-treatment customers affected by Hurricane Melissa. Paramount, however, has not issued a formal revenue or profit forecast for the new financial year.

Net profit increased to $99.1 million from $26.1 million, although the improvement was supported substantially by $138.1 million in other operating income rather than higher sales.

The largest disclosed item was the write-off of a vendor liability of approximately $54 million after Paramount was informed that the obligation had been settled by the vendor’s parent company. Other operating income included a $33-million unrealised foreign-exchange gain, $33.9 million from services and $10.5 million arising from the termination of a lease.

All were reflected in Paramount’s audited profit, but some may not recur at the same level. A calculation using the audited figures shows that before other operating income and expenses were taken into account, gross profit after administrative, selling and distribution expenses fell to approximately $77.8 million from $153.2 million a year earlier.

Paramount also increased its provision for customer debts that may not be collected to $96.2 million from $50.4 million. At the end of May, approximately $215.9 million — nearly half of gross trade receivables — had been outstanding for more than 90 days.

World.title: Honours Overdue: The music icons Jamaica still hasn’t recognised
World.content:
Recipients of the National Honours and Awards will be announced this week by the government of Jamaica. Today, we look at stalwarts of the country’s music industry whose contributions have never been recognised.

Earl “Chinna” Smith

Arguably the most prolific session musician in the history of reggae, Smith has played on classic songs by Dennis Brown (Westbound Train, Cassandra), Bob Marley (Rastaman Vibration), and Burning Spear (Marcus Garvey). His licks can also be heard on Grammy-winning albums by Ziggy Marley and The Melody Makers and Lauryn Hill, as well as Amy Winehouse’s first album. In October 2023, Rolling Stone Magazine named Smith at #182 on its 250 Greatest Guitarists of All Time.

Lynn Taitt

The Trinidadian guitarist is credited with starting rocksteady. He reportedly directed the 1966 recording session that resulted in Take it Easy by Hopeton Lewis, the song many musicologists believe launched that genre. Taitt played on numerous hit songs including the Shank I Sheck rhythm; (007) Shantytown and Israelites by Desmond Dekker and The Aces; Stop That Train by Keith and Tex; and Walk The Street at Night by Derrick Harriott. Lynn Taitt — who was named at #204 on Rolling Stone Magazine’s 250 Greatest Guitarists of All Time in 2023 — died in 2010.

The Abyssinians

The legendary roots trio are best known for the seminal Sata Masa Gana, the 1971 song considered by many to be reggae’s official anthem. Bernard Collins, Donald Manning and Lynford Manning comprised the most famous version of the group, which still tours with Donald in its lineup. Declaration of Rights and Forward On To Zion are other famous songs by The Abyssinians.

Tenor Saw

Maybe the most original dancehall singer. His unique yodel made songs like Pumpkin Belly, Golden Hen and Ring The Alarm standards. That sound influenced singers such as Anthony Redrose and King Kong. Tenor Saw died in 1985.

Sister Nancy

A pioneer female deejay who made her name on sound systems before rocking the mic for producer Winston Riley in the early 1980s. It was Riley who produced Bam Bam, the 1983 song that remains her signature. Bam Bam has been used in ads by major companies such as Reebok, and sampled by heavyweight rappers including Jay Z.

Stanley Beckford

The four-star general of mento! Stanley was not only a fixture of the Festival Song Competition (which he won three times), but he had hit songs during the 1970s when mento was shunned as ‘old people music’. Soldering (recorded with The Starlights), Broom Weed and Brown Gal were some of his popular songs. He died in 2007.

Sanchez

The dancehall Sinatra, Sanchez ruled the roost during the 1980s and 1990s with a series of hit songs. They include Loneliness, Baby Can I Hold You, I Can’t Wait, Here I Am and Brown Eye Girl.

Flabba Holt

Bassist and founder of The Roots Radics Band, he is a ‘foundation’ of contemporary dancehall. Gunman (Michael Palmer), Big Ship (Freddie McGregor), Night Nurse (Gregory Isaacs), Police In Helicopter (John Holt) and Wa Do Dem by Eek A Mouse are some of the songs he played on. He can also be heard on albums by Bunny Wailer and Israel Vibration.

The first winner of the Best Reggae Album (then known as Best Reggae Recording) Grammy, this group earned their stripes with edgy Sly and Robbie-produced songs like Plastic Smile, Abortion, General Penitentiary and Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner. Mykal Rose, Duckie Simpson and Puma Jones (who died in 1990) comprised the most successful version of the group.

Wycliffe “Steely” Johnson

One of the godfathers of digital dancehall, this talented keyboardist was a member of The Roots Radics Band before forming a mega partnership with drummer Cleveland Browne, known as Steely and Clevie. They played on and produced countless hit songs including No, No, No by Dawn Penn; Love Is The Answer by Garnet Silk; Fast Car by Foxy Brown and Trailer Load A Girls by Shabba Ranks. Steely died in 2009.

The Grace Thrillers

Formed in the early 1970s by Noel Willis, this group were the first successful exponents of what became gospel-reggae. Spiritual songs like Can’t Even Walk, Jesus and He’s Alive were played in dancehalls and drew ‘forwards’ from the most hardened ‘rude bwoys’.

Winston Wallace

This former educator and trade unionist wrote Land of My Birth, the unofficial national anthem of Jamaica. That song, by Eric Donaldson, won the Festival Song Competition in 1978. The previous year, they won that contest with Sweet Jamaica. Land of My Birth transcends ‘Festival’, and is played at national events in Jamaica and its Diaspora.

World.title: German anti-terror police investigate explosive drone found at Leipzig airport
World.content:
Officials told WELT — which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer group — that the device’s detonator failed to function, preventing an explosion. They also said the drone was found just meters from a Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. According to the report, it contained Semtex, the explosive used in the bomb that brought down Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988, killing all 259 people on board and 11 on the ground.

Leipzig airport hosts the base of operations of NATO’s Strategic Airlift International Solution (SALIS), which gives participating countries access to Antonov cargo planes to transport military equipment. The airport is DHL’s largest European air hub and serves as an aircraft maintenance base for some Ukrainian Antonov aircraft.

According to WELT, security authorities have internally classified the incident as an attempted attack. No suspects had been detained as of Wednesday evening.

Germany’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt interrupted his summer vacation in Italy to meet officials in Leipzig.

Saxony’s Interior Minister Armin Schuster described the incident in a statement as “very serious security incident.”

Ukraine’s ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, assumed Moscow could be behind the incident. “I hope that all the authorities in Germany will now establish the facts as well. But who else could it have been besides Russia?” he posited on WELT TV.

Russia’s embassy to Germany didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Lennart Pfahler contributed reporting from Berlin. This article has been updated.

World.title: Washington holds up approval for France’s US ambassador pick amid human rights spat
World.content:
According to two people familiar with the matter, the Trump administration took offense at a social media post from France’s mission to the U.N. in Geneva that criticized Washington’s decision to side with Russia and North Korea against the renewal of U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk’s mandate.

“The U.S. used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore,” wrote the French mission on X last month. “And the world no longer listens to it.” The post prompted the U.S. delegation to walk out of a U.N. Security Council meeting in protest.

“The United States is very disappointed in the irresponsible and disrespectful rhetoric from the French,” said an official from the Department of State in response to a written question about Lechevallier’s clearance process. “We are responding appropriately to their comments.”

Türk, an Austrian national who has been high commissioner since 2022, has drawn U.S. ire for his criticism of the country’s immigration policy and Israel’s war in Gaza.

Two of the individuals also expressed hope that the dispute, which was first reported by Reuters, would blow over and Washington would not block Lechevallier’s appointment.

Love-hate relationship

The spat illustrates the volatile relationship between the U.S. and its oldest ally France. While Macron and Trump have shared moments of camaraderie in front of the cameras, they have polar opposite world views and regularly spar over NATO, Ukraine and trade relations.

World.title: Malta leads fight against EU bid to tax Big Gambling
World.content:
But the campaign has run into strong opposition from Malta. The tiny island in the Mediterranean Sea, with a population of just over half a million people, is home to a burgeoning betting sector. It says that higher taxes will cripple its gambling industry, boost illegal operators and drive firms outside the bloc.

“[Malta] will not accept the introduction of any EU-level taxes designed to sustain the bloc’s spending,” the country’s Prime Minister, Robert Abela, told the Maltese Parliament in June.

But Shilton, who lost more than £1 million in betting on horse racing over 45 years and now runs his own gambling addiction charity, dismisses the arguments by Malta and the gambling lobbies as “window dressing.” He’s in favor of higher taxes as he wants to shrink advertising revenue that is used to lure in new gamblers.

“Deep down they’re after everybody’s money. Simple as that,” he told POLITICO during a visit to Brussels in June.

Former England goalkeeper Peter Shilton lost more than £1 million in betting on horse racing over 45 years and now runs his own gambling addiction charity. | David Cannon/Allsport/Getty Images

The topic has split the EU’s 27 governments, pitting gambling-heavy Southern European countries against their more supportive Western European peers, led by France. Capitals are already fighting even though the Commission hasn’t yet issued a formal proposal for the possible tax, which would ultimately need to be unanimously approved by governments.

It’s one of numerous budget battle lines being drawn, with Ireland — which is steering the talks as chair of the rotating Council presidency — set to restart negotiations to facilitate an overall deal on the EU budget before the end of the year.

World.title: Former European Parliament President Klaus Hänsch has died
World.content:
Klaus Hänsch speaks in Bonn, Germany in 2009. | Rastrojo via Wikimedia

The German Social Democrat served as head of the Parliament from 1994 to 1997.

Former European Parliament President Klaus Hänsch has died, current Parliament President Roberta Metsola confirmed on Wednesday.

“His Parliament mourns the loss of a champion of Europe, who took office at a time of profound change for our continent, and who never stopped believing in the potential of this project,” wrote Metsola in a social media post.

“At our last meeting just a few weeks ago, his unwavering optimism shone through as he described his ongoing efforts to promote civic engagement and nurture young European leaders. Europe will miss him. May he rest in peace,” she added.

Hänsch, a German Social Democrat, served as Parliament president from 1994 to 1997, and was an MEP from 1979 to 2009.

He was 87 years old.

World.title: Das Phantom Tom Rohrböck
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler widmen sich in dieser Sonderfolge einem mysteriösen Politikberater, der seit der AfD-Gründung im Hintergrund mitzumischen scheint und der selbst behauptet, als bezahlter Söldner für Nachrichtendienste und Großunternehmen zu arbeiten. Gemeinsam mit der Investigativ-Journalistin Katja Riedel (WDR) beleuchten die beiden, wie der angebliche Strippenzieher intern agiert und unter anderem Personalentscheidungen durch gezielte Desinformation beeinflusst haben soll.

Sie diskutieren die Hintergründe des jüngsten Kontaktverbots, das der AfD-Bundesvorstand auf Druck von Funktionären wie Björn Höcke und Stephan Protschka gegen Rohrböck verhängt hat. Dabei gehen Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler auch der Frage nach, warum viele Parteimitglieder regelrecht Angst vor seinem Einfluss haben und inwieweit dieses Phantom aktuell wieder in interne Machtkämpfe verwickelt ist.

Es geht auch um undurchsichtige Finanzquellen, die Rohrböcks luxuriösen Lebensstil und seine Einladungen an AfD-Funktionäre ermöglichen. Sie sprechen mit Katja Riedel auch über Anlagen in Liechtenstein, verschwundene Gelder von ahnungslosen Kleinanlegern und mögliche Verbindungen zum verstorbenen Milliardär August von Finck.

Der Film „Geheimes Netzwerk: Das rechte Phantom“ vom NDR ist hier online zu sehen.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

World.title: EU to transfer €1.4B in profits from frozen Russian assets to Ukraine
World.content:
The latest transfer follows another deadly night of missile attacks on Kyiv.

The European Union has collected €1.4 billion in revenue from immobilized Russian central bank assets and will channel the proceeds to Ukraine, the European Commission announced Wednesday.

In a press release, the Commission said the payment, received Monday, was the “fifth transfer of its kind.” Since the assets have been immobilized, they have generated a total of €8 billion in windfall profits.

Brussels said 95 percent of the latest tranche would go through the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism, helping Kyiv repay EU and G7 loans, while the remaining 5 percent would flow through the European Peace Facility to meet Ukraine’s “pressing military and defence needs.”

World.title: Self-driving startup approved to take taxi passengers in London
World.content:
Wayve said its vehicles “are designed to operate autonomously, and will do the driving,” though under TfL’s rules, a licensed PHV driver must be present and responsible for the vehicle at all times.

“Safety is our top priority,“ a TfL spokesperson said. “Any new vehicle licensed to carry passengers on London’s roads must align with our Vision Zero goal of eliminating all deaths and serious injuries from collisions on London’s streets by 2041.”

Successive U.K. governments have sought to make the country a European pioneer in self-driving technology.

The Department for Transport opened a permitting scheme for companies to operate commercial robotaxi services without a human driver in May. Applications for that scheme — which is separate from TfL’s PHV regime — continue to be assessed by central government with input from local transport authorities including TfL.

Getting licenses isn't the only obstacle facing robotaxi services. A survey by the London Assembly’s Transport Committee this month identified widespread opposition to autonomous passenger vehicles among the capital’s inhabitants, with just 29 percent of Londoners saying they support the roll out.

World.title: Italy to spend billions more on energy and defense, finance minister says
World.content:
Giorgetti said Italy will request to spend an additional 0.6 percent of gross domestic product on green energy investments and 0.9 percent on defense — the full amount that is envisaged under the new fiscal guidelines.

The additional defense spending will “include both new multi-year investment programs and proposals to reallocate resources already provided for under current legislation,” Giorgetti told MPs. Italy's parliament is expected to approve Giorgetti's request to the Commission on Wednesday.

The extra flexibility is aimed at reducing dependence on fossil fuels and moving toward NATO’s target to spend 5 percent of GDP on defense. With 2 percent of GDP allocated to defense in 2025, Italy is among the alliance’s spending laggards.

However, the decision to raise military spending is set to inflame political tensions within the country ahead of a crucial election year that will see incumbent Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni seek a second mandate.

The governing coalition is split on the issue, and the right-wing League party — from which Giorgetti himself hails — has repeatedly campaigned against spending more money to counter the Russian threat.

In a further constraint, the government is under heavy pressure from the right-wing, Russia-friendly National Future party led by former Gen. Roberto Vannacci, which is eating into support for the other governing parties, according to the polls.

World.title: IDF to continue to 'operate proactively' in Gaza, Israeli military chief says
World.content:
The Israel Defense Forces will continue to "operate proactively" in Gaza, according to Eyal Zamir, the chief of the general staff of the Israeli military.

 

Zamir made the comments following an operational tour on Wednesday, during which he met with several senior Israeli commanders who briefed him on the situation on the ground, per a statement shared by the military.

“In the Gaza Strip, we have struck a blow against Hamas, significantly weakened it and altered the security situation,” Zamir said. “The IDF will continue to operate proactively and in accordance with the principle we have established – to eliminate threats and, in all circumstances, to defend the communities and their residents, and to safeguard their security".

His statement came after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel had not agreed to a US-backed plan for Gaza, which would see Israeli forces withdraw from territory and the disarmament of the Hamas militant group.

"President Trump and his team think they can get Hamas to disarm and demilitarise in Gaza," Netanyahu said in a video message on Tuesday.

"We are looking into that. They sent us a draft, we did not agree," he continued, adding: "It is not our draft. We sent our comments".

Trump announced last week that his Board of Peace had reached what he called a "historic" agreement on the "complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza," which he said would pave the way for the transition to a new Palestinian government.

According to Trump, the deal would see Israeli forces withdraw from Gaza while an International Stabilization Force would work with a new Palestinian police unit to run the territory.

Jennifer Gavito, a nonresident senior fellow with the Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council, said "external actors" would be "indispensable in the success of this proposal."

"Egypt and Qatar will have to continue to lean heavily on Hamas to fulfill its commitments," Gavito said, adding that Trump would also have to put "tremendous pressure on Netanyahu" in order for the plan to succeed.

The Israel-Gaza war broke out after Hamas's October 7 attacks on Israel in 2023, which killed more than 1,200 people and saw 251 others taken hostage into Gaza.

Israel launched a military campaign into Gaza in the wake of the attacks, which has killed more than 73,000 people, per Gaza's health ministry.

World.title: Leftist Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeats establishment candidate in shock Michigan primary victory
World.content:
Progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic party's Senate primary election in the US state of Michigan on Wednesday, highlighting key internal differences over the party's direction.

 

El-Sayed narrowly defeated moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens - who was backed by many of the party's senior establishment figures such as Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer - in what became an expensive proxy battle over the party's course.

He will now go on to face Republican Mike Rogers in November in a bid to keep the Senate seat with the Democrats. November's elections will determine the makeup of Congress for US President Donald Trump's remaining time in power.

"We won," El-Sayed wrote in a post on X. "I am so proud to be your Democratic nominee for US Senate. Let's win in November".

Both El-Sayed and Stevens - the latter of whom reportedly received tens of millions in backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and affiliated groups - have moved quickly to champion party unity since the result was announced.

"I love Michigan and am so proud to have put up my hand to serve," Stevens wrote in a post on social media, adding that she had spoken with El-Sayed and had vowed to offer her "full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers this November."

In response, El-Sayed thanked Stevens for running and said he looked forward to "uniting this fall."

"Because what unites us is so much bigger than what divides us," he added.

During his campaign, El-Sayed, who trained as a doctor before working in public health, focused on affordability and healthcare, pledging "Medicare for All" and saying he would work to "get money out of politics" and "put money in your pocket."

His campaign website says he is running for the US Senate as he believes "life in America shouldn’t be this hard."

"As your Senator, Abdul will fight to build a government that works for you, not Elon Musk, Donald Trump, or their billionaire friends," it added.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump called the result "great news for the Republican Party" while labelling El-Sayed as "a communist loser who hates Jews and Israel."

World.title: Basque Country halves colon cancer deaths with screening programme
World.content:
Screening for colon cancer using a simple test for hidden blood in faeces can save thousands of lives. That is the conclusion of one of the largest studies carried out to date in Spain, which finds that this programme of early detection is associated with a 50% reduction in mortality from colorectal cancer among people aged 50 to 69.

 

The research, published this Wednesday in "JAMA Network Open (source in Spanish)", tracked how the disease evolved over 21 years in a population of almost 2.2 million people in the Basque Country. The findings show that the fall in deaths began just three years after the screening programme was introduced and has been sustained ever since.

As well as cutting mortality, the programme has made it possible to detect 70.8% of tumours at stages I and II, when the chances of cure are far higher and treatment is less aggressive.

The study, led by Dr Luis Bujanda, examined mortality data recorded between 2004 and 2024. Over that period there were 438,134 deaths from all causes, of which 16,298 were linked to colorectal cancer.

In the age group covered by the screening programme, 50 to 69 years, the mortality rate fell from 39.7 to 19.8 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, a decrease of 50.1%. In the population as a whole, mortality also dropped, from 32.8 to 23.1 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants.

The researchers identified a turning point in 2012, just three years after the programme began, strengthening the link between screening and the reduction in deaths from colorectal cancer. They also estimate that, without the introduction of this early detection system, mortality among people aged 50 to 69 would have been 46.2% higher.

A simple test that can detect cancer before symptoms appear

The screening programme is based on the faecal immunochemical test (FIT), a non-invasive test that detects small amounts of hidden blood in faeces, one of the earliest signs of a possible cancer or precancerous lesions. In the Basque Country, this test is offered every two years to men and women aged 50 to 69 who have no symptoms. If the result is positive, a colonoscopy is carried out to confirm the diagnosis.

Over the study period, the programme led to the detection of 4,892 cases of colorectal cancer. More than seven in ten were diagnosed at stages I or II, when treatment options are more effective and survival is significantly higher.

Support for early detection programmes

Colorectal cancer is one of the most common tumours and a leading cause of cancer death in Spain and worldwide. However, detecting it early greatly increases the chances of cure and even makes it possible to remove polyps before they turn into a malignant tumour.

For the authors, the results support the long-term benefits of organised screening programmes using the faecal immunochemical test as a public health strategy to reduce mortality from colorectal cancer.

They nevertheless stress that this is an observational study. This means the results show an association between the rollout of the programme and the fall in mortality, but do not allow a cause-and-effect relationship to be established with the same degree of certainty as a clinical trial.

Even so, the scale of the decline observed and its persistence for more than two decades reinforce the value of screening as one of the main tools for tackling this type of cancer.

World.title: Ukraine’s former ambassador to US faces anti-corruption probe
World.content:
Olha Stefanishyna, Ukraine's former ambassador to the US, is under investigation in an anti-corruption case, with the High Anti-Corruption Court holding a hearing on the matter in Kyiv on Wednesday.

 

Ukraine’s state broadcaster Suspilne reports that the National Anti-Corruption Bureau and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) served Stefanishyna with a new notice of suspicion on 5 August.

According to the SAPO prosecutor, Stefanishyna – a former ambassador to the US and ex–deputy prime minister for European and Euro-Atlantic integration – is accused of failing to declare two apartments and cash used to pay for renovations, airline tickets and the rent on another apartment.

She is also alleged to have failed to disclose her use of a car registered to one of her subordinates.

The prosecutor says her spending exceeded her income and savings.

Stefanishyna responded in a statement on Facebook, saying she viewed the investigation “calmly and without unnecessary emotion”.

“Any procedural actions are part of the lawful work of the law enforcement system and do not amount to a finding of guilt,” she wrote.

She added that she had “addressed many of the issues now being raised in the media, including those concerning real estate” and had provided journalists with “all the necessary documents” regarding the apartment that consequent questions.

“The burden of proving allegations lies with those who make them,” she wrote. “As for me, I will do what I must: calmly and lawfully defend my position. I have no doubt about the outcome.”

Zelenskyy dismissed Stefanishyna from her post on 3 August in a presidential decree that gave no reason for the move.

Speculation that she could leave one of Kyiv’s most important ambassadorial roles because of a corruption probe has circulated since a surprise wartime government reshuffle began in mid-July.

Stefanishyna said she decided to step down from her job in Washington for “personal reasons”.

Her planned departure was widely seen by analysts as a trigger for the reshuffle, with now ex-prime minister Yuliia Svyrydenko, who was later dismissed, expected to succeed Stefanishyna as Ukraine’s ambassador to Washington.
