World.title: From “rapid response” to possible law: who are Georgia’s national values being protected from?
World.content:
The Georgian government has not ruled out introducing legislation against what it describes as the erosion of national identity. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the proposed rules could cover insults directed at saints, monarchs and prominent public figures. No draft law has been introduced yet. However, experts argue that the groundwork is already being laid. Members of the ruling team have already begun discussing penalties and possible regulation of the media.

As the ruling Georgian Dream party debates possible punishment for insulting national values, it is worth examining what such measures could cover and what Russia’s experience suggests.

From assaults to a campaign to “protect national values”

The debate over possible legislation followed an attack on comedian Onise Okriashvili over a joke he made on YouTube. Late on 22 July, a man assaulted him near his home in Tbilisi. The attacker, Niko Khurtsilava, said he acted because Okriashvili had insulted Georgian national culture.

Even before the assault, pro-government television channels had launched a media campaign against Okriashvili. They broadcast a clipped excerpt from his YouTube show in which he referred to renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze using obscene language.

The writer’s grandson, Nodar Macharashvili, publicly backed the attacker. A few days after the incident, MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, who also described himself as Khurtsilava’s friend, announced the creation of a new movement that would provide “rapid response” to insults directed at sacred values, ancestors, religion and history.

“If protecting our culture and national identity requires it, we will not shy away from any threat. We are ready to take responsibility for every action we take and, if necessary, even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

He did not specify what he meant by “rapid response”. He also declined to answer journalists’ questions about the use of physical violence and vigilantism.

On 28 July, the group applied to the Public Registry to register its newly established organisation under the name National Generation.

A week after the attack on Okriashvili, on 30 July, another initiative group emerged to “protect national values”. It brought together actor Giorgi Shanidze, director Giorgi Sikharulidze and Kote Mzhavia, director of the Batumi Theatre.

Unlike the first movement, this group called for legal mechanisms rather than “rapid response”. Its members said the law should protect the church, sacred sites, historical heroes and national values.

“Freedom of expression is a fundamental value. However, that right cannot become a tool for insulting the sacred symbols and core values that form the country’s historical, cultural and spiritual foundation,” Giorgi Shanidze said.

The statement refers to “externally funded destructive groups” whose activities, it says, are creating confrontation between the Georgian nation and small minority groups.

“To prevent the situation from escalating further and reaching the point where even the wise Georgian people could lose patience, responsible steps must be taken and the existing problems must be resolved through legal and peaceful means,” the statement says.

The group plans to hold consultations with lawyers, historians, artists and athletes before drafting a legislative proposal.

However, neither the bill nor its concept has been published, so it remains unclear which actions could become punishable. The proposed form of liability and possible penalties also remain unknown.

What could a law on national values include?

On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: Georgian scam call centres: old fraudsters, new address? An investigation
World.content:
Georgian scam call centres that came under the spotlight during an international investigative project in 2025 have reportedly resumed operations from a new location. According to the investigative outlet Monitor, people linked to AK Group have relocated to an office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street in Tbilisi.

The outlet says its journalists conducted covert surveillance at the address for six months. They say they identified several of the same individuals who had been seen near AK Group’s previous office last year. According to Monitor, the footage also shows some of the same vehicles that regularly appeared at the company’s former location.

Journalists say they repeatedly spotted vehicles used by Akaki Kevkhishvili, who is widely believed to be the real operator of AK Group. The cars carried the registration numbers AK100KK and AK200KK. Investigators seized one of them in 2025 as part of the ongoing criminal investigation.

According to Monitor, AK Group’s registered owner and director, Meri Shotadze, also regularly visited the same address. She used two different vehicles, one of which investigators have also seized, while the other is registered to another person.

The investigation also claims that several agents who previously worked at AK Group’s former office have reappeared at the new location. They include Anzhelika Chkhapelia, who allegedly used the alias Marina Novikova; Misha Bayramov; Valerian Gigauri; Giorgi Gotman; and Ketevan Malashkhia, who allegedly used the alias Ashley Moriarty. According to Monitor, Malashkhia is a cousin of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife. The outlet also identified a Belarusian citizen, Lita, who had previously denied working at the call centre.

The journalists also say they identified security staff at the new office who had previously been seen outside AK Group’s former premises. They named former law enforcement officer Manuchar Gegia and former Zugdidi traffic police chief Levan Gogia.

According to the outlet, the office on Mirian Mepe Street closed after it announced the publication of its latest investigation. Both floors of the building are now being offered for rent.

Monitor says the premises had been leased since 2022 by RTM Imports, a company owned by Irakli Kvlividze, the brother of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife.

The journalists say they informed the Prosecutor’s Office on 1 July 2026 that AK Group’s managers and employees had been regularly operating from the office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street. According to Monitor, prosecutors have not clarified whether they investigated the information or whether the inquiry into the alleged fraud is still ongoing.

Background

In 2025, Monitor and more than 32 international media organisations published an investigation into AK Group’s activities. According to the report, the group employed 85 people and defrauded more than 6,100 people across Europe and Canada between 2022 and 2025. The journalists estimated that the operation generated more than $35 million in revenue over that period.

After the investigation was published, law enforcement authorities opened a criminal inquiry into organised fraud and the laundering of proceeds from crime on an especially large scale. Prosecutors have charged 11 people in the case.

In a separate bribery case, authorities also arrested former Georgian State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. Prosecutors accuse him, in one of the counts, of providing protection to the call centres. A court has also frozen the assets and company shares of the alleged organisers and employees of the call centre network.

Investigation continues

According to Monitor, the Prosecutor’s Office told the outlet that it had requested legal assistance from Germany to help identify potential victims. Prosecutors also said they had sought additional information from journalists involved in the investigation, but claimed they had declined to cooperate.

In a written response, the Prosecutor’s Office said that “the final decision in the case largely depends on information and materials to be obtained from abroad through legal assistance.”

A separate Monitor investigation found that Akaki Kevkhishvili and Meri Shotadze had previously worked at another call centre, 100 Marketing Solutions. Authorities began investigating the company in 2023 and froze its shares as part of the inquiry. However, a court lifted the freeze in 2026.

Are Georgian scam call centres still operating?

World.title: Armenia approves new government as Pashinyan promises appointments based on merit
World.content:
Armenia approves new government

Alongside the opening of Armenia‘s 9th parliamentary term, the country formed a new government. In line with the constitution, Nikol Pashinyan took office as prime minister. He headed the electoral list of the Civil Contract party, which won a parliamentary majority.

The party submitted the required nomination documents for its leader to President Vahagn Khachaturyan, who then signed a decree appointing Pashinyan as prime minister.

On the previous day, at the proposal of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and by decree of President Vahagn Khachaturyan, Deputy Prime Ministers Mher Grigoryan and Tigran Khachatryan were reappointed to their posts.

Most cabinet ministers were also reappointed.

Changes were made in the prime minister’s office. Former chief adviser to the prime minister and former Armenian ambassador to the United States, Lilit Makunts, has been appointed chief of staff. Her predecessor, Araik Harutyunyan, became an MP with the ruling Civil Contract faction on August 2.

At the same time, Pashinyan announced that he plans to appoint graduates of leading universities from around the world, selected through the government’s talent pool, to senior positions in the government.

“You will soon see these decisions implemented in practice,” the prime minister said.

Almost all ministers kept their portfolios

At Prime Minister Pashinyan’s recommendation, the following ministers retained their posts:

Defence – Suren Papikyan,

Internal Affairs – Arpine Sargsyan,

Foreign Affairs – Ararat Mirzoyan,

Territorial Administration and Infrastructure – David Khudatyan,

Environment – Hambardzum Matevosyan,

Health – Anahit Avanesyan,

Education, Science, Culture and Sport – Zhanna Andreasyan,

Justice – Srbuhi Galyan,

Labour and Social Affairs – Arsen Torosyan,

Economy – Gevorg Papoyan,

Finance – Vahe Hovhannisyan.

Only High-Tech Industry Minister Mkhitar Hayrapetyan did not keep his post. Pashinyan had previously said that Hayrapetyan himself had decided to step down.

David Tadevosyan replaced him. The prime minister introduced the new minister to ministry staff today. Mkhitar Hayrapetyan also attended the meeting. He said he would remain available around the clock if the new minister or his team needed advice.

“I am ready to contribute my modest knowledge and experience whenever you feel the need,” the former minister said.

David Tadevosyan graduated from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia. Between 2012 and 2014, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned a Master of Science in Engineering and Management.

Before taking up the ministerial post, Tadevosyan served as acting director of International Radio Network CJSC. Between 2024 and 2025, he headed Afeyan Initiatives for Armenia, an organisation founded by Armenian-American businessman, scientist and philanthropist Noubar Afeyan. Earlier in his career, Tadevosyan worked for the mining company Vallex Group, the Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Chemical Technologies, and SberSpinoff.

More than 1,000 applications for the government’s talent pool

On 15 June, shortly after his Civil Contract party won the 2026 parliamentary elections, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan invited graduates of the world’s leading universities to join the government. He encouraged them to put their knowledge and professional experience to work in public administration.

Today, the prime minister said the initiative had attracted strong interest, with the government receiving 1,141 applications.

“Following the initial screening, 459 candidates – around 40% of all applicants – advanced to the second stage. The average age of the candidates is 34,” Pashinyan said.

The prime minister announced that the government would create a talent pool based on interview results and professional assessments. Officials will match the selected candidates’ education, work experience and professional skills with the specific needs of the public administration system.

He added that candidates included in the talent pool could receive offers for positions in the public sector or other forms of cooperation during the course of this year.

Armenia approves new government

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘It’s important to understand what kind of hell government is leading us into’
World.content:
Lasha Tugushi, head of the Liberal Academy, has commented on Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s claim that Georgian politicians have never used harsher rhetoric towards Russia than they do today, either before or after the 2008 war. Tugushi argues that the prime minister is repeating a familiar narrative promoted by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

According to Tugushi, the government is trying to present itself as the only force capable of “saving” the country, while linking the events of 2008 and 2022 forms part of that political strategy.

According to Tugushi, the suggestion that Georgia was ever pro-Russian is “nonsense”, as portraying Russia in a positive light has always been regarded as shameful in Georgian society.

Earlier, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement linking the war in Ukraine to Georgia’s domestic politics and the country’s opposition. According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Lasha Tugushi said: “Anti-Russian sentiment existed in Georgia long before this. I remember the 1990s, when hostility towards Russia was very strong. The same was true after the war in Abkhazia. I cannot agree with the prime minister’s view that the key turning points were 2008 and 2022.

“I do not remember Georgia ever being pro-Russian. That is nonsense. What’s more, in respectable society it has always been considered shameful to say that Russia is a good country or to speak positively about Russian symbols.

“As for the focus on 2008 and 2022, that is part of a political game in which the leaders of Georgian Dream repeat a familiar narrative: that there is only one benevolent political force capable of saving Georgia – Georgian Dream. Everyone else, they claim, is either an enemy or a traitor seeking to drag the country into a devastating war.”

“But let’s remember who suspended Georgia’s EU integration, who is pursuing an anti-European policy today, who is confronting the ambassadors of Western countries, the European Parliament and the OSCE, who is picking fights with Sweden and France. Who came up with the scare story about the ‘deep state’? Georgian Dream did all of that.

“That does not mean the previous government made no mistakes or that everything was perfect. We need to understand that politics cannot be viewed in black-and-white terms. Things should be called by their proper names. The previous government has plenty of its own sins, and it paid the price for them. But today we see countries that were once on a par with Georgia moving closer to EU membership, while we, instead of advancing towards integration, are drifting further away from the West.”

“There are two main pillars on which the current government relies.

The first is fear – the claim that enemies want to open a second front in Georgia.

The second is the argument that our Georgian identity is under threat.

These are the two narratives they use to frighten people and rely on a fearful public in order to remain in power indefinitely.

But the fact is that they are not succeeding in their campaign against democracy to the extent they would like. It is crucial to see clearly what kind of hell this government is leading us into and what it actually looks like.

Over the past few years, Georgian Dream has taken many steps backwards and not a single step forward. This is an anti-national path. It is building authoritarianism and working against the Georgian people. I have many questions. For example, can Georgian Dream correct the grave mistakes it has made? I would like to believe it can find that path and that at least something will change.”

On Georgian Dream’s policies

World.title: Queensland builder fined over rust-coloured canal pollution
World.content:
Monique Luchterhand and her family have always enjoyed fishing and catching crabs in the waterways outside their Palm Beach home.

Now, they are too worried to eat anything they catch.

For the past six months, an orange stain in the canal has left residents questioning what is flowing into one of the Gold Coast's most prized waterways.

"We recently got a tinny, and it's completely stained the base of it," Ms Luchterhand said.

"We thought it was just mud and just that naturally occurring discolouration but then noticed it wasn't going away — it just looks horrible.

"We've tried pressure-hosing it, but it's not coming off."

Monique Luchterhand says the pollution has stained their tinny. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

The Luchterhands live on a canal near Tahiti Avenue and Seventh Avenue at Palm Beach, where the orange staining has also appeared along the banks.

"My son still fishes, but we don't let him eat what he catches anymore. He just catches them for fun and puts them back," Ms Luchterhand said.

" It's definitely something we have to be conscious of … because you just worry about what the contamination is. "

Ms Luchterhand said residents were left in the dark about the cause of the discolouration and had not yet been notified by the Gold Coast council.

Residents say they have yet to be notified by the council of the cause of the pollution. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

In July, a City of Gold Coast spokesperson told the ABC the canal discolouration had been caused by dewatering from a nearby construction site on Sixth Avenue.

Dewatering is the process of removing groundwater from a construction site to dry out the area so work can be carried out safely.

Last Friday, the council said it had fined Brisbane-based builder LPS Group.

"The city has been working closely with the party responsible and has issued a penalty infringement notice (PIN) totalling $17,270, as well as an enforcement notice," a council spokesperson said.

"City officers continue to monitor the site and undertake water-quality testing to ensure any discharged water complies with relevant approvals and conditions."

The council spokesperson said it had already issued eight PINs for development-related water-quality offences across the city this year.

Sherpa Group's development on Sixth Avenue in Palm Beach. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

Improvements being made

LPS Group is the builder contracted by Gold Coast developer Sherpa Group to deliver its $67 million luxury apartment project at 7–9 Sixth Avenue.

Sherpa Group founder Christie Leet said it was working with its builder, LPS Group, to improve its dewatering processes.

"We are aware of a small number of complaints in relation to the discharge of treated underground water from our site entering Tallebudgera Creek via Seventh Avenue," Mr Leet said.

"We wish to convey to the community that the dewatering discharge test results remain compliant.

"However, as an added measure we have asked our builder for extra dewatering tanks to be installed onsite with more routine cleaning of the tanks beyond what is required under the management plan."

Mr Leet said the company had been in "detailed discussions" with City of Gold Coast to ensure its dewatering program continued to comply with local laws.

"Dewatering occurs on every development site on the Gold Coast, and we are committed to ensuring the highest standard of water management across the projects we deliver," he said.

"We are aware of some discolouration of sand within a local canal and are working closely with council to improve the aesthetics of this."

LPS Group did not respond to the ABC's request for comment.

Expert urges caution

Griffith University water scientist Matthew Currell said the reddish water could occur when iron sulphides in the ground were exposed to oxygen during dewatering.

"When you dewater the sub-surface, often you're exposing sediments to oxygen for the first time in a very long time," Professor Currell said.

" That will often lead to the oxidation of metals like iron, which gives the water its reddish colour. "

Matthew Currell says the discolouration occurs when iron is exposed to oxygen. (Four Corners: Maddy King)

He said the discolouration could also be an early warning sign that acid sulphate soils, a common issue along Australia's east coast, had been disturbed.

"When those sulphides get exposed to air, they release not just iron, but also it can sometimes lead to acidic run-off, which can then mobilise other metals into the water and cause environmental harm," he said.

While Professor Currell said he had not reviewed the canal's water-quality data and could not say whether that process was occurring in this case, he said the Gold Coast was a recognised risk area.

"I'd be very careful about getting in the water if it is discoloured like that," he said.

Ms Luchterhand said she understood there was a strong need for development to cater to the city's growing population but urged the council to ensure there were strict processes in place to stop pollution from entering the city's waterways.

"The waterways are part of the reason why people want to live here so it's really important that council stay on top of that and keep them clean and pure for us all to enjoy," she said.

World.title: Farmers welcome barn owl baby boom after mouse plague
World.content:
Farmers and wildlife groups have reported an increase in barn owl sightings in Western Australia's Midwest and Wheatbelt regions.

Experts suspect the area's recent mouse plague has caused a spike in owls, which are fledging at this time of the year.

Barn owl boom

Chapman Valley hobby farmer Melanie Pugh discovered seven baby barn owl chicks inside a grain silo on her property last month.

A Howatharra hobby farmer discovered young barn owls inside a silo in July. (Supplied: Melanie Pugh)

Ms Pugh said the baby birds were fed by their parent for a few weeks before they fledged one by one.

"I did a bit of research about owls, because I'd heard that it's rare to have big clutches," Ms Pugh said.

"Apparently seven is extremely rare unless the food is plentiful."

Ms Pugh said the presence of the owls coincided with a notable drop in mice on the property, which had been inundated amid a plague earlier this year.

The farmer had been trapping about 150 mice each day in May, which reduced to about 10 mice each day by late July.

The presence of barn owls coincided with a notable drop in mice at a Midwest property.

"In my research, it said the mother owl has to feed each chick five mice a night, plus herself, for 10 weeks," she said.

"It's nice to have owls, because they're rare and they're beautiful."

Meanwhile, wildlife group Carnaby's Crusaders has reported an "explosion" of barn owls breeding in artificial hollows near Moora, in WA's Wheatbelt.

Dean Arthurell said four clutches were recorded on a recent visit, each with three to five eggs or nestlings, which indicated an abundance of food.

Barn owls were discovered breeding and hatching in artificial hollows near Moora, in WA's Wheatbelt. (Supplied: Dean Arthurell)

"There's a dramatic increase in food resources, so the barn owls are really making the most of it," he said.

"They are finding habitat in proximity to said food source, being the increase in rodents that we're seeing through the wheatbelt."

The nesting boxes had been installed to assist endangered Carnaby's cockatoos, but Mr Arthurell said the barn owls were welcome visitors.

"The owls are well and truly through their breeding process, so we hope for the most part that these guys will largely be done by the time that Carnaby's are ready to investigate and lay," he said.

Barn owls eggs were discovered in artificial bird boxes in the Wheatbelt. (Supplied: Dean Arthurell)

Barn owls are the most widespread terrestrial bird, occurring on every continent except Antarctica.

They are known to experience booms and busts in population depending on food availability.

The Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions said it did not have any programs that record barn owl numbers and was not aware of any recent increase in activity.

However, several more wildlife groups in the Midwest and Wheatbelt said increasing numbers of barn owls were being brought to them and spotted in the environment, which they linked to the mouse plague.

Morawa's worst-ever mouse plague leaves streets covered in mice A farming town in Western Australia is battling an unprecedented mouse plague that is damaging crops and contaminating homes and businesses, while raising serious health and economic concerns in the community.

"When there's a huge smorgasbord of food, you're going to find that these birds of prey are going to have two clutches of chicks that year, because they have the food out there," wildlife carer Michelle Jones said.

Bait-use falling

Ms Jones said a drop in the use of an owl-killing rodenticide in recent years may also have contributed to the apparent surge in owl numbers.

A barn owl has made itself at home in Walkaway, Geraldton. (Supplied: Katie Anne Thoars)

Ms Jones said following an awareness campaign by advocates, large portions of the community had switched out deadly second-generation anticoagulant poisons for owl-safe mice baits and traps.

"Not many chicks came through in 2024," she said.

"Now we've had this huge turnaround with people using safer options."

However, raptor carer Janelle Ende warned the barn owl boom would be followed by intense competition for food and habitat.

Ms Ende, who runs wildlife rehabilitation organisation Just Raptors, said she expected a rise in starving and displaced juveniles, which would likely end up in the wrong place or being harassed by other bird species.

Raptor rehabilitator Janelle Ende has three barn owls in her care, and expects more to come. (Supplied: Janelle Ende)

She said mice had stopped breeding as temperatures dropped during winter and numbers would continue to decline.

"You always see this after a mouse plague. You get birds handed in [to wildlife rehabilitators]," Ms Ende said.

She said anyone who sees a barn owl in the wrong place should not disturb it and alert a local wildlife carer who can assess it.

She said anyone wanting to encourage owls to their property can install a home-made owl box.

World.title: Austria hits record temps, wildfires in Greece, Albania as Europe feels heat
World.content:
The temperature in Austria reached a record high on Wednesday, while Hungarians were asked to curb their power use as the latest heatwave and drought took their toll on central and southern Europe.

Europe, the world's fastest-warming continent, has been ravaged by record-breaking heat and destructive wildfires this summer, with France and Spain particularly hard hit in recent weeks.

The focus of the heatwave has now shifted further east, with Albanian emergency services battling a wildfire in the southern region of Mallakaster.

Italy also placed its major cities under a red heat alert as temperatures climbed to around 40 degrees Celsius in some areas.

Tourists in Rome huddle together in the shade amid sweltering conditions in the Italian capital. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

The heat prompted the Vatican to move Pope Leo's first weekly general audience after the July break indoors, rather than hold it in St Peter's Square.

Visitors to Rome welcomed the decision as they sought relief from the sweltering conditions.

"I suppose it's better to hold it indoors because of the heat," said Diego Amaya, a tourist from Mexico.

Austria hits record high temp again

The temperature hit a record 41.2C in the Austrian town of Bad Deutsch-Altenburg near the border with Slovakia, national weather service GeoSphere Austria said. The previous record of 41C was set on Tuesday in nearby Vienna.

Across the border in Hungary, companies and households cut power consumption this week after a government appeal to ease pressure on the grid amid the severe drought. The capital, Budapest, is set to face the peak of the heatwave over the next two days, with temperatures already rising close to 40C on Wednesday.

A government official distributes bagged water to pedestrians in Budapest on Sunday. (MTI via AP Photo: Zsolt Szigetvary)

Dwindling water levels on the Danube have forced Hungary to largely shut down its sole nuclear plant, which uses the river's waters for cooling, creating an energy crisis that has stretched power supply capacity to its limits.

The Danube river is so low that Nazi warships are emerging Europe's second-longest river is carrying less water than it has in decades, revealing shipwrecks and shutting down nuclear reactors.

Slovenia's only nuclear power plant, Krsko, which supplies neighbouring Croatia as well, said on Wednesday it would begin reducing reactor output overnight due to exceptionally high temperatures and low flows on the Sava River, which flows into the Danube.

The plant will initially cut generation to 80 per cent of capacity.

Further west, water levels on the Rhine River in Germany have hit new lows, with some cargo services stopping and other sailings continuing, but with greatly reduced loads.

The Rhine is a route for commodities, including grains, ores and petrol.

Wildfires burn in Albania, Greece

In Albania's southern Mallakaster region, wildfires forced the evacuation of about 15 families along with their livestock and pets, while ground and aerial crews fought to stop the flames reaching homes near a village.

Efforts continued to tame another wildfire, likely caused by lightning, in rocky, mountainous terrain south of the Albanian city of Gjirokaster.

In neighbouring Greece, a wildfire, possibly caused by vibrating electricity conductors and fanned by gale-force winds, has burned thousands of hectares of farmland near a popular holiday destination north-west of Athens.

The blaze appeared largely contained on Wednesday, but hundreds of firefighters remained in the area to prevent flare-ups as six helicopters doused scattered smoking spots.

Greek firefighters approach towering flames on Mount Kithairon, north-west of Athens. (AP Photo: Petros Giannakouris)

In Moldova, where temperatures are likely to hit 38C on Thursday with no rain expected, President Maia Sandu urged residents to cut electricity use during evening peak hours and to conserve water.

"It is one thing to water your vegetable garden, quite another your lawn," Ms Sandu said on a podcast.

" Having no water in [Moldova's capital] Chișinău for several days would be a real catastrophe. I hope it won't come to that. "

Prime Minister Vasile Tofan told Moldovan television that neighbouring Ukraine was unable to provide power at agreed rates and Romania was also unable to supply it, even at three times the price at peak hours.

The hot, dry summer is also having a worrying impact on agriculture.

Britain's cereal harvest is on track to be the worst since comparable records began in 1984, according to an analysis published on Wednesday, as crops wither after one of the driest and hottest spring-summer periods on record.

Reuters

World.title: Vollering win sets up three-way Tour de France Femmes fight
World.content:
Dutch rider Demi Vollering won a sprint finish against her two main rivals to take stage five of the Tour de France Femmes, with Switzerland's Marlen Reusser coming in second to hold on to the overall lead.

Poland's Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) looked to have stolen a march with 300 metres remaining, but Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) took off in pursuit and hit the front close to the line.

"I knew Kasia would go early, because she always does," Vollering said after Wednesday's win.

"I knew Marlen would gamble, so I let her gamble a bit to try and make her work, but she didn't. I gave it everything until the final sprint, and I needed every single metre in the last finish straight."

A gruelling up-and-down 140-km ride from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais with eight categorised climbs brought the expected shake-up in the general classification, but the top two remained the same.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Reusser, who won Tuesday's individual time trial to move into yellow, holds a 12-second lead over 2023 winner Vollering, with Niewiadoma-Phinney moving up to third overall, one minute 17 seconds behind the leader.

Last year's winner Pauline Ferrand-Prévot struggled on the final climbs, and the French rider is now five minutes behind Reusser.

Mountains classification leader Puck Pieterse took maximum points on the first six climbs, and was part of a 19-rider breakaway with over 75 km remaining, but they were reeled in by the yellow-jersey group after the penultimate climb.

Niewiadoma-Phinney, the 2024 winner, appeared set to win her first Tour de France stage, but Vollering had other ideas and put in a blistering finish.

Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney have always finished on the final podium since the race began in 2022, and are well on course to do so again, with Reusser defending a slender lead with four stages left.

"Marlen has not won a Tour yet, and she will have to work for it as well. I'm sure it will be a hard battle, because she is not the rider who you can beat easily, because she is very strong," Vollering said.

Thursday's stage six is a 153.4-km hilly ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhône.

Reuters

World.title: LIV Golf secures lifeline 'lead investor' for player-driven future
World.content:
LIV Golf has secured a "lead investor" to keep the lights on, and the league will move forward with players becoming majority equity holders, chief executive Scott O'Neil has announced.

A signed agreement is in place with the unnamed investor and has been approved by the LIV Golf board, O'Neil said.

The transaction is expected to close in September. No details on the amount of capital infusion were announced.

Multiple reports said LIV Golf will return next season with 10 events: five international and five in the United States.

Dark clouds have been looming over the PGA Tour and DP World Tour rival since Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced this spring that it will stop funding the league at the end of 2026.

The PIF reportedly invested $US5 billion ($7 billion) in the project since it launched in 2022.

LIV Golf cancelled its New Orleans event in June and reportedly has nixed its season-ending team championship, scheduled for later this month in Michigan. At least one report said that the league was considering filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.

On Wednesday, local time, O'Neil said the new agreement will "play a key role in supporting the path forward for the League's next era, driven by and for the players".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We're also seeing strong interest from more than a dozen additional parties to potentially serve as minority investors, creating a multi-partner model built for long-term stability and growth," he said.

"Notably, our next chapter will make our players the majority equity holders in LIV Golf, a first for a major global sports league, and gives the League the foundation to keep growing the game worldwide. We anticipate finalising terms in the coming weeks, with the goal of entering a transaction in September.

"In the meantime, our focus is on delivering a great week for fans and players at Bedminster and finishing the 2026 season strong."

No details on the framework for the players' proposed equity stakes were provided.

Ever since the PIF pulled the financial plug, LIV Golf had been in the market for investments between $250 and $350 million, according to Sportico.

LIV Golf returns to action with its New York tournament this weekend, beginning Thursday at Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey.

Reuters

World.title: Exposure to pesticides at work could raise risk of ALS, study finds
World.content:
Workers exposed to pesticides could have up to a 70 per cent greater risk of developing the fatal motor neurone disease ALS, a study has found.

Researchers say global rates of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) have increased along with the use of pesticides, as pressures on food systems grow.

The study comes after Australia's chemical regulator brought in new restrictions on the use of the herbicide paraquat, which has previously been linked to Parkinson's disease.

Men who have been exposed to pesticides at work may be twice as likely to develop the disease as those with no exposure, the scientists found after reviewing data relating to ALS.

There was no apparent increase in risk for women, according to the paper published in the international medical journal, the BMJ.

The authors said while the causes of ALS were not well understood, their results "add to the evidence suggesting that occupational exposure to pesticides may increase the risk of ALS".

Chemicals subject of lawsuits

Pesticides are a range of chemical substances used to destroy weeds, insects and other organisms such as fungi, diseases or rodents.

Farming industries such as grains and horticulture are heavily reliant on synthetic pesticides such as paraquat and glyphosate, which have been subject to scrutiny in recent decades.

Tens of thousands of lawsuits alleging links between glyphosate and cancer have been filed in the United States, while Australia's Federal Court considered a class action against Bayer, which produces the glyphosate product Roundup.

A sign warns the public that pesticides are in use. (ABC Radio Perth: Emma Wynne)

While few law courts — including the Federal Court — have found the scientific links between chemical contact and disease to be proven, dozens of countries have banned or restricted the use of glyphosate.

In June, Australia's chemical regulator announced new restrictions to the use of the herbicide paraquat, which some neurologists have linked to Parkinson's disease.

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority said "the weight of evidence does not show that paraquat exposure through approved uses increases the risk of developing Parkinson's disease".

But the regulator imposed "significant" restrictions on the pesticide's use, including lower application rates, to safeguard the environment and wildlife.

In response, major paraquat manufacturer Syngenta announced it was pulling the herbicide from sale in Australia, blaming "regulatory constraints … and [an] increasingly expensive supply chain".

Pesticides critical for agriculture

Australia's peak agriculture group says many farmers who are reliant on chemical pesticides support further health research.

Cotton is one of the most pesticide-dependent crops. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

National Farmers' Federation president Hamish McIntyre said agricultural workers were conscious of the risks of working with chemicals.

But he said farm chemicals were critical to maintain food and fibre production.

"I've been working with pesticides since the early 1980s and we've been trained appropriately and we continue to improve our skills and training with pesticides," Mr McIntyre said.

"We support continued research into all areas around pesticide application and its effectiveness, and also how it's interacting with our environment."

'Not a eureka moment'

Associate professor Rachel Tan, a motor neurone disease specialist not involved in the study published in the BMJ, said the findings supported the case that workplace pesticide exposure was linked to a higher risk of ALS.

But she said further research was needed around which specific chemicals may be responsible.

Motor neurone disease researcher Rachel Tan. (Supplied)

"The overall evidence base is not entirely consistent, some studies are finding no clear association, some studies are finding that this association is more driven by men than women," Dr Tan said.

"Some of the most important questions that we will need to find out is what components of pesticides might increase the person's risk, whether longer exposure to pesticides increased that risk further."

RMIT professor of analytical chemistry, Oliver Jones, said people "don't need to panic" over the study's findings, which he said relied on previous studies and contained no new experimental data.

He said there was "unlikely" to be a single cause of motor neurone diseases.

"While reducing exposure to pesticides is a sensible general precaution, the paper is not a eureka moment about the risks of pesticide exposure," Dr Jones said.

World.title: Some parents helping their underage kids gamble, study finds
World.content:
Parental behaviour could be a significant contributing factor in teenage gambling rates, a study has found.

According to the Australia Institute, 600,000 Australian teens below the age of 18 gamble per year and researchers from CQUniversity's Appleton Institute and Experimental Gambling Research Laboratory sought parents' perspectives.

Their findings were published in two papers: one in the International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction in 2025 and the other in the Journal of Gambling Studies in 2026.

The research showed examples of the parental facilitation of gambling, including behaviours at home that endorsed or encouraged the practice.

"These are things like parents talking about their own gambling wins, asking their teenager to pick numbers for the Lotto or Keno," author Cassy Dittman said.

"It was even things like putting on a bet for their teenager for sports or racing events, or even allowing the teenagers to use their own online account to gamble.

"And that was something we found was relatively common among parents."

Cassie Dittman says her research shows parental facilitation is a major factor in rates of adolescent gambling. (Supplied: CQUniversity)

Dr Dittman said the key finding was that the more parents engaged in facilitative behaviours, the more likely teens were to gamble and go on to display risky or problem levels of gambling.

"That parental facilitation gambling came out above and beyond as the strongest factor in predicting adolescent gambling problems," she said.

"Just how strong that effect was was really surprising."

Morgan Harrington says parental attitudes to illegal teenage gambling speaks to the broader normalisation of the practice. (Supplied: Australia Institute)

Poor regulation leading to 'normalisation'

Australia Institute research manager Morgan Harrington, who published a paper in 2025 on teenage gambling, said parental attitudes indicated a "broader normalisation" of gambling in Australia.

24yo who placed first bet at 15 says he's lost $900k to gambling From footy tips to Taylor Swift bets, teenagers are being lured into gambling. Almost 34 per cent of Australian teens gamble and everyone from teachers, experts, to the young people themselves are sounding the alarm.

"With the saturation level of gambling advertising that we have in Australia, and because online gambling has put a casino in every pocket, all of this contributes to a real, profound cultural shift in Australia in which gambling is coming to be seen as a normal part of everyday life," he said.

Dr Harrington said Australians were the world's most prolific gamblers. They lose $35 billion a year, not including the social and mental health costs.

"I think any notion that this is somehow part of our cultural DNA or that Australians just love a punt ignores the reality that we have some of the laxest regulations," he said.

"We've allowed a culture to evolve where people are coming to accept this as a normal part of society but, if we had stronger regulations, we might be able to claw back some of the losses."

The You win some, you lose more report was handed down in 2023 after an inquiry into online gambling and gambling harm in Australia. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

Dr Harrington said the government had failed to act on the landmark parliamentary inquiry and subsequent report, You win some, you lose more, which made 31 recommendations.

Those included a total advertising ban, the establishment of a national regulator and the prohibition of inducements "without delay".

"Until we have that kind of reform, we can only expect Australia's losses to continue to mount," Dr Harrington said.

Parents not concerned

Dr Dittman said her research showed parents knew their underage children were gambling, despite that being illegal.

"Close to 30 per cent of parents reported their adolescent was engaging in some form of monetary gambling in the past 12 months," she said.

Even kids want gambling ads banned, so why won't the government do it? The government's proposed cThe government's proposed crackdown on gambling ads doesn't go as far as most Australians want. When you run the numbers, it's a win for the betting industry.rackdown on gambling ads doesn't go as far as most Australians want. When you run the numbers, it's a win for the betting industry.

Dr Dittman said the behaviours included buying a scratchie or lotto ticket, playing poker machines and sports betting.

The research also showed parents were more concerned about bullying, mental health concerns and substance abuse issues than gambling, which ranked as being of the least concern among 11 issues.

Dr Dittman said parents gambling with their teens, or co-gambling, was happening frequently.

"Around two-thirds of parents who had gambled in the past 12 months indicated that their adolescent was present with them when they had gambled," she said.

"That's sort of suggesting to young people that gambling might be something of a social activity, potentially a harmless activity and something that might be a low-risk activity."

A spokesperson for the Department of Social Services said the government had worked with state and territory governments to introduce measures that protect children and young people.

"These include mandatory pre-verification which requires the verification of a customer’s identity when they register for any new online wagering account, before they can place a bet," they said.

"The Government has also delivered important reforms to reduce young people's exposure to gambling-like content in video games.

"A new public awareness campaign, with a focus on at-risk groups expected to include young men and teenagers, will ensure more people are better informed about the impacts of online gambling and the supports available."

World.title: Tony Burke cancelled his immigration speech. His constituents have plenty to say
World.content:
PoliticsNSWImmigration Tony Burke cancelled his immigration speech. His constituents have plenty to say Mostafa Rachwani August 6, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Steven Theodoridis is adamant: if Tony Burke goes ahead with limiting family visa applications, it’ll “wreck him”. Dressed in a Bulldogs jersey, the manager of Mastika Gelato & Cafe said that it was families that needed to stay together and be brought to Australia together, as long as it was “direct family”. Mastika Gelato and Dessert Bar manager Steven Theodoridis said “People are happier with their families around them, they work harder, and their families help their businesses … we need to be protecting families not breaking them up.” Sitthixay Ditthavong “So no extended family like cousins or in-laws. But wives, husbands, sons, daughters, sisters and brothers are OK. “People are happier with their families around them, they work harder, and their families help their businesses. I believe in families, and we need to be protecting families not breaking them up.”



Community concern comes after Burke’s speech announcing a significant immigration crackdown was delayed after cabinet ministers raised questions about the political backlash and unresolved economic costs. The policy announcement was due to focus on firmer controls of the migration system by stopping people taking advantage of it through manoeuvres such as overstaying or using the family system. There is already a heavy backlog of demand for family visas as part of the permanent visa stream, with more than 100,000 people facing a 17-month wait for partner visas. Theodoridis’ shop is in the heart of Belmore, a key suburb in Burke’s electorate of Watson, which also takes in heavily multicultural areas such as Lakemba, Bankstown and Punchbowl. These are areas with historically high levels of immigration, with a mix of recent migrants alongside families that have called the area home for generations. And Burke has depended on these residents to maintain his vice-like grip on his seat since he won it in 2004.



Burke has dominated the seat, often winning it at a canter and with double-figure margins, and very rarely facing any real threat. But his insistence on forging ahead with the immigration policy threatens his support among the many prominent migrant groups in the area. Lebanese Muslim Association general secretary Gamel Khier said the organisation was worried about the potential impacts of the policy. Burwood Road barber Ali Alekdeh said “If we don’t have immigrants, there will be no health workers, no labourers. Immigrants built this country”. Sitthixay Ditthavong “The LMA is worried that minority communities will be severely impacted by these proposed reforms. Family migration is an important hope for many Australians with family overseas,” he said. Along Burwood Road, many businesses and residents expressed some doubts about the policy, with barber Ali Alekdeh adamant Burke was making a mistake.



“If we don’t have immigrants, there will be no health workers, no labourers. Immigrants built this country, they are taxi drivers and Uber drivers. Who will be around? Hospitals will fall apart without immigrants.” Alekedeh insisted the system was working as intended and that a political focus on immigration was “a fake problem”. “They come here, they pay taxes, they buy houses, they do everything by the rules. What’s the problem? Pauline Hanson is just playing with his (Burke’s) head.” “It’s a bullshit issue. There’s never enough immigrants. They (the government) just need to relax.” He wasn’t alone in expressing concern at how the government’s clampdown would impact small businesses. Across the road, at newly opened restaurant Rusty’s, owner Melike Kaya said she struggled to hire workers.



“I have tried to get local workers, it isn’t for the lack of trying. I tried, but the majority of the applicants aren’t locals. They’re recent migrants. They’ve come here looking for a better life, so what happens when that stops?” Kaya, a Liberal voter, was cooking a pasta sauce as she said she also felt that locals would likely be “upset” with Burke for pursuing the policy, and that it could change their vote. Owner of Rusty’s restaurant, Melike Kaya, says of Labor: “As a small business owner, I think that they make it harder and harder for us to actually thrive”. Sitthixay Ditthavong “They promise a whole bunch, and then I don’t see them deliver what they promise. And I think that, as a small business owner, I think that they make it harder and harder for us to actually thrive,” she said of Labor. “They don’t stick to their word.”



She wasn’t alone in voicing her concern at the impact immigration was having, with another business owner saying “screening” needed to improve. The business owner, who asked to remain anonymous so she could speak freely, claimed migrants were exploiting the goodwill of the Australian government. Related Article Immigration Needs work: Burke’s plans for migration overhaul delayed due to cabinet questions “I’m a second generation wog, and my parents built this country, and I hate what is happening to Australia,” she said. “People are coming here, and they aren’t assimilating, they isolate themselves and aren’t part of the community. “Australia needs to be respected as a country,” she went on. “Australia is a Christian country in the end, and we should be independent of other countries and their dramas.”



“Labor needs to dig deeper into who they are bringing to this country. It hurts watching all this fall apart.”

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Coalition will force Albanese to cede ground on gambling reforms; Government looks to crack down on illegal e-bikes
World.content:
Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said national cabinet would continue to discuss data centre policy, but the federal government would ultimately set energy reforms with or without state consent.

Bowen laid down the law to the states and territories at the National Press Club yesterday, saying: “The Commonwealth will not be standing by and letting a race to the bottom of states falling over themselves to attract data centres at the cost to household bills, reliability, or emissions.

The Queensland and Northern Territory governments have objected to requiring data centres to fully offset their electricity use with investments in renewable energy.

“I always prefer to work with my state and territory colleagues. Always have had excellent relations with Coalition ministers at the state level in New South Wales and Tasmania, for example,” Bowen told Radio National.

“And where a state or territory says, ‘Look, we agree with most of what you’re trying to do here, but you know, we’d rather do it this way’, [I] always try and find a way to accommodate and find consensus, and that’s always been my approach. But what we’re not going to do is let one state or one territory dictate to the rest of the Commonwealth or the other states.”

World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip, Wall Street steady as oil slides on Hormuz deal hopes; SpaceX tumbles Damian Troise Updated August 6, 2026 — 6:32am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Stocks meandered to a mixed finish on Wall Street and remained close to their records, while oil prices held steady. The uncertain trading on Wall Street followed two days of big gains that gave the week and August a strong start. Several big technology companies slumped, though, ultimately weighing down the market. Relief washed over global markets after Trump said the US and Iran held productive talks – but it was short-lived. Bloomberg The S&P 500 fell 12.97 points, or 0.2 per cent, to close at 7,723.55. The index spent most of the day higher after surging to a record on Tuesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 263.24 points, or 0.5 per cent, to 54,349.12, reaching another record. The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a dip of 6 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.9 per cent on Wednesday to close at a record high. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.60¢. “The coiled spring investors have been waiting for has finally released, with the S&P 500 Index surging to record highs for the first time in two months,” said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, in a report.



Related Article Opinion

Aviation Jetstar really wants to charge you for everything but the seat Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation The Nasdaq fell 221.55 points, or 0.8 per cent, to 26,363.44. The index was weighed down by big technology companies losing ground, including a 4 per cent drop for Google’s parent company, Alphabet, and a 1.1 per cent drop for Microsoft. Uncertainty about the direction of the US war with Iran continues hanging over the market. President Donald Trump said a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could come as early as Wednesday. But there have been many stops and starts during the five-month old conflict that has stifled the global supply of oil and rattled energy markets. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 0.1 per cent to $US79.45 a barrel. Oil prices have been swinging for months and were as high as $US102 per barrel at one point during the conflict, jolting already stubbornly high inflation. Higher oil prices pushed gasoline prices higher and increased shipping costs for a wide range of products. Wall Street has been generally rising as companies head into the closing stretch of their latest round of earnings reports with sharp overall gains. Three-quarters of the companies within the S&P 500 have reported results so far, and Wall Street expects profit growth of 50 per cent when they are all finished.



The Walt Disney Co. rose 3.6 per cent after easily beating Wall Street’s profit forecasts, helped by a $US1 billion ($1.4 billion) box office haul from Toy Story 5 and theme park revenue. Booking Holdings jumped 6.6 per cent after reporting that strong travel demand drove profit and revenue growth during its most recent quarter. Elon Musk’s SpaceX fell 13.6 per cent following the release late of its first quarterly report as a public company, which showed that it sharply boosted spending on artificial intelligence. The company did help give semiconductor giant Nvidia a 3.4 per cent boost after announcing it would exclusively use that company’s chips for its artificial intelligence technology. That announcement weighed on Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 7 per cent. Musk had previously said that SpaceX and his electric vehicle company, Tesla, would use chips from both Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia. Treasury yields slipped in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 4.61 per cent from 4.63 per cent from late Tuesday.



European markets were mixed. Strong corporate profits and expectations for more growth ahead have been steering stocks higher. Wall Street has also been worried about stock prices becoming unjustifiably high, especially within the technology sector and for companies focused on artificial intelligence. Profit growth, especially for some of the big chipmakers, like Nvidia, could help justify some of the big investments those companies are making in AI. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Burning billions: SpaceX’s sales are soaring, but its spending even more so Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist AI-focused companies, with their big market values, have been behind many of the big market swings and most of Wall Street’s gains. “The market appears to be moving from rewarding companies for AI spending to assessing the revenue and earnings that these investments can generate,” said Brian Therien, analyst, investment strategy, at Edward Jones, in a report.



Inflation concerns have been hanging over markets and the Federal Reserve. The central bank has been holding its key benchmark rate steady as it monitors the costs and the impact on the economy. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise rates at least once before the end of 2026. Household spending remains resilient, despite the stress from higher costs on everything from gas to groceries. The jobs market has been one of the stronger areas of the economy, though growth has been slowing. Wall Street will get another update on Friday with the monthly employment report for July.
