World.title: After 30 years of ‘magic’ with Tina Fey, Tracy Morgan says this will be their greatest trick
World.content:
The spotlight is squarely on Tracy Morgan in The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tracy Morgan is experiencing déjà vu. Twenty years ago, he was playing Tracy Jordan – an erratic, child-at-heart celebrity who causes chaos on Tina Fey’s hit sitcom 30 Rock. Now he’s acting in another eccentric comedy backed by the same creative heavyweight. Only this time, the spotlight is squarely on him. Related Article ★★★★

Review Loved 30 Rock? This cracker new comedy is the 2026 equivalent The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins, a new mockumentary sitcom, reunites Morgan with 30 Rock writers Robert Carlock and Sam Means as showrunners, and Fey as executive producer. The comedian plays the titular star, a disgraced former pro footballer who hires a washed-up documentary director (Daniel Radcliffe) to film his life in a bid to redeem his reputation. Replete with absurdist one-liners and mad-cap pop culture references, it’s like watching an updated version of 30 Rock. But what about the man behind these characters? As culture writer Nell Geraets learnt in this conversation, he’s just as eccentric. Despite 30 Rock being regarded as one of the greatest sitcoms of all time, he now has his sights set even higher. NG: The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins has reconnected you with many of the creators and writers of 30 Rock – Sam Means, Robert Carlock and Tina Fey (the latter two who you also worked with a decade prior on Saturday Night Live). What was it like creating comedy with them again? TM: We’ve always made beautiful music together. That’s my family, and we get each other’s voices. They get my voice, and they know exactly how to put me in a position to win. I love the things they have me saying. All of them are pure masterminds … It’s a labour of love. We’ve been proven to do great work together. Loading



This show does feel like a blast from the past. It has been 13 years since the 30 Rock finale aired. There used to be waves of network sitcoms, but they’re much rarer these days. Did it feel like you were filling a gap in the market by making Reggie Dinkins? I felt that immediately. When we first started this project, I just wanted to do good old-fashioned TV, and have everyone put something out there that everyone in the household can just watch together – put the phones down, let’s just watch some good old-fashioned TV like we used to. The cast of 30 Rock (from left): Tina Fey, Jack McBrayer, Jane Krakowski, Alec Baldwin and Tracy Morgan. But the industry’s obviously changed a lot since 30 Rock aired. Did you notice any differences between making a sitcom today versus making one in the 2000s? I didn’t look at it like that. I didn’t see any difference. I said, ‘Let’s do the same formula, but let’s just update it’. And look what we’ve done. Nothing’s changed. You still like this? You like Reggie Dinkins just like you like 30 Rock? [Reporter nods, and Morgan relaxes into his seat, satisfied] There you go … It’s humanity. Nothing’s changed. ‘Tracy Jordan took me to the moon. Reggie Dinkins is going to take me to Mars.’ Tracy Morgan So many people know you as the hilariously out-of-touch Tracy Jordan from 30 Rock. What impact would you say that role has had on your career?



Tracy Jordan took me to the moon. Reggie Dinkins is going to take me to Mars. People used to refer to me as Tracy Jordan, now they’re referring to me as Reggie Dinkins. He’s a pretty funny guy. The thing that’s good about that is it’s the same sense of humour. So, you feel like Tracy Jordan sent you on a trajectory that inevitably led you to Reggie? Yes, you only get one sense of humour. You only laugh at one thing, you only laugh at one kind of funny. You don’t laugh at a million funnies. Everything ain’t funny to you, but this happens to be funny to you … Reggie Dinkins, Tracy Jordan: same one sense of humour. Before Reggie Dinkins there was 30 Rock’s Tracy Jordan (right). NBC It feels like everything Tina Fey touches turns to gold. What is it about her comedy that has managed to remain so relevant over time? She’s a very smart lady. When it comes to showbusiness, she has the Midas touch. Everybody doesn’t have the Midas touch. She has found her Nirvana. You have to find your Nirvana. Do you understand what I’m saying? Like find your peace?



Imagine. I can’t stand when somebody with no abracadabra is trying to tell me what to do with my magic. You ain’t got no abracadabra, and you’re trying to tell me what to do with my magic? I ain’t never seen you pull a bunny out no hat. [Tina’s] constantly pulling bunnies out of a hat. Magic. It’s all magic. Daniel Radcliffe, Erika Alexander and Tracy Morgan in The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins. Scott Gries/NBC You’re obviously no stranger to sitcoms, having been part of 30 Rock, The Last O.G. and so on. What drew you to the mockumentary style this time around? I just love looking down the barrel [of the camera]. I think that’s hilarious, when we’re directly in your home. And all of us know when to do it and how to do it. It makes it funnier because you [the audience] become a part of the show. One of the greatest parts of Reggie Dinkins is the dynamic between you and Daniel Radcliffe. Your characters are so different, yet they have such great chemistry. That comes from Robert [Carlock] and Tina [Fey], along their travels meeting people, and going, “hmm, how could we put this guy from the UK with this street guy from Brooklyn and make that funny?” And they did. Daniel Radcliffe and Tracy Morgan become unexpected friends in The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins. NBC



What was it like building that dynamic with Radcliffe? Chemistry, it’s all chemistry. We’re not a team; we are family. The day before we started shooting, we had dinner at my house, so everybody could hit the ground running, and everybody could be comfortable with each other. And that’s how it turned out. By the time they turned the cameras on, we were already comfortable with each other. We were already having fun. What’s your favourite thing about him? Everything. He’s the sweetest person. He’s very generous, he’s kind, he’s helpful, and he’s always right there. We can’t wait to get back to work [together] now. This season is going to be hilarious for you … The thing about Reggie Dinkins is it gets funnier and funnier. Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in August I can see how much you love this show and everyone in it. It was like that with 30 Rock. We learnt so much from Tina Fey. Everybody did their job. We’re a family.

World.title: Psychiatrists cast doubt on court secrecy orders that protect accused
World.content:
NationalJustice Psychiatrists cast doubt on court secrecy orders that protect accused Wendy Tuohy and Erin Pearson August 6, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is no way to reliably predict the risk to the mental health of accused people from media reporting of their cases, senior psychiatrists say, as community disquiet about “psychological safety”-based secrecy orders grows. The psychiatrists say mental health clinicians cannot forecast potential behaviour, including self-harm or suicide, and that the reports relied upon by judges when considering suppression applications are inexact at best. Last December The Age obtained a document circulating among barristers that offers advice on how to get suppression orders and what to ask psychiatrists to include. Michael Howard/Jessica Shapiro Specialists including Melbourne University Professor Steve Ellen say it is virtually impossible to discern between the impact of the general stress of appearing in court as an accused and the stress of publication as part of Australia’s open justice system. “Predicting suicide is incredibly hard, it is an extremely rare event [per capita] and the list of risk factors is long; the ability to quantify the risk of suppression over disclosure, versus all the other risks, is minimal,” Ellen said. “It is not even close to an exact science.”



Ellen, the former head of general hospital and emergency psychiatry at The Alfred hospital, said that while psychiatrists may reasonably conclude a person is vulnerable, “it is far harder to say that naming them, rather than the prosecution itself, is the decisive additional factor”. Related Article Courts Melbourne businessman found guilty of rape, but his name remains a secret “We are relying on a very uncertain art to inform the courts, and this uncertain art is being used to undermine one of the key principles of justice.” The comments come as the identities of alleged perpetrators in several prominent rape or sexual assault cases have successfully argued for suppression of their identities for significant periods. Tom Silvagni, son of football great Stephen Silvagni, had rape proceedings suppressed for 18 months before he was was found guilty of two counts in late 2025 – after which the gag order was lifted.



The name of Ralph Carr, a celebrity agent found guilty of rape on July 28, was suppressed for more than three years to protect his pyschological safety. He was found to have raped a 27-year-old woman who wanted to work for him and the suppression order was lifted on Monday. Loading The identity of a Melbourne doctor accused of filming women and children naked in showers at the Harold Holt Swim Centre in Glen Iris was suppressed for three months after he argued that publication would harm the mental health of his child. Ellen said “at least two-thirds of defendants would have some mental health issues caused by the court experience”, but this did not mean they should win a suppression order. He first raised his concerns in a Substack post in March, when Monash University research revealed that 521 court suppression orders had been granted in Victoria in 2023.



A senior psychiatrist, who cannot be named because of the office he holds, also questioned psychiatry’s ability to reliably predict any added impact for defendants from being named, or any behavioural flow-ons. Related Article Courts Doctor charged with filming naked pool patrons wins three-month secrecy order “Most of medical science is not an exact science, and psychiatry is the least exact science when it comes to [predicting outcomes],” he said. “Almost 100 per cent of well settled people with no mental health issues when they commit a crime could go to court and say, ‘this is stressful, and my information should be suppressed’,” he said. This was not a basis for suppression, he said, “because everybody gets stressed going to court. Even when I go to court as an expert witness, I get stressed.”



Related Article Exclusive

Press freedom Court secrecy rules to be reviewed over suppression order complaints The expert said suppressing names of sex offenders puts community members at potential risk. Melbourne University Law School Associate Professor Jason Bosland said it is difficult to challenge psychological opinions in court because of the nature of the expertise. “It is very difficult for anyone to challenge the evidence of a psychologist or a psychiatrist,” he said. “You can cross-examine them but to challenge their expert opinion and really convince the judge the psychiatrist is wrong is a really difficult thing to do. “The scales aren’t evenly balanced in terms of the way these cases play out from an evidence perspective,” he said. He agreed with Ellen that such experts were effectively providing evidence “beyond the scope of the discipline”.



“Projecting into the future as to how a person will react is … not really the purpose of psychiatry,” Bosland said. The fact “the same person is doing [the psychiatric reports] again and again” should raise alarm bells, he added. Bosland and the two psychiatrists said the appearance of special treatment was created by mental health-based suppression orders being sought and granted to well-connected clients with the means to pay for them and specialised legal counsel. Former Supreme Court Judge Betty King has come out against mental health-based court suppressions. Vince Caligiuri Bosland said it erodes the public’s faith in the justice system when a convicted rapist cannot be named, “and it creates a perception that certain people are receiving favourable treatment; that is really corrosive, and I think the courts should be concerned about that”. Last December, The Age revealed a document circulating among barristers describing how to keep high-profile clients out of the spotlight, including what to ask psychiatrists to include in reports.



Related Article Justice ‘It’s wrong’: Former judge says mental health suppression orders threaten court system Criminologist and Australian Research Council Future Fellow Professor Marie Segrave said there was a privileging of the defendant’s psychological safety over that of the victim-survivor in cases where the perpetrator’s identity was protected. She said doing so, sometimes even after conviction,“raises a lot of concerns around how the justice system is operating and also creates significant concern around justice for victim-survivors.” “This idea that people are protected who have harmed them, and been found guilty of harming them, is likely also producing significant harm, and we need to investigate this further,” Segrave said. Swinburne University law lecturer and chief executive of the Rape and Sexual Assault Research and Advocacy group, Dr Rachael Burgin, pointed out that accused rapists could ask for their names to be suppressed and then also, through defence lawyers, subpoena victims’ counselling notes.



She said the privacy imbalance amounts to “systems abuse” of victims. “In the context where victim-survivors’ counselling records are essentially public property in sex offence matters, we’re doing a lot to protect the perpetrators’ mental health, but not a lot to protect the mental health of the victim-survivor,” she said. “This isn’t justice.” Barrister Greg Barns, SC, spokesperson for the Australian Lawyers Alliance, said suppression orders more broadly were often necessary to secure a fair trial, and while there was a view that some gag orders were handed out like confetti, the reality is most cases are not subject to secrecy orders. “The reality also is that suppression orders are inevitable in a society where the media is now so all-pervasive, including highly unregulated social media,” Barns said. “It’s become unfashionable to support an accused, but they have a right to fair trial.



“Like a lot of things in our legal system, it’s a question of balance. “Whilst some people may have a concern that it seems that high-profile defendants appear to get suppression orders when others might not, the reality is that if you are high profile the chances of you being subjected to some form of harassment [are] heightened.” Barns said the media plays a crucial role in the criminal justice system, but with that role comes responsibility. But Kate Wright, chair of Sexual Assault Services Victoria, said it was already rare to get sexual assault cases to court, and a strong deterrent was the spotlight in trials on victims’ behaviour – with little concern for their mental health. Adding protection of the alleged perpetrator’s identity, based on the risk to mental health of being tried, was “incredibly off-putting for anyone considering reporting sexual assault.”



“Survivors’ mental health concerns are not given the same credence or consideration, that’s what we’re seeing,” she said. “It is really reinforcing the messages to the community around shame and blame of victim-survivors, and that we are prioritising the perpetrator above the victim-survivor. They are the last consideration when they should be the first.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: TV’s best spy drama is completely flying under the radar
World.content:
Michael Fassbender as Martian in The Agency, a spy show that gently forces us to consider America’s waning global influence.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

No one in the world loves spy dramas more than my father-in-law, a man who will only commit hours of his life to a show if someone is getting double-crossed, preferably while travelling on a fake passport to a far-flung corner of the globe. He doesn’t discriminate. Any series will do. Homeland, Slow Horses, The Americans, The Night Manager, Day of the Jackal – you name it, he’s seen it. So imagine my surprise when I asked for his thoughts on The Agency – perhaps the best spy drama on TV, which is now in its second season – and was met with nothing but a confused look. Related Article ★★★★★

Streaming Binge all six seasons of this remarkable drama while you can I peppered him with prompts: “The Agency? Michael Fassbender? A CIA agent in London? The spy show that gently forces us to consider America’s waning global influence while hinting we might be on the brink of a new world order?” He assured me he had not seen the show but would add it to the list. Sadly, this was not an isolated incident. The Agency is so successfully undercover that very few people are across it (either that, or no one pays for Paramount+). But I refuse to live in a world where The Agency flies under the radar. So, like any self-respecting CIA agent, my mission is to recruit as many assets as possible. First it was my father-in-law, and now it’s your turn. Loading What is The Agency about?



At its core, the series operates inside the paranoid, fluorescent-lit pressure cooker of London Station, the CIA’s primary European hub. Fassbender plays Brandon Colby, codename “Martian”, a senior covert operative abruptly recalled to London after six years living a double life in Ethiopia, leaving behind his married lover, Sudanese anthropologist Samia Zahir (Jodie Turner-Smith). Editor's pick Streaming On Ted Lasso, she’s ruthless. Off camera, she’s ‘quite a goofy nugget’ Promoted to deputy director of operations, Martian must navigate the psychological bends of re-entering civilian life, reconnecting with his estranged daughter and shedding his cover identity. This delicate balance unravels spectacularly when Samia, Martian’s only weak spot, turns up in London. Before long, the usually protocol-obsessed CIA agent is breaking the rules to keep the relationship alive. Beyond Martian’s personal tailspin, the walls of London Station house a network of operatives whose entire existences are defined by transactional relationships. Richard Gere brings significant heft to station chief Bosko, the man responsible for keeping the White House happy, which usually involves making sure no one dies and the mission comes in under budget (yes, even the CIA is cost-cutting). Meanwhile, Henry Ogletree (Jeffrey Wright) serves as the counter-intelligence chief and Martian’s direct boss. A lifelong agent, Ogletree is understandably suspicious of everyone and everything, all of the time. But The Agency comes into its own when dealing with the junior agents, like Danny (Saura Lightfoot-Leon), an academic recruited by Martian. Jodie Turner-Smith as Samia Zahir, Martian’s married lover, in The Agency. In many ways, Danny is an audience surrogate, curious about the CIA but naive to its inner workings. Together, the pair present as a classic case of before and after. Danny is the wide-eyed recruit convinced she can change the world, and Martian knows from brutal experience that the work only ever changes the person doing it. And rarely for the better. “People are fascinated by the kind of people that go into this line of work and what kind of people come out of it at the end,” Fassbender recently told the BBC. “Martian was once idealistic and full of hope, then his moral compass gets eroded by the things he has to do and the sacrifices that go into it.”



Editor's pick Analysis

Streaming Netflix is pumping out true-crime rubbish. It’s up to you to stop it How is this different from any other spy show? Sorry Ethan Hunt, James Bond and all the other male spies with similar-sounding names: The Agency is not a world of Aston Martins, vodka martinis and high-speed chases. Instead, the series frames contemporary espionage as a chess match fought across multiple fronts simultaneously, from African resource diplomacy to Eastern European proxy networks. Written by brothers Jez and John Butterworth (who also penned the criminally underrated 2010 political drama Fair Game), The Agency is unafraid of borrowing plot lines from the current news cycle. In season one, a CIA asset goes missing in Russian-occupied Ukraine, requiring high-level negotiations to spare his life. In season two, Danny goes undercover in Tehran to target Iranian nuclear facilities because the US government is obsessively monitoring uranium enrichment operations tied to the Fordow plant. Sound familiar? Richard Gere as Bosko, Ambreen Razia as Blair, Dominic West as the unnamed CIA Director and Jeffrey Wright as Henry in The Agency. And much like the modern geopolitical landscape, the minute one crisis is averted, another appears in its place. Much of the action takes place in situation rooms and intelligence briefings, which admittedly sounds low-energy but really isn’t.



Take it from me: watching Fassbender’s Martian unpack the importance of diplomatic plausible deniability is just as exciting as Daniel Craig emerging from the sea in Speedos. Editor's pick Review What to stream this week: A five-star post-Epstein thriller, plus five more picks French provenance, American confidence If you’ve ever watched Antiques Roadshow, you’ll know that the most valuable cultural artefacts often have a French provenance, and so it is with The Agency. The American series is a remake of Eric Rochant’s Le Bureau des Légendes (The Bureau) – available on SBS On Demand and well worth the watch – often cited as the gold standard of the genre. And when I say remake, I mean remake in the truest sense: the first season of The Agency is almost beat-for-beat the same as The Bureau. This would usually be a cause for concern, but given The Bureau boasts a 96 per cent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, the “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” approach makes sense. Richard Gere as Bosko in The Agency. Rather than coming across as a cheap Hollywood knock-off, The Agency has pulled off a rare balancing act, maintaining the original’s French sensibilities while ramping up the production values. Alex Berger, a producer of The Bureau, says the US series “respected what we did originally” while upping “the scope, the scale and the ambition”. “We did the first season for €15 million ($24.6 million) in 2013, and the first season of The Agency is over 10 times that,” he told Variety. Money well spent, I reckon.

World.title: Tony Burke cancelled his immigration speech. His constituents have plenty to say
World.content:
PoliticsNSWImmigration Tony Burke cancelled his immigration speech. His constituents have plenty to say Mostafa Rachwani August 6, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Steven Theodoridis is adamant: if Tony Burke goes ahead with limiting family visa applications, it’ll “wreck him”. Dressed in a Bulldogs jersey, the manager of Mastika Gelato & Cafe said that it was families that needed to stay together and be brought to Australia together, as long as it was “direct family”. Mastika Gelato and Dessert Bar manager Steven Theodoridis said “People are happier with their families around them, they work harder, and their families help their businesses … we need to be protecting families not breaking them up.” Sitthixay Ditthavong “So no extended family like cousins or in-laws. But wives, husbands, sons, daughters, sisters and brothers are OK. “People are happier with their families around them, they work harder, and their families help their businesses. I believe in families, and we need to be protecting families not breaking them up.”



Community concern comes after Burke’s speech announcing a significant immigration crackdown was delayed after cabinet ministers raised questions about the political backlash and unresolved economic costs. The policy announcement was due to focus on firmer controls of the migration system by stopping people taking advantage of it through manoeuvres such as overstaying or using the family system. There is already a heavy backlog of demand for family visas as part of the permanent visa stream, with more than 100,000 people facing a 17-month wait for partner visas. Theodoridis’ shop is in the heart of Belmore, a key suburb in Burke’s electorate of Watson, which also takes in heavily multicultural areas such as Lakemba, Bankstown and Punchbowl. These are areas with historically high levels of immigration, with a mix of recent migrants alongside families that have called the area home for generations. And Burke has depended on these residents to maintain his vice-like grip on his seat since he won it in 2004.



Burke has dominated the seat, often winning it at a canter and with double-figure margins, and very rarely facing any real threat. But his insistence on forging ahead with the immigration policy threatens his support among the many prominent migrant groups in the area. Lebanese Muslim Association general secretary Gamel Khier said the organisation was worried about the potential impacts of the policy. Burwood Road barber Ali Alekdeh said “If we don’t have immigrants, there will be no health workers, no labourers. Immigrants built this country”. Sitthixay Ditthavong “The LMA is worried that minority communities will be severely impacted by these proposed reforms. Family migration is an important hope for many Australians with family overseas,” he said. Along Burwood Road, many businesses and residents expressed some doubts about the policy, with barber Ali Alekdeh adamant Burke was making a mistake.



“If we don’t have immigrants, there will be no health workers, no labourers. Immigrants built this country, they are taxi drivers and Uber drivers. Who will be around? Hospitals will fall apart without immigrants.” Alekedeh insisted the system was working as intended and that a political focus on immigration was “a fake problem”. “They come here, they pay taxes, they buy houses, they do everything by the rules. What’s the problem? Pauline Hanson is just playing with his (Burke’s) head.” “It’s a bullshit issue. There’s never enough immigrants. They (the government) just need to relax.” He wasn’t alone in expressing concern at how the government’s clampdown would impact small businesses. Across the road, at newly opened restaurant Rusty’s, owner Melike Kaya said she struggled to hire workers.



“I have tried to get local workers, it isn’t for the lack of trying. I tried, but the majority of the applicants aren’t locals. They’re recent migrants. They’ve come here looking for a better life, so what happens when that stops?” Kaya, a Liberal voter, was cooking a pasta sauce as she said she also felt that locals would likely be “upset” with Burke for pursuing the policy, and that it could change their vote. Owner of Rusty’s restaurant, Melike Kaya, says of Labor: “As a small business owner, I think that they make it harder and harder for us to actually thrive”. Sitthixay Ditthavong “They promise a whole bunch, and then I don’t see them deliver what they promise. And I think that, as a small business owner, I think that they make it harder and harder for us to actually thrive,” she said of Labor. “They don’t stick to their word.”



She wasn’t alone in voicing her concern at the impact immigration was having, with another business owner saying “screening” needed to improve. The business owner, who asked to remain anonymous so she could speak freely, claimed migrants were exploiting the goodwill of the Australian government. Related Article Immigration Needs work: Burke’s plans for migration overhaul delayed due to cabinet questions “I’m a second generation wog, and my parents built this country, and I hate what is happening to Australia,” she said. “People are coming here, and they aren’t assimilating, they isolate themselves and aren’t part of the community. “Australia needs to be respected as a country,” she went on. “Australia is a Christian country in the end, and we should be independent of other countries and their dramas.”



“Labor needs to dig deeper into who they are bringing to this country. It hurts watching all this fall apart.”

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Coalition will force Albanese to cede ground on gambling reforms; Government looks to crack down on illegal e-bikes
World.content:
Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said national cabinet would continue to discuss data centre policy, but the federal government would ultimately set energy reforms with or without state consent.

Bowen laid down the law to the states and territories at the National Press Club yesterday, saying: “The Commonwealth will not be standing by and letting a race to the bottom of states falling over themselves to attract data centres at the cost to household bills, reliability, or emissions.

The Queensland and Northern Territory governments have objected to requiring data centres to fully offset their electricity use with investments in renewable energy.

“I always prefer to work with my state and territory colleagues. Always have had excellent relations with Coalition ministers at the state level in New South Wales and Tasmania, for example,” Bowen told Radio National.

“And where a state or territory says, ‘Look, we agree with most of what you’re trying to do here, but you know, we’d rather do it this way’, [I] always try and find a way to accommodate and find consensus, and that’s always been my approach. But what we’re not going to do is let one state or one territory dictate to the rest of the Commonwealth or the other states.”

An hours-long siege has ended in tragedy after a man and woman were found dead in an outback home.

Several streets in Charleville, 600 kilometres west of Toowoomba in Queensland, were thrust into lockdown after police were called to investigate reports of a serious assault at the home about 6pm on Wednesday.

Residents in a three-street block were forced to retreat into their homes for nearly eight hours as specialist police surrounded the area.

The emergency public safety declaration was revoked just before 2am on Thursday.

A 45-year-old man and a 23-year-old woman were found dead in the home.

World.title: ASX set to dip, Wall Street steady as oil slides on Hormuz deal hopes; SpaceX tumbles
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip, Wall Street steady as oil slides on Hormuz deal hopes; SpaceX tumbles Damian Troise Updated August 6, 2026 — 6:32am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stocks meandered to a mixed finish on Wall Street and remained close to their records, while oil prices held steady. The uncertain trading on Wall Street followed two days of big gains that gave the week and August a strong start. Several big technology companies slumped, though, ultimately weighing down the market. Relief washed over global markets after Trump said the US and Iran held productive talks – but it was short-lived. Bloomberg The S&P 500 fell 12.97 points, or 0.2 per cent, to close at 7,723.55. The index spent most of the day higher after surging to a record on Tuesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 263.24 points, or 0.5 per cent, to 54,349.12, reaching another record. The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a dip of 6 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.9 per cent on Wednesday to close at a record high. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.60¢. “The coiled spring investors have been waiting for has finally released, with the S&P 500 Index surging to record highs for the first time in two months,” said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, in a report.



Related Article Opinion

Aviation Jetstar really wants to charge you for everything but the seat Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation The Nasdaq fell 221.55 points, or 0.8 per cent, to 26,363.44. The index was weighed down by big technology companies losing ground, including a 4 per cent drop for Google’s parent company, Alphabet, and a 1.1 per cent drop for Microsoft. Uncertainty about the direction of the US war with Iran continues hanging over the market. President Donald Trump said a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could come as early as Wednesday. But there have been many stops and starts during the five-month old conflict that has stifled the global supply of oil and rattled energy markets. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 0.1 per cent to $US79.45 a barrel. Oil prices have been swinging for months and were as high as $US102 per barrel at one point during the conflict, jolting already stubbornly high inflation. Higher oil prices pushed gasoline prices higher and increased shipping costs for a wide range of products. Wall Street has been generally rising as companies head into the closing stretch of their latest round of earnings reports with sharp overall gains. Three-quarters of the companies within the S&P 500 have reported results so far, and Wall Street expects profit growth of 50 per cent when they are all finished.



The Walt Disney Co. rose 3.6 per cent after easily beating Wall Street’s profit forecasts, helped by a $US1 billion ($1.4 billion) box office haul from Toy Story 5 and theme park revenue. Booking Holdings jumped 6.6 per cent after reporting that strong travel demand drove profit and revenue growth during its most recent quarter. Elon Musk’s SpaceX fell 13.6 per cent following the release late of its first quarterly report as a public company, which showed that it sharply boosted spending on artificial intelligence. The company did help give semiconductor giant Nvidia a 3.4 per cent boost after announcing it would exclusively use that company’s chips for its artificial intelligence technology. That announcement weighed on Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 7 per cent. Musk had previously said that SpaceX and his electric vehicle company, Tesla, would use chips from both Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia. Treasury yields slipped in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 4.61 per cent from 4.63 per cent from late Tuesday.



European markets were mixed. Strong corporate profits and expectations for more growth ahead have been steering stocks higher. Wall Street has also been worried about stock prices becoming unjustifiably high, especially within the technology sector and for companies focused on artificial intelligence. Profit growth, especially for some of the big chipmakers, like Nvidia, could help justify some of the big investments those companies are making in AI. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Burning billions: SpaceX’s sales are soaring, but its spending even more so Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist AI-focused companies, with their big market values, have been behind many of the big market swings and most of Wall Street’s gains. “The market appears to be moving from rewarding companies for AI spending to assessing the revenue and earnings that these investments can generate,” said Brian Therien, analyst, investment strategy, at Edward Jones, in a report.



Inflation concerns have been hanging over markets and the Federal Reserve. The central bank has been holding its key benchmark rate steady as it monitors the costs and the impact on the economy. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise rates at least once before the end of 2026. Household spending remains resilient, despite the stress from higher costs on everything from gas to groceries. The jobs market has been one of the stronger areas of the economy, though growth has been slowing. Wall Street will get another update on Friday with the monthly employment report for July.
