World.title: After 30 years of ‘magic’ with Tina Fey, Tracy Morgan says this will be their greatest trick
World.content:
The spotlight is squarely on Tracy Morgan in The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tracy Morgan is experiencing déjà vu. Twenty years ago, he was playing Tracy Jordan – an erratic, child-at-heart celebrity who causes chaos on Tina Fey’s hit sitcom 30 Rock. Now he’s acting in another eccentric comedy backed by the same creative heavyweight. Only this time, the spotlight is squarely on him. Related Article ★★★★

Review Loved 30 Rock? This cracker new comedy is the 2026 equivalent The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins, a new mockumentary sitcom, reunites Morgan with 30 Rock writers Robert Carlock and Sam Means as showrunners, and Fey as executive producer. The comedian plays the titular star, a disgraced former pro footballer who hires a washed-up documentary director (Daniel Radcliffe) to film his life in a bid to redeem his reputation. Replete with absurdist one-liners and mad-cap pop culture references, it’s like watching an updated version of 30 Rock. But what about the man behind these characters? As culture writer Nell Geraets learnt in this conversation, he’s just as eccentric. Despite 30 Rock being regarded as one of the greatest sitcoms of all time, he now has his sights set even higher. NG: The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins has reconnected you with many of the creators and writers of 30 Rock – Sam Means, Robert Carlock and Tina Fey (the latter two who you also worked with a decade prior on Saturday Night Live). What was it like creating comedy with them again? TM: We’ve always made beautiful music together. That’s my family, and we get each other’s voices. They get my voice, and they know exactly how to put me in a position to win. I love the things they have me saying. All of them are pure masterminds … It’s a labour of love. We’ve been proven to do great work together. Loading



This show does feel like a blast from the past. It has been 13 years since the 30 Rock finale aired. There used to be waves of network sitcoms, but they’re much rarer these days. Did it feel like you were filling a gap in the market by making Reggie Dinkins? I felt that immediately. When we first started this project, I just wanted to do good old-fashioned TV, and have everyone put something out there that everyone in the household can just watch together – put the phones down, let’s just watch some good old-fashioned TV like we used to. The cast of 30 Rock (from left): Tina Fey, Jack McBrayer, Jane Krakowski, Alec Baldwin and Tracy Morgan. But the industry’s obviously changed a lot since 30 Rock aired. Did you notice any differences between making a sitcom today versus making one in the 2000s? I didn’t look at it like that. I didn’t see any difference. I said, ‘Let’s do the same formula, but let’s just update it’. And look what we’ve done. Nothing’s changed. You still like this? You like Reggie Dinkins just like you like 30 Rock? [Reporter nods, and Morgan relaxes into his seat, satisfied] There you go … It’s humanity. Nothing’s changed. ‘Tracy Jordan took me to the moon. Reggie Dinkins is going to take me to Mars.’ Tracy Morgan So many people know you as the hilariously out-of-touch Tracy Jordan from 30 Rock. What impact would you say that role has had on your career?



Tracy Jordan took me to the moon. Reggie Dinkins is going to take me to Mars. People used to refer to me as Tracy Jordan, now they’re referring to me as Reggie Dinkins. He’s a pretty funny guy. The thing that’s good about that is it’s the same sense of humour. So, you feel like Tracy Jordan sent you on a trajectory that inevitably led you to Reggie? Yes, you only get one sense of humour. You only laugh at one thing, you only laugh at one kind of funny. You don’t laugh at a million funnies. Everything ain’t funny to you, but this happens to be funny to you … Reggie Dinkins, Tracy Jordan: same one sense of humour. Before Reggie Dinkins there was 30 Rock’s Tracy Jordan (right). NBC It feels like everything Tina Fey touches turns to gold. What is it about her comedy that has managed to remain so relevant over time? She’s a very smart lady. When it comes to showbusiness, she has the Midas touch. Everybody doesn’t have the Midas touch. She has found her Nirvana. You have to find your Nirvana. Do you understand what I’m saying? Like find your peace?



Imagine. I can’t stand when somebody with no abracadabra is trying to tell me what to do with my magic. You ain’t got no abracadabra, and you’re trying to tell me what to do with my magic? I ain’t never seen you pull a bunny out no hat. [Tina’s] constantly pulling bunnies out of a hat. Magic. It’s all magic. Daniel Radcliffe, Erika Alexander and Tracy Morgan in The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins. Scott Gries/NBC You’re obviously no stranger to sitcoms, having been part of 30 Rock, The Last O.G. and so on. What drew you to the mockumentary style this time around? I just love looking down the barrel [of the camera]. I think that’s hilarious, when we’re directly in your home. And all of us know when to do it and how to do it. It makes it funnier because you [the audience] become a part of the show. One of the greatest parts of Reggie Dinkins is the dynamic between you and Daniel Radcliffe. Your characters are so different, yet they have such great chemistry. That comes from Robert [Carlock] and Tina [Fey], along their travels meeting people, and going, “hmm, how could we put this guy from the UK with this street guy from Brooklyn and make that funny?” And they did. Daniel Radcliffe and Tracy Morgan become unexpected friends in The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins. NBC



What was it like building that dynamic with Radcliffe? Chemistry, it’s all chemistry. We’re not a team; we are family. The day before we started shooting, we had dinner at my house, so everybody could hit the ground running, and everybody could be comfortable with each other. And that’s how it turned out. By the time they turned the cameras on, we were already comfortable with each other. We were already having fun. What’s your favourite thing about him? Everything. He’s the sweetest person. He’s very generous, he’s kind, he’s helpful, and he’s always right there. We can’t wait to get back to work [together] now. This season is going to be hilarious for you … The thing about Reggie Dinkins is it gets funnier and funnier. Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in August I can see how much you love this show and everyone in it. It was like that with 30 Rock. We learnt so much from Tina Fey. Everybody did their job. We’re a family.

World.title: Psychiatrists cast doubt on court secrecy orders that protect accused
World.content:
NationalJustice Psychiatrists cast doubt on court secrecy orders that protect accused Wendy Tuohy and Erin Pearson August 6, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is no way to reliably predict the risk to the mental health of accused people from media reporting of their cases, senior psychiatrists say, as community disquiet about “psychological safety”-based secrecy orders grows. The psychiatrists say mental health clinicians cannot forecast potential behaviour, including self-harm or suicide, and that the reports relied upon by judges when considering suppression applications are inexact at best. Last December The Age obtained a document circulating among barristers that offers advice on how to get suppression orders and what to ask psychiatrists to include. Michael Howard/Jessica Shapiro Specialists including Melbourne University Professor Steve Ellen say it is virtually impossible to discern between the impact of the general stress of appearing in court as an accused and the stress of publication as part of Australia’s open justice system. “Predicting suicide is incredibly hard, it is an extremely rare event [per capita] and the list of risk factors is long; the ability to quantify the risk of suppression over disclosure, versus all the other risks, is minimal,” Ellen said. “It is not even close to an exact science.”



Ellen, the former head of general hospital and emergency psychiatry at The Alfred hospital, said that while psychiatrists may reasonably conclude a person is vulnerable, “it is far harder to say that naming them, rather than the prosecution itself, is the decisive additional factor”. Related Article Courts Melbourne businessman found guilty of rape, but his name remains a secret “We are relying on a very uncertain art to inform the courts, and this uncertain art is being used to undermine one of the key principles of justice.” The comments come as the identities of alleged perpetrators in several prominent rape or sexual assault cases have successfully argued for suppression of their identities for significant periods. Tom Silvagni, son of football great Stephen Silvagni, had rape proceedings suppressed for 18 months before he was was found guilty of two counts in late 2025 – after which the gag order was lifted.



The name of Ralph Carr, a celebrity agent found guilty of rape on July 28, was suppressed for more than three years to protect his pyschological safety. He was found to have raped a 27-year-old woman who wanted to work for him and the suppression order was lifted on Monday. Loading The identity of a Melbourne doctor accused of filming women and children naked in showers at the Harold Holt Swim Centre in Glen Iris was suppressed for three months after he argued that publication would harm the mental health of his child. Ellen said “at least two-thirds of defendants would have some mental health issues caused by the court experience”, but this did not mean they should win a suppression order. He first raised his concerns in a Substack post in March, when Monash University research revealed that 521 court suppression orders had been granted in Victoria in 2023.



A senior psychiatrist, who cannot be named because of the office he holds, also questioned psychiatry’s ability to reliably predict any added impact for defendants from being named, or any behavioural flow-ons. Related Article Courts Doctor charged with filming naked pool patrons wins three-month secrecy order “Most of medical science is not an exact science, and psychiatry is the least exact science when it comes to [predicting outcomes],” he said. “Almost 100 per cent of well settled people with no mental health issues when they commit a crime could go to court and say, ‘this is stressful, and my information should be suppressed’,” he said. This was not a basis for suppression, he said, “because everybody gets stressed going to court. Even when I go to court as an expert witness, I get stressed.”



Related Article Exclusive

Press freedom Court secrecy rules to be reviewed over suppression order complaints The expert said suppressing names of sex offenders puts community members at potential risk. Melbourne University Law School Associate Professor Jason Bosland said it is difficult to challenge psychological opinions in court because of the nature of the expertise. “It is very difficult for anyone to challenge the evidence of a psychologist or a psychiatrist,” he said. “You can cross-examine them but to challenge their expert opinion and really convince the judge the psychiatrist is wrong is a really difficult thing to do. “The scales aren’t evenly balanced in terms of the way these cases play out from an evidence perspective,” he said. He agreed with Ellen that such experts were effectively providing evidence “beyond the scope of the discipline”.



“Projecting into the future as to how a person will react is … not really the purpose of psychiatry,” Bosland said. The fact “the same person is doing [the psychiatric reports] again and again” should raise alarm bells, he added. Bosland and the two psychiatrists said the appearance of special treatment was created by mental health-based suppression orders being sought and granted to well-connected clients with the means to pay for them and specialised legal counsel. Former Supreme Court Judge Betty King has come out against mental health-based court suppressions. Vince Caligiuri Bosland said it erodes the public’s faith in the justice system when a convicted rapist cannot be named, “and it creates a perception that certain people are receiving favourable treatment; that is really corrosive, and I think the courts should be concerned about that”. Last December, The Age revealed a document circulating among barristers describing how to keep high-profile clients out of the spotlight, including what to ask psychiatrists to include in reports.



Related Article Justice ‘It’s wrong’: Former judge says mental health suppression orders threaten court system Criminologist and Australian Research Council Future Fellow Professor Marie Segrave said there was a privileging of the defendant’s psychological safety over that of the victim-survivor in cases where the perpetrator’s identity was protected. She said doing so, sometimes even after conviction,“raises a lot of concerns around how the justice system is operating and also creates significant concern around justice for victim-survivors.” “This idea that people are protected who have harmed them, and been found guilty of harming them, is likely also producing significant harm, and we need to investigate this further,” Segrave said. Swinburne University law lecturer and chief executive of the Rape and Sexual Assault Research and Advocacy group, Dr Rachael Burgin, pointed out that accused rapists could ask for their names to be suppressed and then also, through defence lawyers, subpoena victims’ counselling notes.



She said the privacy imbalance amounts to “systems abuse” of victims. “In the context where victim-survivors’ counselling records are essentially public property in sex offence matters, we’re doing a lot to protect the perpetrators’ mental health, but not a lot to protect the mental health of the victim-survivor,” she said. “This isn’t justice.” Barrister Greg Barns, SC, spokesperson for the Australian Lawyers Alliance, said suppression orders more broadly were often necessary to secure a fair trial, and while there was a view that some gag orders were handed out like confetti, the reality is most cases are not subject to secrecy orders. “The reality also is that suppression orders are inevitable in a society where the media is now so all-pervasive, including highly unregulated social media,” Barns said. “It’s become unfashionable to support an accused, but they have a right to fair trial.



“Like a lot of things in our legal system, it’s a question of balance. “Whilst some people may have a concern that it seems that high-profile defendants appear to get suppression orders when others might not, the reality is that if you are high profile the chances of you being subjected to some form of harassment [are] heightened.” Barns said the media plays a crucial role in the criminal justice system, but with that role comes responsibility. But Kate Wright, chair of Sexual Assault Services Victoria, said it was already rare to get sexual assault cases to court, and a strong deterrent was the spotlight in trials on victims’ behaviour – with little concern for their mental health. Adding protection of the alleged perpetrator’s identity, based on the risk to mental health of being tried, was “incredibly off-putting for anyone considering reporting sexual assault.”



“Survivors’ mental health concerns are not given the same credence or consideration, that’s what we’re seeing,” she said. “It is really reinforcing the messages to the community around shame and blame of victim-survivors, and that we are prioritising the perpetrator above the victim-survivor. They are the last consideration when they should be the first.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: TV’s best spy drama is completely flying under the radar
World.content:
Michael Fassbender as Martian in The Agency, a spy show that gently forces us to consider America’s waning global influence.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

No one in the world loves spy dramas more than my father-in-law, a man who will only commit hours of his life to a show if someone is getting double-crossed, preferably while travelling on a fake passport to a far-flung corner of the globe. He doesn’t discriminate. Any series will do. Homeland, Slow Horses, The Americans, The Night Manager, Day of the Jackal – you name it, he’s seen it. So imagine my surprise when I asked for his thoughts on The Agency – perhaps the best spy drama on TV, which is now in its second season – and was met with nothing but a confused look. Related Article ★★★★★

Streaming Binge all six seasons of this remarkable drama while you can I peppered him with prompts: “The Agency? Michael Fassbender? A CIA agent in London? The spy show that gently forces us to consider America’s waning global influence while hinting we might be on the brink of a new world order?” He assured me he had not seen the show but would add it to the list. Sadly, this was not an isolated incident. The Agency is so successfully undercover that very few people are across it (either that, or no one pays for Paramount+). But I refuse to live in a world where The Agency flies under the radar. So, like any self-respecting CIA agent, my mission is to recruit as many assets as possible. First it was my father-in-law, and now it’s your turn. Loading What is The Agency about?



At its core, the series operates inside the paranoid, fluorescent-lit pressure cooker of London Station, the CIA’s primary European hub. Fassbender plays Brandon Colby, codename “Martian”, a senior covert operative abruptly recalled to London after six years living a double life in Ethiopia, leaving behind his married lover, Sudanese anthropologist Samia Zahir (Jodie Turner-Smith). Editor's pick Streaming On Ted Lasso, she’s ruthless. Off camera, she’s ‘quite a goofy nugget’ Promoted to deputy director of operations, Martian must navigate the psychological bends of re-entering civilian life, reconnecting with his estranged daughter and shedding his cover identity. This delicate balance unravels spectacularly when Samia, Martian’s only weak spot, turns up in London. Before long, the usually protocol-obsessed CIA agent is breaking the rules to keep the relationship alive. Beyond Martian’s personal tailspin, the walls of London Station house a network of operatives whose entire existences are defined by transactional relationships. Richard Gere brings significant heft to station chief Bosko, the man responsible for keeping the White House happy, which usually involves making sure no one dies and the mission comes in under budget (yes, even the CIA is cost-cutting). Meanwhile, Henry Ogletree (Jeffrey Wright) serves as the counter-intelligence chief and Martian’s direct boss. A lifelong agent, Ogletree is understandably suspicious of everyone and everything, all of the time. But The Agency comes into its own when dealing with the junior agents, like Danny (Saura Lightfoot-Leon), an academic recruited by Martian. Jodie Turner-Smith as Samia Zahir, Martian’s married lover, in The Agency. In many ways, Danny is an audience surrogate, curious about the CIA but naive to its inner workings. Together, the pair present as a classic case of before and after. Danny is the wide-eyed recruit convinced she can change the world, and Martian knows from brutal experience that the work only ever changes the person doing it. And rarely for the better. “People are fascinated by the kind of people that go into this line of work and what kind of people come out of it at the end,” Fassbender recently told the BBC. “Martian was once idealistic and full of hope, then his moral compass gets eroded by the things he has to do and the sacrifices that go into it.”



Editor's pick Analysis

Streaming Netflix is pumping out true-crime rubbish. It’s up to you to stop it How is this different from any other spy show? Sorry Ethan Hunt, James Bond and all the other male spies with similar-sounding names: The Agency is not a world of Aston Martins, vodka martinis and high-speed chases. Instead, the series frames contemporary espionage as a chess match fought across multiple fronts simultaneously, from African resource diplomacy to Eastern European proxy networks. Written by brothers Jez and John Butterworth (who also penned the criminally underrated 2010 political drama Fair Game), The Agency is unafraid of borrowing plot lines from the current news cycle. In season one, a CIA asset goes missing in Russian-occupied Ukraine, requiring high-level negotiations to spare his life. In season two, Danny goes undercover in Tehran to target Iranian nuclear facilities because the US government is obsessively monitoring uranium enrichment operations tied to the Fordow plant. Sound familiar? Richard Gere as Bosko, Ambreen Razia as Blair, Dominic West as the unnamed CIA Director and Jeffrey Wright as Henry in The Agency. And much like the modern geopolitical landscape, the minute one crisis is averted, another appears in its place. Much of the action takes place in situation rooms and intelligence briefings, which admittedly sounds low-energy but really isn’t.



Take it from me: watching Fassbender’s Martian unpack the importance of diplomatic plausible deniability is just as exciting as Daniel Craig emerging from the sea in Speedos. Editor's pick Review What to stream this week: A five-star post-Epstein thriller, plus five more picks French provenance, American confidence If you’ve ever watched Antiques Roadshow, you’ll know that the most valuable cultural artefacts often have a French provenance, and so it is with The Agency. The American series is a remake of Eric Rochant’s Le Bureau des Légendes (The Bureau) – available on SBS On Demand and well worth the watch – often cited as the gold standard of the genre. And when I say remake, I mean remake in the truest sense: the first season of The Agency is almost beat-for-beat the same as The Bureau. This would usually be a cause for concern, but given The Bureau boasts a 96 per cent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, the “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” approach makes sense. Richard Gere as Bosko in The Agency. Rather than coming across as a cheap Hollywood knock-off, The Agency has pulled off a rare balancing act, maintaining the original’s French sensibilities while ramping up the production values. Alex Berger, a producer of The Bureau, says the US series “respected what we did originally” while upping “the scope, the scale and the ambition”. “We did the first season for €15 million ($24.6 million) in 2013, and the first season of The Agency is over 10 times that,” he told Variety. Money well spent, I reckon.

World.title: City Rail Link opening date officially revealed - but billboards got in first
World.content:
City Rail Link - a project that has been discussed in one way or another for 100 years - is finally opening.

The CRL is New Zealand's largest transportation infrastructure project, and construction has been going on for the past 10 years.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop and Auckland mayor Wayne Brown made the formal announcement of its opening date of 13 September at one of the new stations - Karanga-a-Hape Station - on Thursday morning.

But that wasn't before billboards announcing the opening date of the $5.5 billion project were put up in error around the CBD in the early morning hours.

An AT spokesperson told RNZ they were put up in error and only supposed to be displayed the official announcement.

"It was a mistake by the billboard provider," they said.

At the announcement, Bishop said he was "thrilled" to announce the opening date, marking a turning point for Auckland.

In just five and a half weeks' time, Bishop said trains would be running all the way through the middle of the city, creating faster journeys and seeing more frequent trains.

People won't have to worry about missing the train because another would be arriving just a few minutes later.

Bishop said the project had been talked about since the 1920s and he was proud to be the minister who got to deliver it.

He said it had not been easy.

Wayne Brown and Chris Bishop at the announcement. LUCY XIA / RNZ

Aucklanders have had to live with the project for a decade, disrupting local businesses and closing roads, meaning communities experiences hardships.

But Bishop said once people jump on the first train, they would realise it's all been worth it.

At the announcement, Brown said "finally, we did something ahead of time".

"We announced it this morning, accidentally."

Brown said the project would change the way Auckanders travel and make a better, faster and cheaper way for people to get around.

He said he had strong feelings on how much the project had cost but it was an investment that would ultimately get Auckland moving.

Auckland's City Rail Link opens on 13 September. RNZ / Irra Lee

Auckland Transport chief executive Stacey van der Putten said the early announcement of the opening date was disappointing.

"Things happen, it's a bummer", she said.

Van der Putten said it was a "content loading issue" with the advertising supplier and the issue had been raised.

She said mistakes happen and while it happened on the actual day of the announcement, "it's a bummer".

Bishop said, "at the end of the day, who cares?"

He joked that he hoped AT would get some "cost savings on future ".

CRL open days

Auckland Transport, City Rail Link Limited and KiwiRail will be opening the new stations to the public through a series of 'First Look' events. These will be free, ticketed sessions, but numbers will be limited.

They will be held over consecutive Saturdays in August: 8 August - First Look at Maungawhau, 15 August - First Look at Karanga-a-Hape, 22 August - First Look at Te Waihorotiu.

The free tickets for these will be available one week ahead of each event.

World.title: Cabinet blocked minister's plan to scrap Pacific seasonal worker cap, documents show
World.content:
Immigration Minister Erica Stanford wanted to scrap annual limits on Pacific migrant workers under the Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme, but apparently could not get the sign-off from Cabinet.

Stanford made her case in a meeting last month, according to papers released on Wednesday, proposing it would reduce administration costs for RSE employers, while increasing remittances sent back to the Pacific.

Stanford recently announced a swathe of technical changes to the RSE scheme, such as allowing workers to apply for migrant exploitation protection visas, and extending how long an employer could stay in the scheme if they treated their staff properly.

Her office told RNZ Pacific it was considered, but ultimately put aside ahead of the announcement. A decision on the proposal was absent from the decision minutes, suggesting it never got past the committee stage.

Stanford's office argued that a limitless scheme would foster a "manageable" increase in workers, though it noted it could further crowd out New Zealand workers - a common criticism of the seasonal worker schemes.

"On balance, I consider this risk low and able to be mitigated," the proposal read.

"Officials will monitor RSE volumes and proportions of the overall workforce and I expect regular reporting on volumes will help identify if there is a need to resume using the cap."

A disdain for the cap from the horticulture industry was flagged, in that the process of allocating how many workers an employer could hire was unfair and complex.

RNZ / Nick Monro

Mixed views

It was noted Pacific partners had mixed views on the proposal, but that no partners expressed "strong concerns" about removing it.

Meanwhile, employers regard the number of beds they can provide as their own effective cap, the paper argued.

It suggested employers were generally prioritising New Zealand workers - who still make up three-quarters of the horticulture workforce, thus explaining why the number of RSE workers coming to New Zealand is typically a few thousand fewer than the cap itself.

"Worker volumes have plateaued since 2022 despite cap increases," it noted.

"Since the cap was first met in 2013, it has consistently been increased in response to demand, suggesting it has rarely been an effective or enduring mechanism for limiting RSE volumes."

Increasing the cap from 19,500 to 20,750 workers for the 2024/25 season featured in the National-ACT coalition agreement when the current term of government began. That level remains today.

At the last general election in 2023, the ACT Party campaigned on scrapping limits, while Stanford's National party campaigned on a smaller increase.

ACT celebrated the RSE changes in a press release from its Agriculture spokesperson, Andrew Hoggard, last week.

"Fruit doesn't wait around for forms to be processed. When it's ready to pick, growers need workers in the orchard," he said.

World.title: New Caledonia's new president unveils cabinet portfolios
World.content:
The president of New Caledonia's government unveiled of his "collegial" cabinet ministers on Wednesday, with the announcement of how the portfolios are now distributed among the 11-member team.

President Milakulo Tukumuli, 42, announced his cabinet line-up at a news conference, following his election by the French Pacific territory's Congress on 31 July.

Tukumuli said his main priority was to address major issues facing New Caledonia, including pressing economic ones, such as the dire situation faced by domestic transport airline Air Calédonie.

Apart from the president's traditional civil security and external relations portfolios, has now taken over the sensitive health, social protection regimes and transport portfolios. He will also be his government's spokesperson.

New Caledonia government's cabinet ministers. Supplied / Gouvernement de la Nouvelle-Calédonie

No more portfolio redundancies

Other sensitive portfolios have also been assigned to pro-France cabinet members, such as Christopher Gygès (who is also the vice-president and retains economy-related key attributions, including economy, tax and telecommunications).

Gygès will also be in charge of customs, "economic attractiveness", external trade and "food sovereignty".

New Caledonia’s government minister Christopher Gygès holds a press conference on 13 June 2024. Government of New Caledonia

Milakuli's predecessor, Alcide Ponga, is now in charge of nickel mining-related and energy matters, a sector severely affected by a profound crisis for the past four years with two of the three smelters currently mothballed while a process is underway to identify potential buyers.

Pro-France Nina Julié becomes minister for education, youth and sports and childhood protection.

Laurent Bonnefond takes charge of urbanism and land-use planning, a topic also related to New Caledonia's reconstruction process after the destructive riots and civil unrest that caused over €2.2 billion in material damage, as well as 14 dead and a drop of an estimated 13.5 percent of the French territory's Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

Philippe Blaise also joins New Caledonia's 19th cabinet to take care of the budget, finance and the public service.

In the same collegial government, some members are also representing the pro-independence camp.

These are veteran politician Gilbert Tyuienon (from Union Calédonienne -UC- party), who has been tasked to attend to labour, employment vocational training and social dialogue matters.

From the same camp, newcomer Johanito Wamytan is now in charge of a revamped fisheries, ocean and the Coral Sea natural park, as well as research and climate issues.

Ernest Déméné is now the new minister for culture, equality and citizenship matters.

Méryl Marlier is the new minister for social economy, solidarity and water policies.

Méryl Marlier is the new minister for social economy, solidarity and water policies. Supplied / Gouvernement de la Nouvelle-Calédonie

The only representative of the other pro-independence party, UNI (Union pour l'Indépendance), has been handed over the portfolio of custom, traditional affairs, as well as indigenous Kanak cultural heritage. He is also in charge of relations with the Customary Senate, New Caledonia's version of a Great Council of Chiefs.

Keywords: efficiency, reforms

The main aim of the cabinet's portfolios organisation was now to "be efficient to redress New Caledonia" and "avoid never-ending portfolio redundancies".

Some terms such as "tourism" and "agriculture" have therefore disappeared from the list of portfolios.

Tukumuli said this was for the sake of "coherence" and cost-effectiveness, and these matters would be directly addressed and dealt with by New Caledonia's three provinces, under their respective jurisdictions.

Get the country back on its feet

"[New Caledonia] is in a quasi bankruptcy situation. We need about 13 billion French Pacific Francs (US$125 million) before the end of this month and we don't have that kind of money right now", he told local reporters, alluding to a potential "shut down" situation.

Tukumuli is due to pronounce his general policy maiden speech before New Caledonia's Congress at a yet unspecified date in the coming days.

The May 2024 and civil unrest caused over €2.2 billion in material damage to the French Pacific territory's economy. AP / Nicolas Job

Planned visit to Paris

Tukumuli is also planning to lead a bipartisan delegation in Paris later this month, in order to seek fresh deals and support from France, especially on the immediate financial support side.

One of the mooted options would be to request that some of the loans contracted be turned into non-refundable grants.

Since the May 2024 destructive unrest, France has also launched a series of financial packages, some by way of loans, others by grants, to help New Caledonia recovers from one of its gravest economic and social crises in its recent history.

"After Covid, we borrowed 50 billion French Pacific Francs, (CFP, around US$486m), then another 140 billion CFP (US$1.3b) after the May 2024 riots, so we have a debt of about 190b CFP. So it's this debt that we have to get cancelled," Tukumuli said.

Air Calédonie is targeted by blockades on its domestic outer island airports, due to a protest movement launched early March 2026. RNZ Pacific/Walter Zweifel

Domestic air transport crisis

Meanwhile, specifically on domestic air transport, which is on the verge of collapse, he is due to fly to the Loyalty Islands on Thursday to resume talks with protesters and other stakeholders.

"I think we have to take a bit of perspective, to see the bigger picture," he said, suggesting not only the air transport issue, but the whole transport sector should be considered as a whole "mobility framework".

Air Calédonie is targeted by blockades on its domestic outer island airports, due to a protest movement launched early March 2026 by a collective of customers who are protesting against the decision to transfer all domestic operations from the small airport of Magenta, in Nouméa, to the international airport of La Tontouta, over 50 kilometres away from the capital.

The measures was perceived as necessary to mutualise costs with Air Calédonie's international branch, Air Calédonie International (or AirCalin), operating from its base of La Tontouta airport.

The blockades initially affected flights from Nouméa to all airports on the three Loyalty Islands (Maré, Lifou and Ouvéa), as well as on the Isle of Pines (off the capital Nouméa).

Since March, traffic has been allowed to resume Lifou and the Isle of Pines.

On Monday and Tuesday this week, on Ouvéa and Maré Islands, marches were organised by islanders who voiced their anger against the remaining airport blockades that have been ongoing since 2 March.

Placards were brandished, denouncing the fact that passengers were "taken hostage" by the blockades, which severely affects not only passengers, but also freight as well as education or medical emergencies to and from the main island of Grande Terre.

Tourism sector companies are also severely affected.

"This is untenable ... Ouvéa is a dead island, it's agonising," Ouvéa Mayor Maurice Tillewa told local media, invoking the basic notion of freedom of movement.

But Air Calédonie has also filed for bankruptcy and placed the company under judicial supervision from a Trade Tribunal, which is now tasked to review the company's situation every six months to decide whether it is allowed to continue operations or be liquidated.

This bi-yearly ruling will also depend on the company's performance and sustainability.

"The airstrips on Ouvéa and Maré need to re-open to allow (Air Calédonie) to stay alive", Tukumuli said.

"It is in great difficulty because it once transported about 300,000 passengers per year and now, after the (May 2024) riots, it's gone down to 180,000 and the figure for this year look like 120,000.

World.title: New primary industry ventures revealed for foreign investors in New Zealand
World.content:
Overseas investment into primary industries like forestry and farming continues to play a part in the New Zealand economy.

The investment is part of tens of billions of dollars of foreign capital that entered the economy last year, according to the Overseas Investment Office.

Among the overseas investors snapping up forests was furniture giant Ikea's investor, while a Bay of Plenty mixed farm was bought by a Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints subsidiary.

Details of the purchases are included in the latest applications approved by Land Information New Zealand/Toitū te Whenua's Overseas Investment Office (OIO) in June.

Ikea's Ingka Investments Forest Assets of the Netherlands has bought the 350-hectare Taringatura Forest in Southland, adding to its 43,000 hectare forest portfolio in Aotearoa - for more production forestry, from local parties Benmore Two and Benmore Two Forest Partnership.

"The Applicants will acquire the land, and hold a forestry right over the land, respectively," said the OIO decision, that noted consent was granted as the national interest test was met.

"[They] intend to continue using the land for forestry purposes."

Sustainable Forestry, owned by German insurer and financier HDI Haftpflichtverband der Deutschen Industrie V.a.G. will also acquire the 893-hectare Mangapapa Forest at Tangarakau near Stratford from local firm, New Street Capital.

The land will continue to be used for forestry, the OIO said.

Another, majority Japanese-owned company ANZCO Foods has bought a property neighbouring its Eltham beef plant in Taranaki for staff accommodation.

The country's largest gold producer, mostly North American-owned Oceana Gold, has acquired freehold interest in sensitive land for its open pit and underground gold mine.

The location has been withheld under the Official Information Act, but it was likely either its Waihi or Macraes sites.

Late last month, RNZ reported that Farmland Reserve, owned by the Mormon Church, had bought its second kiwifruit orchard in Bay of Plenty.

This one was also a large dairy farm named Koromiko Dairies near Pukehina that would be run by Craigmore Sustainables, as was its first orchard purchase in New Zealand, and would undergo a roughly $32 million redevelopment. Grazing livestock may continue on the site, a Craigmore spokesperson said.

Between 2025/26, Land Information said more than $24 billion in transactions came through its OIO.

Logging and forestry sectors dominated consent application numbers, followed by accommodation then electricity supply.

Though they excluded consents for homes foreign investors would live in.

World.title: Nine new secondary school subjects announced by government
World.content:
The government has announced nine new secondary school subjects that will be developed by industry groups.

They include tourism, construction and built environment, and energy and infrastructure.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said the subjects would be available for students in Years 12-13 from 2029 when they would form part of a new qualification replacing the NCEA.

The full list of subjects were:

Next-gen manufacturing

Applied intelligent systems

Construction and built environment

Energy and infrastructure

Engineering technology

Food and fibre systems

Health services and care

Hospitality food and beverage

Tourism

"These subjects are being developed with industry to give students an exciting range of options, so businesses know young people are building the skills their sectors need, and students can gain knowledge that sets them up for work, trades, training or university," Stanford said.

The subjects would be developed by Industry Skills Boards, which were originally set up to oversee tertiary qualifications and apprenticeships for specific industries.

Energy and Infrastructure Industry Skills Board chief executive Philip Aldridge said the new subjects would give industry a direct role in shaping student's pathways.

"Students make better choices when they can see where study can take them," Aldridge said in a statement.

"New Zealand's energy and infrastructure sectors will need more skilled people to deliver the services our country depends on every day. These subjects will help prepare students for careers in industries that are central to New Zealand's economic growth and productivity."

Civil Contractors New Zealand chief executive Alan Pollard said the change would help students better understand the careers available in civil construction.

World.title: Auckland's coldest day in five years as power use hits another record
World.content:
Many places in the country will be waking up to freezing weather on Thursday, with MetService warning of double-digit negative temperatures in parts of the south.

They coincided with record power use on Wednesday night.

MetService says Auckland has had its coldest temperatures in five years overnight.

Whenuapai Airport recorded -1.7C on Thursday, and Auckland Airport was 1.5C before 5am.

Metereologist Luis Fernandes said Auckland could be set for even lower temperatures on Thursday evening.

Frost in Auckland on Thursday morning. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

Aoraki Mount Cook has hit -10 this morning, with Twizel and Alexandra at -9.

People in Taumarunui woke up to a temperature of -6 - the third coldest on record.

Invercargill has also reached its coldest this year, at -5.3C early this morning.

Other parts of the North Island that saw sub-zero temperatures overnight, including Taupō and Hamilton.

In the South Island, Christchurch, Queenstown and Alexandra all recorded temperatures below -3C.

MetService meteorologist Katie Lyons said widespread frosts were forecast.

"We've got a big ridge of high pressure which is giving a lot of clear skies, and that means cold temperatures, good cooling so people will be waking up to lots of frosts around the country," she said.

Whenuapai Airport recorded -1.7C on Thursday. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

"Places like Auckland could be anywhere between -2C all the way up to 4C. The likes of Wellington it could be anywhere between 0C and 4C."

Transpower said power use on Wednesday night broke through the previous record.

Transpower's live data shows New Zealand's power grid hit 7463 megawatts last night - a new record.

Yesterday morning, the peak hit 7247 MW for the power grid manager.

It was expecting there could be another record demand for electricity on Thursday.

The power grid operator issued a notice to power companies advising there would be a potential shortfall of energy at peak times over the next couple of days.

Warnings were in place on Thursday and Friday between 7.30am and 8.30am.

Lyons said the cold snap was expected to end by the weekend.

"For most places into Friday that cold will continue," she said.

"The West Coast of the South Island will be the first to slowly see those temperatures rise into Friday, and then for the rest of the country on Saturday it will feel like more of a return to normal as we get the next frontal feature moving in from the Tasman with some northwesterly winds."

'We're absolutely ecstatic' - skifield boss

Whakapapa ski-field. Supplied/ Ruapehu Alpine Lifts

Whakapapa general manager of operations Steve "Youngman" Manunui said it was -7C at the ski-field's base area on Thursday - ideal conditions for snowmaking.

Whakapapa GM discusses Mt Ruapehu ski season Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The lingering impact of Covid-19 and financial pressures had made this a make-or-break season for Whakapapa and Turoa, he said.

It was under new ownership and was seeing the best start to the season since before the pandemic.

"We're absolutely ecstatic with the start to the winter, best start since pre-Covid actually."

The El Niño phase was delivering cooler, drier temperatures, he said.

The cycle of storms over the last three weeks had been welcome and in between there had been some fine sunny spells that had drawn large numbers of customers.

Manunui said the skifields were in an ideal location in the middle of the North Island, so they were able to attract customers from all over the North Island.

"The good thing is these weather patterns look like they're going to continue for a wee while ... we're setting ourselves up nicely for spring and traditionally we go right through to Labour weekend.

World.title: Commerce Commission takes Foodstuffs South Island to court
World.content:
The Commerce Commission says it is taking Foodstuffs South Island to court, alleging "far-reaching anti-competitive conduct that deprived customers of cheaper prices".

The competition watchdog alleged it implemented and enforced a widespread restriction on independently owned Pak'nSave stores discounting selected products.

Consumer boss discusses Foodstuffs SI Com Com court action Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Foodstuffs South Island is a co-operative, and the owner of New World, Pak'nSave and Four Square in the south.

Under the franchise model, individual South Island Pak'nSave supermarkets are supposed to be able to compete on pricing, discounts and promotions, Commerce Commission chair John Small said.

"Instead, we allege FSSI (Foodstuffs South Island) applied guidelines and rules that stopped these independently owned and operated supermarkets from offering certain discounts unless they received prior approval," he said.

The commission believed the conduct constituted resale price maintenance, which was prohibited under the Commerce Act.

It said Foodstuffs South Island centrally set a "super deal" promotion price for a product, and did not allow franchisees from discounting below the price, unless Pak'nSave obtained prior approval.

The commission said franchisees were also not allowed to discount any other product in the same category below the "super deal" promotional price.

The accusations also included that Foodstuffs South Island set an "every day low price" centrally, primarily for shelf staple goods, and did not allow Pak'nSaves from applying further discounts on these products without prior approval.

"We will argue the alleged anti-competitive conduct was widespread, with FSSI's guidelines covering all South Island Pak'nSave franchisees for a period of at least several years," Small said.

In a statement, a Foodstuffs South Island spokesperson said it took its responsibilities seriously and had engaged constructively with the Commerce Commission and would continue to do so.

"The allegations relate to specific promotional programmes and do not change Pak'nSave's focus on helping Kiwis get their groceries at New Zealand's lowest prices.

"It would be inappropriate for us to comment further at this time."

The chief executive of Consumer Jon Duffy told Morning Report the Commerce Commission's crackdown on Foodstuffs South Island was rare.

He said the allegations were serious and in lay-person's terms amounted to "price-fixing".

Duffy said Pak'nSave supermarkets across the South Island were independently-owned in a franchise model, with Foodstuffs South Island the parent company.

"The parent company is accused of requiring Pak'nSaves to set prices at a certain level and not go below those levels. So, those independent franchise owners weren't allowed to offer better discounts to their customers than any other in the group, as I understand it.

"That's kind of a form of price-fixing, but it's known as 'resale price maintenance' under the Commerce Act," Duffy said.

He said the prosecution was part of a move by the Commerce Commission sector review to enforcement.

If the commission was successful in court, Duffy said Foodstuffs South Island could face a fine of up to $10 million or 10 percent of turnover.

"They're not insignificant, however when you look at the scale of Foodstuffs South Island's business, $10m could actually be on the light side."

But, he maintained action by the Commerce Commission sent an important message.

World.title: ASB joins ANZ and BNZ in lifting interest rates
World.content:
ASB has joined ANZ and BNZ in increasing a range of its interest rates.

It is lifting its six-month home loan rate by 10 basis points to 4.79 percent, its one-year rate by 24 basis points to 4.99 percent, its 18-month rate by 26 basis points to 5.25 percent, its two-year rate by 20 basis points to 5.45 percent and its three-year rate by 16 basis points to 5.45 percent.

Some term deposit rates are increasing, too, taking the 24-month rate to 4.2 percent and the 18-month rate to 4.15 percent.

"We're continuing to see volatility in wholesale interest rates, which have climbed over the past month. This has a direct bearing on the rates we offer on lending and deposits, in line with what is happening in markets around the world," ASB executive general manager personal banking Adam Boyd said,

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

"These changes mean we're able to support savers with stronger term deposit rates. We'd also encourage any homeowners with questions about their lending to get in touch. It's important to find the right structure for your circumstances and our team is ready to help you work through your options."

One-year swap rates have risen from about 3 percent to just under 3.4 percent over the past month, and two-year rates have lifted from about 3.3 percent to 3.6 percent.

Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said people were taking longer fixes.

"In late 2024, less than 10 percent of new loans were being fixed beyond 12 months and that number was still less than 20 percent as recently as November 2025. But it's jumped up to the mid-50 percents for the past five months (with the two-year rate very popular), as borrowers look to protect against any further interest rate increases in a world of higher inflation and heightened uncertainty. The shift longer will generally be applying to people re-fixing existing mortgages as they roll over too."

World.title: 'Gone down like a lead balloon': Ex-FA boss on FIFA's World Cup backflip
World.content:
"It's gone down like a lead balloon."

This is David Gallop's view of FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-infamous World Cup privatisation proposal.

"It's so far off passing the pub test that I think it's like he let off a stink bomb in the middle of the pub and people ran screaming, leaving half a schooner behind," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"That's how poorly it's been received."

Mr Gallop has been one of Australia's foremost sport's administrators. He was CEO of the NRL from 2002-2012 before jumping ship to become the boss of Football Federation Australia for seven years until his tenure ended in 2019.

He has watched on this past week as Mr Infantino's failed sell-off plan has evolved into a full-blown crisis over his leadership.

"He's definitely under pressure now … to throw out an idea like this that's gone down so badly," he said.

Mr Infantino's proposal, dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise, would have seen the commercial rights of FIFA's most popular tournaments, including the World Cup, transferred to a private company, and a 20 per cent stake sold to investors, valued at $20 billion.

It's been reported Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law, was one of the private equity figures behind the plan.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump was under scrutiny at the World Cup. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

"Anytime you sell anything, you need to have good, compelling reasons, but particularly so when it comes to something like the World Cup and ... sport in general," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"You've got to know that you really need to do it. You really need the money. What are you getting for the slice of the asset and what are you giving up?

"Clearly people have not liked the idea that private investment, and therefore, a profit motive that comes away from the game to those private investors would be something that FIFA would contemplate."

'One-off sugar hit'

Mr Gallop said privatisation was not inherently wrong but required an overwhelming strategic and financial case to be valid.

"It will be a mistake to burn the furniture to heat the house," he said.

"You need to be setting up your sport and the business of your sport for sustainability, not for a one-off sugar hit of capital.

"These are the questions that have to be answered when one is looking at private sale of these effectively community assets that people feel strongly about."

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's plan to privatise has been met with derision by many football bodies. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

The proposal offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each, but Mr Gallop said FIFA's financial position only heightened questions about why such a proposal had been pursued.

"FIFA has $5 billion in cash now after the World Cup," he said.

" I think that's one of the reasons why a proposal to sell an equity stake has fallen so flat. They're not desperate for money. "

Within three days of the proposal, Mr Infantino and FIFA scrapped the plans.

Europe's UEFA, North America's CONCACAF and Asia's AFC, which Australia is member of, all opposed the plan.

UEFA, CONCACAF, as well as a growing number of national federations have taken it further by withdrawing their support of Mr Infantino's leadership.

Football Australia's chair Anter Isaac and CEO Martin Kugeler both declined an interview with 7.30.

The organisation has welcomed the decision by FIFA to scrap the privatisation proposal but is yet to weigh-in on Mr Infantino's, now under siege, leadership.

Mr Gallop said Australia's influence on the world game came less through political power than integrity.

Infantino's 'blotted copybook'

The integrity of Mr Infantino, like that of his predecessor Sepp Blatter has now been called into question.

Former FIFA President Sepp Blatter's tenure ended due to corruption. (Reuters: Stefan Wermuth)

Mr Infantino was elected in 2016 promising to restore confidence in FIFA, following a number of corruption scandals that occurred under Mr Blatter's 17-year reign as president.

Mr Gallop's time at FA straddled the terms of both men. He was also CEO in 2010, when Australia's bid to host the 2022 World Cup was beaten by Qatar, a decision that was mired in controversy and allegations of corruption.

"There was a bit of a stench around FIFA and Gianni came in with a pitch of transparency, accountability, consultation and putting football first," Mr Gallop said.

" I think it's fair to say this proposal, albeit backflipped on, has blotted his copybook in respect to what people expected from him and from his presidency. "

"[Especially} coming hot off the heels of a number of other contentious decisions, including the lifting of the red card on the USA player during the tournament."

United States' Folarin Balogun's red card was rescinded during the World Cup after a call from Trump to Infantino. (AP: Jeff Chiu)

Despite calls for Mr Infantino's resignation growing louder, Mr Gallop said his tenure at the top of world football might not be over just yet.

"I don't think it's necessarily so that he won't get re-elected. He has some big confederations against him at the moment, but he has others where FIFA has carefully funded development in a lot of smaller nations," he said.

Mr Gallop remembers representing Australia at FIFA congresses, sitting next to the small Caribbean nation of Aruba — "a population of a hundred thousand people."

"Behind us would be Brazil … millions of people, an absolute icon of world football … but everyone gets one vote; that's where your confederation structure comes into play," he said.

Mr Gallop believes the president's political future will depend on whether member associations believe the successes achieved under his leadership outweigh the damage caused by the failed privatisation proposal.

" Whether there's enough credit in the bank for all the good things that FIFA have produced … or whether this has blown them up will remain to be seen. "

Fan outrage

Patrick Clancy, head of the Football Supporters Association in Australia, told 7.30 many fans felt betrayed by the proposal.

Football's governing body has long been at the centre of controversy and corruption allegations. (REUTERS: Arnd Wiegmann )

"He's tried to privatise football at the expense of the game of football," he said.

"It's something that came out of nowhere and is not in line with what anyone has thought of before. And so I think that's the concern; where's it all going?"

His organisation is now very keen to understand where Football Australia stands on Mr Infantino and his leadership.

"These are very troubling times in world football and Football Australia needs to make its position very clear," he said.

Mr Clancy says football supporters want to see the game run properly.

"They want to feel that there is a degree of integrity and they don't want a money-hungry organisation that seems to be interfering with that organic nature of the game," he said.

"Within 24 hours, Infantino and FIFA completely changed the shape of world football.

" They blindsided almost everyone in the game, so goodness knows what's going to happen in the next seven days. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Australia's coach says no tour match ahead of India Test series
World.content:
Australia will again opt for a training camp ahead of the five-Test tour of India rather than play ​a traditional warm-up match before attempting to end a 22-year wait for a Test series victory on the subcontinent.

Australia also chose not to play a tour match before ​the 2023 series, ‌instead training on specially prepared, spin-friendly pitches in Bengaluru before the opening Test.

The decision drew scrutiny after India won the Nagpur opener by an innings ‌and 132 runs, setting the tone for a 2-1 series ⁠victory that allowed the hosts to retain the Border-Gavaskar ‌Trophy.

Ifs, buts and maybes for Australia in India The record books will show that Australia left India without the Border-Gavaskar Trophy, but the series defeat offers plenty of opportunity for introspection ahead of the Ashes.

Head coach Andrew McDonald ​said Australia would scout ‌a location to immerse themselves in conditions similar to India before the series opener in Nagpur starting on January 21.

"We've got a couple of options there," he told Cricket Australia website Cricket.com.au ​on ‌Wednesday.

"We have gone to the UAE previously and we have also gone into India last time into Bengaluru, so we're ⁠just working through what that ‌would look like in terms ‌of how we then manage the individuals."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Australia has not won a Test ‌series in India since 2004 when Adam Gilchrist's side triumphed 2-1.

Australia have a gruelling schedule before they ‌arrive in ​India, with a ⁠two-Test home series starting against Bangladesh in Darwin next week followed by a three-Test tour of South Africa in October and another four-Test home series against New Zealand from December ⁠9.

Fast bowler Michael Neser has been ruled out of the Bengaluru series with a ‌calf strain suffered ‌at training in Brisbane but McDonald said wicketkeeper-batter ​Josh Inglis was expected to be available after recovering from a back spasm.

Reuters

World.title: Tony Modra medical record probe expands to extra staffer
World.content:
Another staff member is being investigated for allegedly inappropriately accessing the private medical records of AFL legend Tony Modra, SA Health has confirmed.

Modra was seriously injured in a truck crash at Back Valley, near Victor Harbor on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula, in June, and later underwent facial surgery.

Last month, SA Health said three staff were being investigated for allegedly inappropriately accessing the private medical records of the former Crow, while a further five employees were also being "assessed" to determine whether their access was "always appropriate".

In a statement, SA Health today said the investigation was ongoing.

Police were called to the scene of the truck crash, near Victor Harbor. (Supplied: SA Police)

"One additional SA Health staff member is under investigation for potential inappropriate access of a patient record, following an audit that identified eight staff members who remain under investigation," the statement said.

"In total, nine staff members are part of the current investigation, which is ongoing."

The alleged breaches are not the first time that concerns have been raised about SA Health staff inappropriately accessing patient records in cases involving high-profile individuals.

In 2016, 13 hospital staff were sanctioned after being caught snooping on the medical records of Cy Walsh, who was charged with the stabbing murder of his father — Crows coach Phil Walsh — before being found not guilty by reason of mental incompetence.

In 2024, ABC News revealed an SA Health investigation had found 18 staff engaged in misconduct or inappropriately accessed the medical records of a patient understood to be Charlie Stevens, the late son of SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens.

Tony Modra was injured while driving a truck at Back Valley in June. (Supplied: 9News Adelaide)

SA Health has previously apologised to Modra's family.

The department has also previously said it regularly conducted audits "to ensure that staff are accessing appropriate information".

"Any staff member who has accessed information inappropriately may be subject to disciplinary processes, which may include termination of their employment," SA Health said previously.

Last month, Modra posted an update on his progress on social media, saying he was "getting out and about" and praising the medical staff involved in his recovery.

World.title: Hawks' Wizard looking to pull off Coleman medal shock
World.content:
Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell has sung the praises of Nick Watson as the 170cm "Wizard" attempts to snare what would be one of the most unlikely and magical Coleman medals in VFL/AFL history.

Watson's five-goal haul in last week's 16-point win over North Melbourne lifted his season tally to 52 goals.

It means Watson became the first player since Syd Dyer and Lou Richards in 1946 to kick 50-plus goals in a season despite being 170cm or shorter.

Sydney's 194cm forward Charlie Curnow leads this year's Coleman medal count with 57 goals, with Gold Coast's 202cm spearhead Ben King (53 goals) in second and Watson lurking in third.

AFL round 21 Saturday live updates Josh Fraser's bid to become Carlton's next full-time coach receives a massive boost as the Blues record a thumping win over the Brisbane Lions.

Hawthorn face Brisbane at the Gabba on Friday night before rounding out their home-and-away campaign against Collingwood and West Coast.

A big finish from Watson could be enough to snare him the Coleman, and although Mitchell says the Hawks won't go out of their way to target him in the next three weeks, they would celebrate his achievement if he gets there.

"It'd be great if it happened," Mitchell said.

"But he's young and he's got plenty of opportunities in front of him.

"I certainly hope that's not the focus of the lads going into a game like this. But I won't be shying away from it if he gets that opportunity, of course."

Watson, fondly dubbed "The Wizard", is already a superstar of the competition despite being just 21 years old and 61 games into his AFL career.

"The level of consistency is probably the best thing that we've got from Wizard this year," Mitchell said.

"And it's probably one season earlier than most. He's certainly maturing. Like, he's 21 years old and he's quite popular, and how he handles that is really impressive."

Third-placed Hawthorn (14-5-1) haven't won at the Gabba since 2016, but they have only played three games at the venue since then.

Mitchell wants his team to use Friday's blockbuster against two-time defending premiers Brisbane (13-7) as an interstate finals rehearsal.

"I think if you look at the ladder most Victorian teams are going to have to win interstate at some point, and this is a start for us," said Mitchell, who earlier this week re-signed with Hawthorn until the end of 2030.

The Hawks have a number of selection queries heading into the crunch clash with Ned Reeves (knee), Karl Amon (knee), Mitch Lewis (concussion) and Henry Hustwaite (face) all under injury clouds.

Meanwhile, an American court has formally dismissed charges against Hawthorn player Connor Macdonald for his off-season misadventure.

Macdonald and teammate Dylan Moore spent a night in a US jail after being charged with trespassing for climbing onto a cherry picker.

Moore's case was wrapped up last month, while Macdonald's case has also now been concluded with the pair having previously agreed to complete a substance abuse counselling program.

"It's probably nice for them to have it off their back," Mitchell said.

"They're both having really good seasons and really pleased with their performances. Sometimes dealing with adversity can make you grow, and I think they've both done that this year."

World.title: Pay war on ice as Australia's netball stars sign truce
World.content:
A pay war has been averted — for now — after Australia's Super Netball players agreed to an updated collective player agreement for 2027.

Under the new collective player agreement (CPA), Super Netball players will receive improved pay and conditions, more time off and greater ability to sign individual sponsorship deals.

The 12-month bridging agreement to the CPA has been agreed between Netball Australia, the Super Netball clubs and the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA).

It means Super Netball clubs can start contracting players and preparing for the 2027 campaign.

Before this week's agreement went through, players had been in contract limbo.

Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026 Messy and drawn-out pay negotiations are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the Aussie Diamonds.

The protracted pay dispute also meant plans to expand Super Netball had been placed on hold until at least 2028, despite a new five-year broadcast deal with the Nine Network starting in 2027.

With the CPA now locked in for 2027, attention will turn to a longer-term deal for 2028 and beyond in coming months, with Netball Australia hoping to avoid a repeat of a drawn-out pay dispute.

The ANPA want a revenue-share model, as well as better pregnancy and parental leave policies as part of a longer-term deal.

Netball Australia interim chief executive Mark Falvo said the 12-month bridging agreement struck the right balance between delivering immediate benefits for players, while also positioning the sport for future growth.

"We are at a pivotal moment for our sport," Falvo said in a statement.

"This agreement gives our players, clubs and the league certainty while we enter a period of significant commercial opportunity for netball.

"There is more work to do on meeting some of the asks for the athletes and the clubs, but this agreement delivers meaningful outcomes for players today while demonstrating our responsibility to balance the long-term sustainability of the league."

The news of the fresh CPA comes on the back of Sports Entertainment Group (SEG), headed by Craig Hutchison, putting the final touches on their takeover of the licence of the Giants Super Netball club.

SEG already owns the Melbourne Mavericks as well as multiple basketball clubs, with the Giants set to become the latest franchise to go under their SEN Teams banner.

The flurry of netball news comes just days after the Australian Diamonds suffered a shock 46-45 semi-final loss to Jamaica at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The Diamonds were hot favourites to snare gold, but had to settle for bronze with a 80-65 win over England in the third-versus-fourth play-off match.

Although New Zealand walked away with the gold medal, their domestic competition faces an uncertain future after losing around $3.7 million in 2026.

With no broadcast deal in place, rumours are bubbling the Premiership in New Zealand could be placed on hold for 2027, or downgraded to amateur status.

It means a flurry of Kiwi players could seek out Super Netball deals for next year as they seek financial security.

New CPA deal:

Increase to the total player payment pool (minimum and maximum amounts) by greater than the Consumer Price Index (CPI)

Players to receive a one-off payment upon the signing of a commercial partner for the Super Netball league

Additional time off through condensing hours for club commitments that will free up an additional two weeks of time off per year

Option for athletes to enter into multi-year contracts

Greater ability for athletes to secure their own individual sponsorship deals

Increased health insurance and meal allowances

AAP

World.title: De Minaur wins all-Australian clash as Popyrin gets through in Montreal
World.content:
Fallen star Alexei Popyrin has dug deep for a morale-boosting victory to join Alex de Minaur in the second round of the Canadian Open in Montreal.

Two years after upstaging the great Novak Djokovic in a seismic US Open triumph, Popyrin has slumped to number 139 in the world as he battles a crisis of confidence.

But after toiling through qualifying just to make the main draw, Popyrin toiled for another two hours and 12 minutes to see off Argentine Roman Andres Burruchaga 4-6, 7-5, 6-3 to notch his first ATP-level win since May in the Masters event.

The breakthrough was only Popyrin's ninth win of a lean 2026 campaign and vaulted the one-time world number 19 into a second-round contest with US seventh seed Taylor Fritz or another Argentine, Thiago Agustin Tirante.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

De Minaur, meanwhile, looked to be cruising before fellow Sydneysider James Duckworth put the world number seven through the wringer late on.

Runner-up in 2023, de Minaur was a set and 3-1 up before Duckworth fought back hard seeking a first win over his countryman in three meetings.

But de Minaur held firm to fend off six set points and progress 6-2, 7-6 (6) and book a third-round date with either Britain's Cameron Norrie or Peru's Ignacio Buse.

"In the first set everything was flowing," de Minaur said after the one-hour, 46-minute dogfight.

"I was up a break, had a couple more chances to go up by a double break and all of a sudden it slips away.

"Then all of a sudden momentum shifts and we got into a battle. So I am glad I was able to sneak through. There are a couple of things I need to tighten up on, but we live to fight another day."

While de Minaur and Popyrin move on, fellow Australian Adam Walton crashed out with a 6-3, 6-4 loss to American Jenson Brooksby.

In the women's WTA event in Toronto, Tahlia Gibson continued her stellar 2026 season with an upset 7-5, 6-1 second-round win over Polish 18th seed Maja Chwalinska.

Gibson's 28th win of a breakout year earned her a crack at Russian 16th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova.

World.title: NRL club claims player Keith Titmuss contributed to training death
World.content:
A rugby league player who died of heat exhaustion at pre-season training contributed to his own death by not managing his weight and diet in the off-season, his former club says.

The family of Keith Titmuss, who died in November 2020 after collapsing during pre-season training, is suing the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles for damages owing from negligence in his death, including failing to implement the NRL heat policy.

In a defence filed in the NSW Supreme Court the club has claimed it was not responsible for the death of the young man because he did not inform coaching and medical staff of his worsened physical state through the off-season.

"NRL training is inherently dangerous," the club wrote in its defence.

"Any injury, loss and damage suffered by [Titmuss's family] … was caused or contributed to by the deceased's own negligence."

Former NRL player's mother speaks on lawsuit The mother of Manly player Keith Titmuss, who died of exertional heat stroke following a 2020 Sea Eagles training session, breaks her silence on her family's multi-million-dollar lawsuit against the NRL club.

Manly Warringah alleged Titmuss failed to properly train or diet during the off-season and put himself in danger by not stopping training when he felt sick.

"Players were instructed … if they were feeling ill or feeling like they were not coping with the physical demands [that] they were to inform coaching staff," the club said.

The club also filed in its defence that it conducted a fitness test on the 20-year-old four days before he died and found "no red flags".

The session at the Sydney Academy of Sport at Narrabeen involved outdoor sprint tests before moving inside for an intense cardio session.

A 100-passes drill and a cardio circuit involving up-downs/burpees, bear crawls and "fireman carries" was conducted inside the facility's dojo, the parties agree.

The temperature was about 21 degrees Celsius during the session but the humidity was 92 per cent, court documents state.

Manly Warringah admitted the dojo was not fitted with air-conditioning but said there were multiple floor-standing fans, the back doors were open and hydration breaks were enforced.

The player's family alleged the fans were not switched on during the session.

There were 10 staff to monitor the 15 players inside, the club said.

NRL player Keith Titmuss died after 'inappropriate' training session, magistrate finds A magistrate who oversaw the inquest into the death of a young Manly Sea Eagles player recommends the NRL consider mandating a two-week period of controlled training acclimatisation after off-season breaks as part of an existing review.

A 2024 coronial inquest into his death concluded the budding NRL player died of exertion heat stroke, with a pre-existing heart condition unlikely to have played a part.

The work-out at the club's Narrabeen gym, which followed an outdoor session, was "more likely than not inappropriate", the coroner found.

Evidence at the inquest was that paramedics at the scene noted Titmuss's temperature at 41.9C, while his heart rate was more than 140 beats per minute.

Titmuss's family claimed the precautions instituted by Manly Warringah were not sufficient to meet its own heat policy guidelines, alleging the club is liable for the young man's death.

"[Manly Warringah] owed a duty of care to the deceased as an employee and … breached the duty of care owed," the statement of claim said.

Titmuss's family alleged the player started to struggle physically after an outdoor sprint test three days prior, which the club denied.

The club instituted a heat policy after former prop Lloyd Perrett said he was planning to sue the club over a training session in late 2017 which left him hospitalised with heat stroke after suffering a seizure.

Manly Warringah and the NRL were contacted for comment.
